Cosmological perturbations

Karim A. Malik Address: Astronomy Unit, School of Mathematical Sciences, Queen Mary, University of London, Mile End Road, \ctyLondon E1 4NS, \cnyUnited Kingdom    David Wands Address: Institute of Cosmology and Gravitation, University of Portsmouth, \ctyPortsmouth PO1 2EG, \cnyUnited Kingdom
Abstract

We review the study of inhomogeneous perturbations about a homogeneous and isotropic background cosmology. We adopt a coordinate based approach, but give geometrical interpretations of metric perturbations in terms of the expansion, shear and curvature of constant-time hypersurfaces and the orthogonal timelike vector field. We give the gauge transformation rules for metric and matter variables at first and second order. We show how gauge invariant variables are constructed by identifying geometric or matter variables in physically-defined coordinate systems, and give the relations between many commonly used gauge-invariant variables. In particular we show how the Einstein equations or energy-momentum conservation can be used to obtain simple evolution equations at linear order, and discuss extensions to non-linear order. We present evolution equations for systems with multiple interacting fluids and scalar fields, identifying adiabatic and entropy perturbations. As an application we consider the origin of primordial curvature and isocurvature perturbations from field perturbations during inflation in the very early universe.

Keywords: 
Cosmology , Perturbation theory , Cosmological inflation

1 Introduction

The standard model of hot big bang cosmology is based upon the spatially homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) model. This successfully describes the average expansion of the universe on large scales according to Einstein’s theory of general relativity, and the evolution from a hot, dense initial state dominated by radiation to the cool, low density state dominated by non-relativistic matter and, apparently, vacuum energy at the present day. This standard model is described by just a handful of numbers specifying the expansion rate, the temperature of the present microwave background radiation, the density of visible matter, dark matter and dark vacuum energy.

But an homogeneous model cannot describe the complexity of the actual distribution of matter and energy in our observed universe where stars and galaxies form clusters and superclusters of galaxies across a wide range of scales. For this we need to be able to describe spatial inhomogeneity and anisotropy. But there are few exact solutions of general relativity that incorporate spatially inhomogeneous and anisotropic matter and hence geometry. Therefore we use a perturbative approach starting from the spatially homogeneous and isotropic FRW model as a background solution with simple properties within which we can study the increasing complexity of inhomogeneous perturbations order by order.

The introduction of a homogeneous background model to describe the inhomogeneous universe leads to an ambiguity in the choice of coordinates. In the FRW model the homogeneous three-dimensional hypersurfaces provide a natural time slicing of four-dimensional spacetime. For instance, hypersurfaces of a uniform density coincide with hypersurfaces with uniform spatial curvature. However in the real, inhomogeneous universe spatial hypersurfaces of uniform density do not in general have uniform spatial curvature, and hypersurfaces of uniform curvature do not have uniform density. In general relativity there is, a priori, no preferred choice of coordinates. Choosing a set of coordinates in the inhomogeneous universe which will then be described by an FRW model plus perturbations amounts to assigning a mapping between spacetime points in the inhomogeneous universe and the homogeneous background model. The freedom in this choice is the gauge freedom, or gauge problem, in general relativistic perturbation theory. It can lead to apparently different descriptions of the same physical solution simply due to the choice of coordinates. This freedom can be a powerful tool as it allows one to work in terms of variables best suited to the problem in hand, however it is important to work with gauge-invariant definitions of the perturbations variables if the results are to be easily assimilated and cross-referenced to the work of others.

In this review we will focus on how one can construct a variety of gauge-invariant variables to deal with perturbations in different cosmological models at first order and beyond. We will emphasise the geometrical meaning of metric and matter perturbations and their gauge-invariant definitions.

Most work to date has been done only to linear order where the perturbations obey linear field equations. Even then we must consistently solve the linear evolution equations, subject to the constraint equations of general relativity which relate the matter variables to the geometry. Beyond first order, the non-linearity of Einstein’s equations becomes evident, making progress much more difficult. But in limiting cases, notably the large scale limit, it is possible to extend some of the simple results of linear theory to higher orders.

Previous reviews on the topic of linear perturbation theory in cosmology include, for example, Refs. [66, 123, 43, 21, 141, 61], and the relevant chapters in Refs. [177, 131, 75, 84]. For second-order perturbation theory see Refs. [129, 15, 126]. For reviews on inflation in particular see, e.g., Refs. [88, 70, 86, 93, 84, 77, 17, 174] and for cosmic microwave background anisotropies see, e.g., Refs. [67, 82, 42, 51] Finally, for reviews on perturbation theory in the context of the higher-dimensional brane-world scenario see, e.g., Refs.  [68, 24, 135, 100, 23] and for perturbation theory in the context of the low-energy string effective action see, e.g., Refs. [85, 34].

For simplicity we work with a flat background spatial metric which is compatible with current observations. For generalisation to spatially hyperbolic or spherical FRW models see other reviews, e.g., Ref.[66]. We use a prime to denote derivatives with respect to conformal time, and we use a comma to denote partial derivatives with respect to comoving spatial coordinates, i.e.,

T,i≡∂T∂xi.T_{,i}\equiv\frac{\partial T}{\partial x^{i}}\,. (1.1)

For further definitions and notation see Appendix A.

2 Perturbations in cosmology

Throughout this review we will assume that our observable Universe can approximately be described by a homogeneous and isotropic Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) spacetime. Thus we assume that the physical quantities can usefully be decomposed into a homogeneous background, where quantities depend solely on cosmic time, and inhomogeneous perturbations. The perturbations thus “live” on the background spacetime and it is this background spacetime which is used to split four-dimensional spacetime into spatial three-hypersurfaces, using a (3+1) decomposition. In addition we work with a spatially flat FRW background, though results can be readily extended to non-zero spatial curvature.

We start this section by defining arbitrary perturbations of tensorial quantities and then proceed by decomposing vectors and tensors into “time” and “space” parts on the spatial hypersurfaces.

2.1 Defining perturbations

Any tensorial quantities can then be split into a homogeneous background and an inhomogeneous perturbation

𝐓⁡(η,xi)=𝐓0​(η)+δ​𝐓​(η,xi).{\bf T}(\eta,x^{i})={\bf T}_{0}(\eta)+\delta{\bf T}(\eta,x^{i})\,. (2.1)

The background part is a time-dependent quantity, 𝐓0≡𝐓0​(η){\bf T}_{0}\equiv{\bf T}_{0}(\eta), whereas the perturbations depend on time and space coordinates xμ=[η,xi]x^{\mu}=[\eta,x^{i}]. The perturbation can be further expanded as a power series,

δ​𝐓​(η,xi)=∑n=1∞ϵnn!​δ​𝐓n​(η,xi),\delta{\bf T}(\eta,x^{i})=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon^{n}}{n!}\delta{\bf{T}}_{n}(\eta,x^{i})\,, (2.2)

where the subscript nn denotes the order of the perturbations, and we explicitly include here the small parameter ϵ\epsilon. In linear perturbation theory, for example, we only consider first-order terms, ϵ1\epsilon^{1}, and can neglect terms resulting from the product of two perturbations, which would necessarily be of order ϵ2\epsilon^{2} or higher, which considerably simplifies the resulting equations. In the following sections we shall omit the small parameter ϵ\epsilon whenever possible, as is usually done to avoid the equations getting too cluttered.

2.2 Decomposing tensorial quantities

It is convenient to slice the spacetime manifold into a one-parameter family of spatial hypersurfaces of constant time, which is the standard (3+1) split of spacetime. This foliation was introduced by Darmois already in 1927 (see Ref. [53]) and popularised by Arnowitt, Deser and Misner [6] (for conditions on the existence of the foliation see e.g. Ref. [172]). We refer to the foliation of spacetime by spatial hypersurfaces of given conformal time as the time-slicing, and the identification of spatial coordinates on each hypersurface as the threading.

Note that the (3+1) split of spacetime precedes the decomposition of 3-dimensional quantities into scalars and vectors, or scalar, vectors, and tensors below.

2.2.1 Vectors

We can split any 4 vector VμV^{\mu} into a temporal and spatial part,

𝒰μ=[𝒰0,𝒰i].{\cal{U}}^{\mu}=\left[{\cal{U}}^{0},{\cal{U}}^{i}\right]\,. (2.3)

Note that 𝒰0{\cal{U}}^{0} is a scalar on spatial hypersurfaces. The spatial part 𝒰i{\cal{U}}^{i} can then be further decomposed into a further scalar part 𝒰{\cal{U}} and a vector part 𝒰veci{{\cal{U}}_{\rm{vec}}^{i}},

𝒰i≡δi​j𝒰,j+𝒰veci,{\cal{U}}^{i}\equiv\delta^{ij}{\cal{U}}_{,j}+{{\cal{U}}_{\rm{vec}}^{i}}\,, (2.4)

where ∂𝒰veci/∂xi=0\partial{{\cal{U}}_{\rm{vec}}^{i}}/\partial x^{i}=0. The denominations scalar and vector part go back to Bardeen [7] and are due to the transformation behaviour of 𝒰{\cal{U}} and 𝒰veci{{\cal{U}}_{\rm{vec}}^{i}} on spatial hypersurfaces. The decomposition of a vector field into potential (or curl-free) part and a divergence-free part in Euclidean space is known as Helmholtz’s theorem. The curl-free and divergence-free parts are also called longitudinal and solenoidal parts, respectively.

In our isotropic (FRW) background, there can be no spatial vector part at zeroth order (as this would correspond to a preferred direction), but there can be a non-zero temporal part,

𝒰(0)0≠0,𝒰(0)i=0.{\cal{U}}^{0}_{(0)}\neq 0\,,\qquad{\cal{U}}^{i}_{(0)}=0\,. (2.5)

A non-trivial vector, with a non-zero spatial part, can appear only at first order. We give examples of vector fields in a FRW background including perturbations in Section 3.1, where we discuss the unit vector field normal to constant-time hypersurfaces and the fluid 4-velocity.

Note that “divergence-free”, etc, is defined with respect to the flat-space metric, rather than using covariant derivatives, since perturbations are defined with respect to the spatially flat background.

2.2.2 Tensors

As for vector fields, we can decompose a rank-2 tensor into a time part and spatial part, but now have also mixed time-space parts.

Consider the metric tensor gμ​νg_{\mu\nu} which we require to be symmetric,

gμ​ν≡gν​μ.g_{\mu\nu}\equiv g_{\nu\mu}\,. (2.6)

The metric tensor has therefore only 10 independent components in 4 dimensions. We first split the metric tensor into a background and a perturbed part, using Eq. (2.1). It then turns out to be useful to split the metric perturbation into different parts labelled scalar, vector or tensor according to their transformation properties on spatial hypersurfaces [7, 162], which are themselves expanded into first and higher order parts using Eq. (2.2).

Our background spacetime is described by a spatially flat FRW background metric

d​s2=a2​[−d​η2+δi​j​d​xi​d​xj],ds^{2}=a^{2}\left[-d\eta^{2}+\delta_{ij}dx^{i}dx^{j}\right]\,, (2.7)

where η\eta is conformal time and a=a⁡(η)a=a(\eta) is the scale factor. The cosmic time, measured by observers at fixed comoving spatial coordinates, xix^{i}, is given by t=∫a⁡(η)​𝑑ηt=\int a(\eta)\,d\eta.

The perturbed part of the metric tensor can be written as

δ​g00\displaystyle\delta g_{00} =\displaystyle= −2​a2​ϕ,\displaystyle-2a^{2}{\phi}\,, (2.8)
δ​g0​i\displaystyle\delta g_{0i} =\displaystyle= a2​Bi,\displaystyle a^{2}B_{i}\,, (2.9)
δ​gi​j\displaystyle\delta g_{ij} =\displaystyle= 2​a2​Ci​j.\displaystyle 2a^{2}C_{ij}\,. (2.10)

The 0−i0-i and the i−ji-j-components of the metric tensor can be further decomposed into scalar, vector and tensor parts

Bi\displaystyle B_{i} =\displaystyle= B,i−Si,\displaystyle B_{,i}-S_{i}\,, (2.11)
Ci​j\displaystyle C_{ij} =\displaystyle= −ψδi​j+E,ij+F(i,j)+12hi​j.\displaystyle-\psi\;\delta_{ij}+E_{,ij}+F_{(i,j)}+\frac{1}{2}h_{ij}\,. (2.12)

where ϕ{\phi}, BB, ψ\psi and EE are scalar metric perturbations, SiS_{i} and FiF_{i} are vector metric perturbations, and hi​jh_{ij} is a tensor metric perturbation, which we will now define.

Scalar perturbations can always be constructed from a scalar, or its derivatives, and background quantities. Any 3-vector, such as B,iB_{,i}, constructed from a scalar is necessarily curl-free, i.e., B,[ij]=0B_{,[ij]}=0.

Vector perturbations are divergence-free. For instance one can distinguish an intrinsically vector part of the metric perturbation δ​g0​i\delta g_{0i}, which we denote by −Si-S_{i}, which gives a non-vanishing contribution to δ​g0​[i,j]\delta g_{0[i,j]}. Similarly we define the vector contribution to δ​gi​j\delta g_{ij} constructed from the (symmetric) derivative of a vector F(i,j)F_{(i,j)}.

Finally there is a tensor contribution to δ​gi​j=a2​hi​j\delta g_{ij}=a^{2}h_{ij} which is both transverse, hi​j,j=0h_{ij,}^{~~~j}=0 (i.e., divergence-free), and trace-free (hii=0h_{i}^{i}=0) which therefore cannot be constructed from inhomogeneous scalar or vector perturbations.

Note that when raising and lowering spatial indices of vector and tensor perturbations we use the comoving background spatial metric, δi​j\delta_{ij}, so that, for instance, hij≡δj​k​hi​kh_{i}^{j}\equiv\delta^{jk}h_{ik}.

The reason for splitting the metric perturbation into these three types is that the governing equations decouple at linear order, and hence we can solve each perturbation type separately. At higher order this is no longer true: we find for example at second order that although the “true” second order perturbations, δ​g2​μ​ν\delta g_{2\mu\nu}, still decouple, but their governing equations have source terms quadratic in the first order variables, δ​g1​μ​ν\delta g_{1\mu\nu}, mixing the different types [127]. Indeed at all higher orders, n>1n>1, the different types of perturbations of order nn decouple, but are sourced by terms comprising perturbations of lower order.

We have introduced four scalar functions, two spatial vector valued functions with three components each, and a symmetric spatial tensor with six components. But these functions are subject to several constraints: hi​jh_{ij} is transverse and traceless, which contributes four constraints, FiF_{i} and SiS_{i} are divergence-free, one constraint each. We are therefore finally left 10 new degrees of freedom, the same number as the independent components of the perturbed metric.

The choice of variables to describe the perturbed metric is not unique. Already at first order there are different conventions for the split of the spatial part of the metric. We follow the notation of Mukhanov et al [123] so that the metric perturbation, ψ\psi, can be identified directly with the intrinsic scalar curvature of spatial hypersurfaces at first order, see later. Sometimes it is useful to work in terms of the trace of the perturbed spatial metric

C=Cii=−3​ψ+∇2EC=C_{i}^{i}=-3\psi+\nabla^{2}E (2.13)

At first order this coincides with the perturbation of the determinant of the spatial metric. Including terms up to second order we have

−12hi​jhi​j−2E,ijhi​j−2Fi,jhi​j.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}h_{ij}h^{ij}-2E_{,ij}h^{ij}-2F_{i,j}h^{ij}\,.

where we have used the general result det(eγ)=eTr⁡(γ)\det(e^{\gamma})=e^{{\rm Tr}(\gamma)}. There are further choices for the way the spatial metric is split into the different perturbation variables at second (and higher) order in the perturbations.

Note that our metric perturbations in Eqs. (2.8–2.12) include all orders. If we write out the complete metric tensor, up to and including second-order in the perturbations we have

g00\displaystyle g_{00} =\displaystyle= −a2​(1+2​ϕ1+ϕ2),\displaystyle-a^{2}\left(1+2{\phi_{{1}}}+{\phi_{{2}}}\right)\,,
g0​i\displaystyle g_{0i} =\displaystyle= a2​(B1​i+12​B2​i),\displaystyle a^{2}\left(B_{1i}+\frac{1}{2}B_{2i}\right)\,,

where the first and second order perturbations B1​iB_{1i} and C1​i​jC_{1ij}, and B2​iB_{2i} and C2​i​jC_{2ij}, can be further split according to Eqs. (2.11) and (2.12).

3 Geometry of spatial hypersurfaces

3.1 Timelike vector fields

The perturbed metric given in Section 2.2.2 implicitly defines a unit time-like vector field orthogonal to constant-η\eta hypersurfaces,

nμ∝∂η∂xμ,n_{\mu}\propto\frac{\partial\eta}{\partial x^{\mu}}\,, (3.1)

subject to the constraint

nμ​nμ=−1.n^{\mu}n_{\mu}=-1\,. (3.2)

In the FRW background this coincides with the 4-velocity of matter and the expansion of the velocity field θ=3​H\theta=3H, where HH is the Hubble expansion rate. We define the conformal Hubble parameter

ℋ≡a​H.{\cal H}\equiv aH\,. (3.3)

In this section we calculate corresponding geometrical quantities for nνn^{\nu}, and thus the space-time, defined by the perturbed metric tensor. Note however that in the perturbed spacetime the vector field nμn^{\mu}, need no longer coincide with the 4-velocity of matter fields at first order and beyond.

Up to and including to second order, the covariant vector field is

nμ=−a⁡[1+ϕ1+12​ϕ2+12​(B1​k​B1k−ϕ12),𝟎],n_{\mu}=-a\left[1+{\phi_{{1}}}+\frac{1}{2}{\phi_{{2}}}+\frac{1}{2}\left(B_{1k}B_{1}^{k}-\phi_{1}^{2}\right),\bm{\mathrm{{0}}}\right]\,, (3.4)

and the contravariant vector field is

n0\displaystyle n^{0} =\displaystyle= 1a​[1−ϕ1−12​ϕ2+32​ϕ12−12​B1​k​B1k],\displaystyle\frac{1}{a}\left[1-\phi_{1}-\frac{1}{2}\phi_{2}+\frac{3}{2}\phi_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}B_{1k}B_{1}^{k}\right]\,,
ni\displaystyle n^{i} =\displaystyle= 1a​[−(B1i+12​B2i)+2​B1​k​C1k​i+ϕ1​B1i].\displaystyle\frac{1}{a}\left[-\left(B_{1}^{i}+\frac{1}{2}B_{2}^{i}\right)+2B_{1k}C_{1}^{ki}+{\phi_{{1}}}B_{1}^{i}\right]\,. (3.5)

Observers moving along the hypersurface-orthogonal vector field, nμn^{\mu}, have a vanishing 3-velocity with respect to the spatial coordinates xix^{i} when the shift vector BiB^{i} is zero. We will refer to these as orthogonal coordinate systems.

3.2 Geometrical quantities

The covariant derivative of any time-like unit vector field nμn_{\mu} can be decomposed uniquely as follows [172]:

nμ;ν=13​θ​𝒫μ​ν+σμ​ν+ωμ​ν−aμ​nν,n_{\mu;\nu}=\frac{1}{3}\theta\,{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}+\sigma_{\mu\nu}+\omega_{\mu\nu}-a_{\mu}n_{\nu}\,, (3.6)

where the spatial projection tensor 𝒫μ​ν{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}, orthogonal to nμn^{\mu}, is given by

𝒫μ​ν=gμ​ν+nμ​nν.{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}+n_{\mu}n_{\nu}. (3.7)

The overall expansion rate is given by

θ=nμ;μ,\theta=n^{\mu}_{~;\mu}\,, (3.8)

the (trace-free and symmetric) shear is

σμ​ν=12​𝒫μα​𝒫νβ​(nα;β+nβ;α)−13​θ​𝒫μ​ν,\sigma_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{2}{\cal{P}}^{~\alpha}_{\mu}{\cal{P}}^{~\beta}_{\nu}\left(n_{\alpha;\beta}+n_{\beta;\alpha}\right)-\frac{1}{3}\theta{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}\,, (3.9)

the (antisymmetric) vorticity is

ωμ​ν=12​𝒫μα​𝒫νβ​(nα;β−nβ;α),\omega_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{2}{\cal{P}}^{~\alpha}_{\mu}{\cal{P}}^{~\beta}_{\nu}\left(n_{\alpha;\beta}-n_{\beta;\alpha}\right)\,, (3.10)

and the acceleration is

aμ=nμ;ν​nν.a_{\mu}=n_{\mu;\nu}n^{\nu}\,. (3.11)

On spatial hypersurfaces the expansion, shear, vorticity and acceleration coincide with their Newtonian counterparts in fluid dynamics [59, 160]. In this subsection we focus on the unit normal vector field nμn^{\mu}, but the expansion, shear, vorticity and acceleration defined in this way can readily be applied to any other 4-vector field, such as the 4-velocity uμu^{\mu}. One can easily verify that the vorticity (3.10) is automatically zero for the hypersurface orthogonal vector field, nμn_{\mu} defined in Eq. (3.4). Note however that the perturbed fluid velocity can have vorticity and this is described by the vector (divergence-free) part of the fluid 3-velocity which we will define in section 4.

The projection tensor 𝒫μ​ν{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu} is the induced 3-metric on the spatial hypersurfaces, and the Lie derivative of 𝒫μ​ν{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu} along the vector field nμn^{\mu} is the extrinsic curvature of the hypersurface embedded in the higher-dimensional spacetime [172, 40]. The extrinsic curvature of the spatial hypersurfaces defined by nμn_{\mu} is thus given by

Kμ​ν≡12​£n​𝒫μ​ν=𝒫νλ​nμ;λ=13​θ​𝒫μ​ν+σμ​ν.K_{\mu\nu}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\pounds_{n}{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}={\cal{P}}_{\nu}^{~\lambda}n_{\mu;\lambda}=\frac{1}{3}\theta\,{\cal{P}}_{\mu\nu}+\sigma_{\mu\nu}\,. (3.12)

At first order we can easily identify the metric perturbations with geometrical perturbations of the spatial hypersurfaces or the associated vector field, nμn_{\mu}.

The intrinsic curvature of spatial hypersurfaces up to first order is given by

R1(3)=4a2​∇2ψ1.{}^{(3)}R_{1}=\frac{4}{a^{2}}\nabla^{2}\psi_{1}\,. (3.13)

The scalar part of the shear (3.9) up to first order is given by

σ1​i​j=(∂i∂j−13∇2δi​j)aσ1,\sigma_{1ij}=\left(\partial_{i}\partial_{j}-\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\delta_{ij}\right)a{\sigma}_{1}\,, (3.14)

where we define the shear potential

σ1≡E1′−B1.{\sigma}_{1}\equiv E_{1}^{\prime}-B_{1}\,. (3.15)

The vector and tensor parts are given by, respectively,

σ1​V​i​j=a⁡(F1​(i,j)′−B1​(i,j)),σ1​T​i​j=a2​h1​i​j′.\displaystyle\sigma_{1{\rm{V}}ij}=a\left(F_{1(i,j)}^{\prime}-B_{1(i,j)}\right)\,,\qquad\sigma_{1{\rm{T}}ij}=\frac{a}{2}h_{1ij}^{\prime}\,. (3.16)

The acceleration up to first order is

ai=ϕ,i.a_{i}={\phi}_{,i}\,. (3.17)

The expansion rate up to first order is given by

θ=3a​[ℋ−ℋ​ϕ−ψ′+13​∇2σ].\theta=\frac{3}{a}\left[{\cal H}-{\cal H}{\phi}-\psi^{\prime}+\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\sigma\right]\,. (3.18)

The intrinsic spatial curvature, shear and acceleration of nμn_{\mu} are given up to second order in Appendix C.

The overall expansion, up to second order is given by

θ=1a[\displaystyle\theta=\frac{1}{a}\Bigg[ 3​a′a−3​a′a​ϕ1+C1​kk′−B1​k,k\displaystyle 3\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}-3\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}{\phi_{{1}}}+{C_{1k}^{~~k}}^{\prime}-B_{1k,}^{~~k} (3.19)
−32​a′a​(ϕ2−3​ϕ12)+12​(C2​kk′−B2​k,k)+ϕ1​(B1​k,k−C1​kk′)\displaystyle-\frac{3}{2}\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}\left({\phi_{{2}}}-3{\phi_{{1}}}^{2}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left({C_{2k}^{~~k}}^{\prime}-B_{2k,}^{~~k}\right)+\phi_{1}\left(B_{1k,}^{~~k}-{C_{1k}^{~~k}}^{\prime}\right)
−32a′aB1​kB1k−2C1k​lC1​k​l′+2C1k​lB1​l,k+2B1lC1​l​k,k−B1kC1​l,kl].\displaystyle-\frac{3}{2}\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}B_{1k}B_{1}^{k}-2C_{1}^{kl}C_{1kl}^{\prime}+2C_{1}^{kl}B_{1l,k}+2B_{1}^{l}C_{1lk,}^{~~~k}-B_{1}^{k}C^{l}_{1~l,k}\Bigg]\,.

Focusing for the moment only on scalar perturbations (neglecting first order vectors and tensors) on large scales (neglecting spatial derivatives) the perturbed part of the expansion simplifies to

δ​θ1\displaystyle\delta\theta_{1} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −3a​(a′a​ϕ1+ψ1′),\displaystyle-\frac{3}{a}\left(\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}\phi_{1}+\psi_{1}^{\prime}\right)\,, (3.20)
δ​θ2\displaystyle\delta\theta_{2} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −3a​[a′a​ϕ2+ψ2′+2​ψ1′​(2​ψ1−ϕ1)−3​a′a​ϕ12].\displaystyle-\frac{3}{a}\left[\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}\phi_{2}+\psi_{2}^{\prime}+2\psi_{1}^{\prime}\left(2\psi_{1}-\phi_{1}\right)-3\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}\phi_{1}^{2}\right]\,. (3.21)

Note that the expansion rate, θ\theta in Eq. (3.19), is defined with respect to proper time (comoving with nμn^{\mu}). The expansion rate with respect to conformal time on large scales is

θcoord≃3​[a′a−ψ1′−12​ψ2′−2​ψ1′​ψ1].\theta_{\rm{coord}}\simeq 3\left[\frac{a^{\prime}}{a}-\psi_{1}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{2}^{\prime}-2\psi_{1}^{\prime}\psi_{1}\right]\,. (3.22)

We see that on large scales (and considering only scalar perturbations) spatially flat hypersurfaces (ψ=0\psi=0) are also uniform coordinate expansion hypersurfaces (on which the perturbed expansion vanishes).

In the following we will often refer to the perturbed logarithmic expansion, or “number of e-foldings”

N≡13​∫θ​𝑑τ=13​∫θcoord​𝑑η=ln⁡a−ψ1−12​ψ2−ψ12.N\equiv\frac{1}{3}\int\theta d\tau=\frac{1}{3}\int\theta_{\rm{coord}}d\eta=\ln a-\psi_{1}-\frac{1}{2}\psi_{2}-\psi_{1}^{2}\,. (3.23)

This quantity, and its perturbation δ​N\delta N becomes a particularly useful quantity to describe the primordial scalar perturbation beyond linear order, as we will discuss in Section 11.

4 Energy-momentum tensor for fluids

We are interested in how the spacetime geometry, described by the metric tensor, is affected by the perturbed matter content, described by the energy-momentum tensor.

The four-velocity of matter, uμu^{\mu}, is defined by

uμ=d​xμd​τ,u^{\mu}=\frac{dx^{\mu}}{d\tau}\,, (4.1)

where τ\tau is the proper time comoving with the fluid, subject to the constraint

uμ​uμ=−1.u_{\mu}u^{\mu}=-1\,. (4.2)

The components of the 4-velocity up to second order are then given by

u0\displaystyle u_{0} =\displaystyle= −a⁡[1+ϕ1+12​ϕ2−12​ϕ12+12​v1​k​v1k],\displaystyle-a\left[1+{\phi_{{1}}}+\frac{1}{2}{\phi_{{2}}}-\frac{1}{2}{\phi_{{1}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v_{1k}v_{1}^{k}\right]\,,
ui\displaystyle u_{i} =\displaystyle= a⁡[v1​i+B1​i+12​(v2​i+B2​i)−ϕ1​B1​i+2​C1​i​k​v1k],\displaystyle a\left[v_{1i}+B_{1i}+\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{2i}+B_{2i}\right)-\phi_{1}B_{1i}+2C_{1ik}v_{1}^{k}\right]\,, (4.3)
u0\displaystyle u^{0} =\displaystyle= a−1​[1−ϕ1−12​ϕ2+32​ϕ12+12​v1​k​v1k+v1​k​B1k],\displaystyle a^{-1}\left[1-{\phi_{{1}}}-\frac{1}{2}{\phi_{{2}}}+\frac{3}{2}{\phi_{{1}}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}v_{1k}v_{1}^{k}+v_{1k}B_{1}^{k}\right]\,,
ui\displaystyle u^{i} =\displaystyle= a−1​(v1i+12​v2i),\displaystyle a^{-1}\left(v_{1}^{i}+\frac{1}{2}v_{2}^{i}\right)\,, (4.4)

The spatial part of the velocity can be split into a scalar (potential) part and a vector (solenoidal) part, order by order, following Eq. (2.4) as

vi≡δi​jv,j+vveci,v^{i}\equiv\delta^{ij}v_{,j}+v_{{\rm vec}}^{i}\,, (4.5)

for each order nn where we refer to v(n)v_{(n)} as the scalar velocity potential, and to v(n)​v​e​civ_{(n)vec}^{i} as the vector part.

Note that viv^{i} is the 3-velocity of matter defined with respect to the spatial coordinates, xix^{i}, and so is not the velocity with respect to the hypersurface-orthogonal vector field nin^{i}, except in orthogonal coordinate systems for which Bi=0B^{i}=0. In comoving orthogonal coordinates, which we will discuss later, vi=0v^{i}=0 and Bi=0B^{i}=0.

4.1 Single fluid

The energy-momentum tensor of a fluid with density ρ\rho, isotropic pressure PP and 4-velocity uμu^{\mu}, defined above in Eq. (4), is defined as [66, 160, 47, 177]

Tμ​ν=(ρ+P)​uμ​uν+P​gμ​ν+πμ​ν.T_{\mu\nu}=\left(\rho+P\right)u_{\mu}u_{\nu}+Pg_{\mu\nu}+\pi_{\mu\nu}\,. (4.6)

The anisotropic stress tensor πμ​ν\pi_{\mu\nu} is split into first and second order parts in the usual way,

πμ​ν≡π(1)​μ​ν+12​π(2)​μ​ν,\pi_{\mu\nu}\equiv\pi_{(1)\mu\nu}+\frac{1}{2}\pi_{(2)\mu\nu}\,, (4.7)

and is subject to the constraints

πμ​ν​uν=0,πμμ=0.\pi_{\mu\nu}u^{\nu}=0\,,\qquad\pi^{\mu}_{~\mu}=0\,. (4.8)

The anisotropic stress vanishes for a perfect fluid or minimally coupled scalar fields, but may be non-zero in the presence of free-streaming neutrinos or a non-minimally coupled scalar field.

We follow Kodama and Sasaki [66] in defining the proper energy density as the eigenvalue of the energy-momentum tensor, and the four velocity uμu^{\mu} as the corresponding eigenvector

Tνμ​uν=−ρ​uμ.\displaystyle T^{\mu}_{~\nu}u^{\nu}=-\rho u^{\mu}\,. (4.9)

The anisotropic stress tensor decomposes into a trace-free scalar part, Π\Pi, a vector part, Πi\Pi_{i}, and a tensor part, Πi​j\Pi_{ij}, at each order according to

πi​j=a2[Π,ij−13∇2Πδi​j+12(Πi,j+Πj,i)+Πi​j].\pi_{ij}=a^{2}\left[\Pi_{,ij}-\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\Pi\delta_{ij}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\Pi_{i,j}+\Pi_{j,i}\right)+\Pi_{ij}\right]\,. (4.10)

We get for the components of the stress energy tensor in the background

T00=−ρ0,Ti0=0,Tji=δji​P0,\displaystyle T^{0}_{~0}=-\rho_{0}\,,\qquad T^{0}_{~i}=0\,,\qquad T^{i}_{~j}=\delta^{i}_{~j}P_{0}\,, (4.11)

at first order,

δ(1)​T00\displaystyle{}^{(1)}\delta T^{0}_{~0} =\displaystyle= −δ​ρ1,\displaystyle-\delta\rho_{1}\,, (4.12)
δ(1)​Ti0\displaystyle{}^{(1)}\delta T^{0}_{~i} =\displaystyle= (ρ0+P0)​(v1​i+B1​i),\displaystyle\left(\rho_{0}+P_{0}\right)\left(v_{1i}+B_{1i}\right)\,, (4.13)
δ(1)​Tji\displaystyle{}^{(1)}\delta T^{i}_{~j} =\displaystyle= δ​P1​δji+a−2​π(1)​ji,\displaystyle\delta P_{1}\delta^{i}_{~j}+a^{-2}\pi_{(1)~j}^{~i}\,, (4.14)

and at second order

δ(2)​T00\displaystyle{}^{(2)}\delta T^{0}_{~0} =\displaystyle= −δ​ρ2−2​(ρ0+P0)​v1​k​(v1k+B1k),\displaystyle-\delta\rho_{2}-2\left(\rho_{0}+P_{0}\right)v_{1k}\left(v_{1}^{~k}+B_{1}^{~k}\right)\,, (4.15)
δ(2)​Ti0\displaystyle{}^{(2)}\delta T^{0}_{~i} =\displaystyle= (ρ0+P0)​[v2​i+B2​i+4​C1​i​k​v1k−2​ϕ1​(v1​i+2​B1​i)]\displaystyle\left(\rho_{0}+P_{0}\right)\Big[v_{2i}+B_{2i}+4C_{1ik}v_{1}^{~k}-2\phi_{1}\left(v_{1i}+2B_{1i}\right)\Big] (4.16)
+2​(δ​ρ1+δ​P1)​(v1​i+B1​i)+2a2​(B1k+v1k)​π1​i​k,\displaystyle\qquad+2\left(\delta\rho_{1}+\delta P_{1}\right)\left(v_{1i}+B_{1i}\right)+\frac{2}{a^{2}}\left(B^{k}_{1}+v_{1}^{k}\right)\pi_{1ik}\,,
δ(2)​Tji\displaystyle{}^{(2)}\delta T^{i}_{~j} =\displaystyle= δ​P2​δji+a−2​π2​ji−4a2​C1i​k​π1​j​k+2​(ρ0+P0)​v1i​(v1​j+B1​j).\displaystyle\delta P_{2}\,\delta^{i}_{~j}+a^{-2}\pi^{~i}_{2~j}-\frac{4}{a^{2}}C^{ik}_{1}\pi_{1jk}+2\left(\rho_{0}+P_{0}\right)v_{1}^{i}\left(v_{1j}+B_{1j}\right)\,. (4.17)

Note, that for compactness of presentation we have not split perturbations into their constituent scalar, vector and tensor parts in the above expressions. The decompositions are given for viv_{i} and πi​j\pi_{ij} in Eqs. (4.5) and (4.10), and given for BiB_{i} and Ci​jC_{ij} in Section 2.2.2, in Eqs. (2.11) and (2.12).

Note that contracting the i−ji-j part of the energy-momentum tensor, Eq. (4.17), including the constraints for the anisotropic stress, Eq. (4.8), guarantees that the anisotropic stress cancels on the trace,

δ(1)​Tkk\displaystyle{}^{(1)}\delta T^{k}_{~k} =\displaystyle= 3​δ​P1,\displaystyle 3\delta P_{1}\,, (4.18)
δ(2)​Tkk\displaystyle{}^{(2)}\delta T^{k}_{~k} =\displaystyle= 3​δ​P2+2​(ρ0+P0)​v1k​(v1​k+B1​k).\displaystyle 3\delta P_{2}+2\left(\rho_{0}+P_{0}\right)v_{1}^{k}\left(v_{1k}+B_{1k}\right)\,. (4.19)

This cancellation is true at all orders.

Coordinate transformations affect the split between spatial and temporal components of the matter fields and so quantities like the density, pressure and 3-velocity are gauge-dependent, as described in Section 6. Density and pressure are 4-scalar quantities which transform as given in Eq. (6.18) in the following section, but the 4-velocity is a 4-vector which transforms described in Section 6.3. The anisotropic stress is gauge-invariant at first order, but becomes gauge-dependent at second order.

4.2 Multiple fluids

In the multiple fluid case the total energy-momentum tensor is the sum of the energy-momentum tensors of the individual fluids

Tμ​ν=∑αT(α)μ​ν.T^{\mu\nu}=\sum_{\alpha}T^{\mu\nu}_{(\alpha)}\,. (4.20)

For each fluid we define the local energy-momentum transfer 4-vector Q(α)νQ^{\nu}_{(\alpha)} through the relation

∇μT(α)μ​ν=Q(α)ν,\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}_{(\alpha)}=Q^{\nu}_{(\alpha)}\,, (4.21)

where the energy-momentum tensor, T(α)μ​νT^{\mu\nu}_{(\alpha)}, is locally conserved only for non-interacting fluids, for which Q(α)ν=0Q^{\nu}_{(\alpha)}=0. Equations (8.2) and (4.21) imply the constraint

∑αQ(α)ν=0.\sum_{\alpha}Q^{\nu}_{(\alpha)}=0\,. (4.22)

Following Refs. [66, 111] we split the energy-momentum transfer 4-vector using the total fluid velocity uμu^{\mu} as

Q(α)μ=Q(α)​uμ+f(α)μ,Q^{\mu}_{(\alpha)}=Q_{(\alpha)}u^{\mu}+f^{\mu}_{(\alpha)}\,, (4.23)

where Q(α)Q_{(\alpha)} is the energy transfer rate and f(α)μf^{\mu}_{(\alpha)} the momentum transfer rate, subject to the constraint

uμ​f(α)μ=0,u_{\mu}f^{\mu}_{(\alpha)}=0\,, (4.24)

From Eq. (4.24) we find for the temporal component of the momentum transfer rate vector f(α)μf^{\mu}_{(\alpha)}

f1​(α)0=0,f2​(α)0=2​f1​(α)k​(v1​k+B1​k),f^{0}_{1(\alpha)}=0\,,\qquad f^{0}_{2(\alpha)}=2f^{k}_{1(\alpha)}\left(v_{1k}+B_{1k}\right)\,, (4.25)

We then find for the temporal components of the energy transfer 4-vector to be at zeroth, first and second order, respectively

Q(α)0\displaystyle Q^{0}_{(\alpha)} =\displaystyle= 1a​Q0​α,\displaystyle\frac{1}{a}Q_{0\alpha}\,, (4.26)
Q(α)0\displaystyle Q^{0}_{(\alpha)} =\displaystyle= 1a​(δ​Q1​α−ϕ1​Q0​α),\displaystyle\frac{1}{a}\left(\delta Q_{1\alpha}-{\phi_{{1}}}Q_{0\alpha}\right)\,, (4.27)
Q(α)0\displaystyle Q^{0}_{(\alpha)} =\displaystyle= 12​a[δQ2​α+Q0​α(3ϕ12−ϕ2)−2ϕ1δQ1​α\displaystyle\frac{1}{2a}\Big[\delta Q_{2\alpha}+Q_{0\alpha}\left(3{\phi_{{1}}}^{2}-{\phi_{{2}}}\right)-2{\phi_{{1}}}\delta Q_{1\alpha} (4.28)
+(v1​k+B1​k)(2af1​(α)k+Q0​αv1k)],\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\left(v_{1k}+B_{1k}\right)\left(\frac{2}{a}f^{k}_{1(\alpha)}+Q_{0\alpha}v_{1}^{k}\right)\Big]\,,

where Q0​αQ_{0\alpha}, δ​Q1​α\delta Q_{1\alpha}, and δ​Q2​α\delta Q_{2\alpha} are the energy transfer to the α\alpha-fluid in the background, at first and at second order, respectively.

For the spatial components of the energy transfer 4-vector, the momentum part, we get at first and second order, respectively

Q(α)i\displaystyle Q^{i}_{(\alpha)} =\displaystyle= 1a​Q0​α​v1i+1a2​f1​(α)i,\displaystyle\frac{1}{a}Q_{0\alpha}v_{1}^{i}+\frac{1}{a^{2}}f^{i}_{1(\alpha)}\,, (4.29)
Q(α)i\displaystyle Q^{i}_{(\alpha)} =\displaystyle= 12​a​[1a​f2​(α)i+δ​Q1​α​v1i+Q0​α​(v2i+2​ϕ1​B1i−4​C1​ki​v1k)],\displaystyle\frac{1}{2a}\Big[\frac{1}{a}f^{i}_{2(\alpha)}+\delta Q_{1\alpha}v_{1}^{i}+Q_{0\alpha}\left(v_{2}^{i}+2{\phi_{{1}}}B_{1}^{i}-4C_{1k}^{~i}v_{1}^{k}\right)\Big]\,, (4.30)

where f1​(α)if^{i}_{1(\alpha)} and f2​(α)if^{i}_{2(\alpha)} are the spatial parts of the momentum transfer rates at first and second order.

Note that the homogeneous and isotropic FRW background excludes a zeroth order momentum transfer.

Using Eq. (2.4) the spatial momentum transfer vector of order nn, fn⁡(α)if^{i}_{n(\alpha)}, can be further decomposed into a scalar and a vector part, according to

fn⁡(α)i≡δi​j​fn⁡(α),j+f^n⁡(α)i.f^{i}_{n(\alpha)}\equiv\delta^{ij}f_{n(\alpha),j}+\hat{f}^{i}_{n(\alpha)}\,. (4.31)

5 Energy-momentum tensor for scalar fields

5.1 Single field

A minimally coupled scalar field is specified by the Lagrangian density

ℒ=−12gμ​νφ,μφ,ν−U(φ),{\cal L}=-\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}\varphi_{,\mu}\varphi_{,\nu}-U(\varphi)\,, (5.1)

where the scalar field kinetic energy is then non-negative for our choice of metric signature.

The energy momentum tensor is defined as

Tμ​ν=−2​∂ℒ∂gμ​ν+gμ​ν​ℒ,T_{\mu\nu}=-2\frac{\partial{\cal L}}{\partial g^{\mu\nu}}+g_{\mu\nu}{\cal L}\,, (5.2)

and we therefore get for a scalar field φ\varphi

Tνμ=gμ​αφ,αφ,ν−δνμ(U(φ)+12gκ​λφ,κφ,λ).T^{\mu}_{~\nu}=g^{\mu\alpha}\varphi_{,\alpha}\varphi_{,\nu}-\delta^{\mu}_{~\nu}\left(U(\varphi)+\frac{1}{2}g^{\kappa\lambda}\varphi_{,\kappa}\varphi_{,\lambda}\right)\,. (5.3)

Comparing to the energy-momentum tensor for a perfect fluids, Eq. (4.6), we can identify the non-linear 4-velocity, density and pressure of the scalar field [165]

uμ\displaystyle u_{\mu} =\displaystyle= φ,μ|gλ​κφ,λφ,κ|,ρ=−gλ​κφ,λφ,κ+U,\displaystyle\frac{\varphi_{,\mu}}{|g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{,\lambda}\varphi_{,\kappa}|}\,,\qquad\rho=-g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{,\lambda}\varphi_{,\kappa}+U\,,
P\displaystyle P =\displaystyle= −gλ​κφ,λφ,κ−U.\displaystyle-g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{,\lambda}\varphi_{,\kappa}-U\,. (5.4)

Note that the anisotropic stress, πμ​ν\pi_{\mu\nu}, is identically zero for minimally coupled scalar fields. In fact we can subdivide the energy-momentum tensor for a single field into that of a stiff kinetic fluid with ρ(φ)=P(φ)=−gλ​κφ,λφ,κ\rho_{(\varphi)}=P_{(\varphi)}=-g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{,\lambda}\varphi_{,\kappa} and a vacuum energy ρ(U)=−P(U)=U⁡(φ)\rho_{(U)}=-P_{(U)}=U(\varphi), which exchange energy-momentum Q(φ)μ=−Q(U)μ=(d​U/d​φ)​∇μφQ^{\mu}_{(\varphi)}=-Q^{\mu}_{(U)}=(dU/d\varphi)\nabla^{\mu}\varphi.

Splitting the scalar field into a homogeneous background field and a perturbation,

φ⁡(η,xi)=φ0​(η)+δ​φ1​(η,xi),\varphi(\eta,x^{i})=\varphi_{0}(\eta)+\delta\varphi_{1}(\eta,x^{i})\,, (5.5)

and using the definitions above we find for the components of the energy momentum tensor of a perturbed scalar field at linear order without specifying a gauge yet

T00\displaystyle T^{0}_{~0} =\displaystyle= −12a−2φ0′2−U0+a−2φ0′(ϕ1φ0′−δφ1′)−U,φδφ1,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}a^{-2}\varphi^{\prime~2}_{0}-U_{0}+a^{-2}\varphi_{0}^{\prime}\left(\phi_{1}~\varphi_{0}^{\prime}-\delta\varphi_{1}^{\prime}\right)-U_{,\varphi}\delta\varphi_{1}\,, (5.6)
Ti0\displaystyle T^{0}_{~i} =\displaystyle= −a−2​(φ0′​δ​φ1,i),\displaystyle-a^{-2}\left(\varphi_{0}^{\prime}\delta\varphi_{1,i}\right)\,, (5.7)
Tji\displaystyle T^{i}_{~j} =\displaystyle= [12a−2φ0′2−U0−U,φδφ1+a−2φ0′(δφ1′−ϕ1φ0′)]δji,\displaystyle\left[\frac{1}{2}a^{-2}\varphi^{\prime~2}_{0}-U_{0}-U_{,\varphi}\delta\varphi_{1}+a^{-2}\varphi_{0}^{\prime}\left(\delta\varphi_{1}^{\prime}-\phi_{1}~\varphi_{0}^{\prime}\right)\right]~\delta^{i}_{~j}\,, (5.8)

where U,φ≡dU/dφU_{,\varphi}\equiv dU/d\varphi and U0=U⁡(φ0)U_{0}=U(\varphi_{0}). By comparing Eq. (5.8) with Eq. (4.14), we see that scalar fields do not support vector or tensor perturbations to first order.

5.2 Multiple fields

For NN minimally coupled scalar fields the Lagrangian density is given by

ℒ=−12∑I(gμ​αφI,αφI,μ)−U(φ1,…,φN).{\cal L}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I}\left(g^{\mu\alpha}\varphi_{I,\alpha}\varphi_{I,\mu}\right)-U({\varphi}_{1},\ldots,{\varphi}_{N})\,. (5.9)

The energy-momentum tensor is

Tμ​ν=∑K=1N[φK,μ​φK,ν−12​gμ​ν​gα​β​φK,α​φK,β]−gμ​ν​U,T_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{K=1}^{N}\left[{\varphi}_{K,\mu}{\varphi}_{K,\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}g^{\alpha\beta}{\varphi}_{K,\alpha}{\varphi}_{K,\beta}\right]-g_{\mu\nu}U\,, (5.10)

where φK{\varphi}_{K} is the KKth scalar field and UU the scalar field potential and φK,μ≡∂φK∂xμ{\varphi}_{K,\mu}\equiv\frac{\partial{\varphi}_{K}}{\partial x^{\mu}}.

Analogous to the energy-momentum tensor for a single field, we can identify the non-linear 4-velocity, density and pressure of each of the scalar fields [111]

u(I)​μ\displaystyle u_{(I)\mu} =\displaystyle= φI,μ|gλ​κ​φI,λ​φI,κ|,\displaystyle\frac{\varphi_{I,\mu}}{|g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{I,\lambda}\varphi_{I,\kappa}|}\,,
ρ(I)\displaystyle\rho_{(I)} =\displaystyle= P(I)=−gλ​κ​φI,λ​φI,κ.\displaystyle P_{(I)}=-g^{\lambda\kappa}\varphi_{I,\lambda}\varphi_{I,\kappa}\,. (5.11)

The energy-momentum transfer to each fluid is Q(I)​μ=(∂U/∂φI)​φI,μQ_{(I)\mu}=(\partial U/\partial{\varphi}_{I}){\varphi}_{I,\mu}.

The total energy-momentum tensor (5.10) is the sum over NN stiff fluids plus the vacuum energy

Tμ​ν=∑I=1Nρ(I)​[2​u(I)​μ​u(I)​ν+gμ​ν]−U​gμ​ν.T_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{I=1}^{N}\rho_{(I)}\left[2u_{(I)\mu}u_{(I)\nu}+g_{\mu\nu}\right]-Ug_{\mu\nu}\,. (5.12)

The anisotropic stress, πμ​ν\pi_{\mu\nu}, is identically zero for any number of minimally coupled scalar fields. The total energy-momentum tensor is only equivalent to that of a single scalar field in the special case where all the 4-velocities of the fields, u(I)​μu_{(I)\mu}, are identical. This is true in the homogeneous FRW cosmology, but in general breaks down when inhomogeneous perturbations are considered.

We split the scalar fields φI{\varphi}_{I} into a background and perturbations up to and including second order according to Eqs. (2.1) and (2.2),

φI​(xμ)=φ0​I​(η)+δ​φ1​I​(xμ)+12​δ​φ2​I​(xμ).{\varphi}_{I}(x^{\mu})={\varphi}_{0I}(\eta)+\delta\varphi_{{1I}}(x^{\mu})+\frac{1}{2}\delta\varphi_{{2I}}(x^{\mu})\,. (5.13)

The potential U≡U⁡(φI)U\equiv U({\varphi}_{I}) can be split similarly according to

U⁡(φI)=U0+δ​U1+12​δ​U2,U({\varphi}_{I})=U_{0}+{\delta U_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}{\delta U_{2}}\,, (5.14)

where

δ​U1\displaystyle{\delta U_{1}} =\displaystyle= ∑KUK​δ​φ1​K,\displaystyle\sum_{K}U_{K}\delta\varphi_{{1K}}\,, (5.15)
δ​U2\displaystyle{\delta U_{2}} =\displaystyle= ∑K,LUK​L​δ​φ1​K​δ​φ1​L+∑KUK​δ​φ2​K.\displaystyle\sum_{K,L}U_{KL}\delta\varphi_{{1K}}\delta\varphi_{{1L}}+\sum_{K}U_{K}\delta\varphi_{{2K}}\,. (5.16)

and we use the shorthand UK≡∂U/∂φKU_{K}\equiv\partial U/\partial{\varphi}_{K}. The energy-momentum tensor, Eq. (5.10), expanded up to second order in the perturbations for the metric tensor Eq. (2.2.2) is given in Appendix B.2.

6 Gauge transformations

We now review how tensorial quantities change under coordinate transformations [7, 162, 121, 26, 108] (see Ref. [142, 177, 163] for earlier work on this subject). While the order of the perturbation is indicated by a subscript, we also keep the small parameter ϵ\epsilon in the following equations whenever appropriate.

A problem which arises in cosmological perturbation theory is the presence of spurious coordinate artefacts or gauge modes in the calculations. Although the gauge modes had been dealt with on a “case by case” basis before, the gauge issue was resolved in a systematic way by Bardeen [7]. The gauge issue will arise in any approach to GR that splits quantities into a background and a perturbation. Although GR is covariant, i.e. manifestly coordinate choice independent, splitting variables into a background part and a perturbation is not a covariant procedure, and therefore introduces a coordinate or gauge dependence. By construction this only affects the perturbations; the background quantities remain the same in the different coordinate systems. Here we assume the difference between the coordinate systems is small, of O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon), however the gauge problem would persist also for finite transformations. Note that the “covariant approach” [46] also corresponds to a choice of gauge, namely the comoving one, which is made explicit by the inclusion of the velocity field [35, 78].

In order to restore covariance as far as possible, we usually wish to eliminate the gauge degrees of freedom. We will show in Section 7 how, by constructing variables corresponding to perturbations in physically defined coordinate systems, the gauge dependencies can be made to cancel out (the quantities so constructed will not change under a gauge transformation).

6.1 Active and passive approaches to gauge transformations

There are two approaches to calculate how perturbations change under a small coordinate or gauge transformation. For the active view we study how perturbations change under a mapping, where the map directly induces the transformation of the perturbed quantities. In the passive view the relation between two coordinate systems is specified, and we calculate how the perturbations are changed under this coordinate transformation. In the passive approach the transformation is taken at the same physical point, whereas in the active approach the transformation of the perturbed quantities is evaluated at the same coordinate point. We will discuss both approaches briefly in the following, but shall use the active approach to calculate the transformation behaviour of the first and second order variables. For a mathematically more rigorous discussion see e.g. Ref. [108].

6.1.1 Active approach

The starting point in the active approach is the exponential map, that allows us to immediately write down how a tensor 𝐓{\bf T} transforms up to second order, once the generator of the gauge transformation, ξμ\xi^{\mu}, has been specified. The exponential map is

𝐓~=e£ξ​𝐓,\widetilde{\bf T}=e^{\pounds_{\xi}}{\bf T}\,, (6.1)

where £ξ\pounds_{\xi} denotes the Lie derivative with respect to ξλ\xi^{\lambda}. The vector field generating the transformation, ξλ\xi^{\lambda}, is up to second order

ξμ≡ϵ​ξ1μ+12​ϵ2​ξ2μ+O⁡(ϵ3).\xi^{\mu}\equiv\epsilon\xi_{1}^{\mu}+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\xi_{2}^{\mu}+O(\epsilon^{3})\,. (6.2)

The exponential map can be readily expanded

exp⁡(£ξ)=1+ϵ​£ξ1+12​ϵ2​£ξ12+12​ϵ2​£ξ2+…\exp(\pounds_{\xi})=1+\epsilon\pounds_{\xi_{1}}+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\pounds_{\xi_{1}}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\pounds_{\xi_{2}}+\ldots (6.3)

where we kept terms up to O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}). Splitting the tensor 𝐓{\bf T} up to second order, as given in Eq. (2.2), and collecting terms of like order in ϵ\epsilon we find that tensorial quantities transform at zeroth, first and second order, respectively, as [121, 26]

𝐓0~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\bf T}_{0}} =\displaystyle= 𝐓0,\displaystyle{\bf T}_{0}\,, (6.4)
ϵ​δ​𝐓1~\displaystyle\epsilon\widetilde{\delta{\bf T}_{1}} =\displaystyle= ϵ​δ​𝐓1+ϵ​£ξ1​𝐓0,\displaystyle\epsilon{\delta{\bf T}_{1}}+\epsilon{\pounds}_{\xi_{1}}{\bf T}_{0}\,, (6.5)
ϵ2​δ​𝐓2~\displaystyle\epsilon^{2}\widetilde{\delta{\bf T}_{2}} =\displaystyle= ϵ2​(δ​𝐓2+£ξ2​𝐓0+£ξ12​𝐓0+2​£ξ1​δ​𝐓1).\displaystyle\epsilon^{2}\left({\delta{\bf T}_{2}}+{\pounds}_{\xi_{2}}{\bf T}_{0}+{\pounds}^{2}_{\xi_{1}}{\bf T}_{0}+2{\pounds}_{\xi_{1}}{\delta{\bf T}_{1}}\right)\,. (6.6)

Note that the background quantities are not affected by the mapping. We will apply Eqs. (6.5) and (6.6) to scalars, vectors, and tensors after discussing the passive approach next.

Applying the map (6.1) to the coordinate functions xμx^{\mu} we get a relation for the coordinates of a point qq in and a point pp as

xμ​(q)=eξλ​∂∂xλ|p​xμ​(p),{x^{\mu}}({{q}})=e^{\xi^{\lambda}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{\lambda}}\big|_{{p}}}\ x^{\mu}({{p}})\,, (6.7)

where we have used the fact that when acting on scalars £ξ=ξμ​(∂/∂xμ)\pounds_{\xi}=\xi^{\mu}(\partial/\partial x^{\mu}) and the partial derivatives are evaluated at pp. The left-hand-side and the right-hand-side of Eq. (6.7) are evaluated at different points. Equation (6.7) can then be expanded up to second-order as

xμ​(q)=xμ​(p)+ϵ​ξ1μ​(p)+12​ϵ2​(ξ1,νμ​(p)​ξ1ν​(p)+ξ2μ​(p)).\displaystyle{x^{\mu}}(q)=x^{\mu}(p)+\epsilon\xi_{1}^{\mu}(p)+\frac{1}{2}\epsilon^{2}\left(\xi^{\mu}_{1,\nu}(p)\xi_{1}^{~\nu}(p)+\xi_{2}^{\mu}(p)\right)\,. (6.8)

Note that we do not need Eq. (6.8) to calculate how perturbations change under a gauge transformation in the active approach, it simply tells us how the coordinates of the points pp and qq are related in this approach.

6.1.2 Passive approach

In the passive approach we specify the relation between two coordinate systems directly, and then calculate the change in the metric and matter variables when changing from one system to the other. As long as the two coordinate systems are related through a small perturbation, the functional form relating them is quite arbitrary.

However, in order to make contact with the active approach, discussed above, we take Eq. (6.8) as our starting point. Note, that all quantities in the passive approach are evaluated at the same physical point. Equation (6.8) can be rewritten to give a relation between the “old” (untilded) and the “new” (tilde) coordinate systems [26, 108],

xμ~(q)=xμ(q)−ϵξ1μ(q)+ϵ212(ξ1μ(q),νξ1ν(q)−ξ2μ(q)),\widetilde{x^{\mu}}(q)=x^{\mu}(q)-\epsilon\xi_{1}^{\mu}(q)+\epsilon^{2}\frac{1}{2}\left({\xi^{\mu}_{1}(q)}_{,\nu}\xi_{1}^{~\nu}(q)-\xi_{2}^{\mu}(q)\right)\,, (6.9)

evaluated at the same physical point qq.

The passive point of view is very popular at first order, see e.g. the original paper by Bardeen [7] and the widely used reviews by Kodama and Sasaki [66], and Mukhanov, Feldman, and Brandenberger [123].

The starting point in the passive approach is to identify an invariant quantity, that allows us to relate quantities to be evaluated in the two coordinate systems. We denote the two coordinate systems by x~μ\tilde{x}^{\mu} and xμx^{\mu} system, and their relation is given by Eq. (6.9). We choose as an example the energy density, ρ\rho, which as a four scalar will not change under a coordinate transformation. However, once it has been split into the background quantity and perturbation at different orders, these variables will change.

The two coordinate systems are related by Eq. (6.9), which we can use to expand the right-hand-side of Eq. (6.11) in a Taylor expansion up to second order. To first order, the two coordinate systems are simply related, using the linear part of Eq. (6.8), by

x~μ=xμ−ξ1μ.\tilde{x}^{\mu}=x^{\mu}-\xi_{1}^{\mu}\,. (6.10)

We get the transformation behaviour of the density perturbation, δ​ρ\delta\rho, from the requirement that the total density, ρ=ρ0+δ​ρ\rho=\rho_{0}+\delta\rho, has to be invariant under a change of coordinate system and therefore has to be the same in the x~μ\tilde{x}^{\mu} and the xμx^{\mu} system, that is

ρ~​(x~μ)=ρ⁡(xμ).\tilde{\rho}(\tilde{x}^{\mu})=\rho(x^{\mu})\,. (6.11)

Expanding both sides of Eq. (6.11) using Eq. (2.1), we get

ρ⁡(xμ)\displaystyle\rho(x^{\mu}) =\displaystyle= ρ0​(x0)+ϵ​δ​ρ1​(xμ)+O⁡(ϵ2),\displaystyle\rho_{0}(x^{0})+\epsilon\delta\rho_{1}(x^{\mu})+O(\epsilon^{2})\,, (6.12)
ρ~​(x~μ)\displaystyle\widetilde{\rho}(\tilde{x}^{\mu}) =\displaystyle= ρ0​(x0~)+ϵ​δ​ρ1~​(xμ~)+O⁡(ϵ2),\displaystyle\rho_{0}\left(\widetilde{x^{0}}\right)+\epsilon\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1}}\left(\widetilde{x^{\mu}}\right)+O(\epsilon^{2})\,, (6.13)
=\displaystyle= ρ0​(x0)+ϵ⁡(−ρ0′​(x0)​ξ10​(xμ)+δ​ρ1~​(xμ))+O⁡(ϵ2).\displaystyle\rho_{0}(x^{0})+\epsilon\left(-\rho_{0}^{\prime}(x^{0})\xi_{1}^{0}(x^{\mu})+\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1}}(x^{\mu})\right)+O(\epsilon^{2})\,.

Note that we use the same background solution ρ0​(η)\rho_{0}(\eta) in both expressions. Thus we obtain the transformation rule at first order

δ​ρ1~=δ​ρ1+ρ0′​ξ10.\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1}}=\delta\rho_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\xi_{1}^{0}\,. (6.14)

Another invariant is the line element d​s2ds^{2}, which allows us to deduce the transformation properties of the metric tensor by exploiting the invariance of d​s2ds^{2}, i.e.,

d​s2=g~μ​ν​d​x~μ​d​x~ν=gμ​ν​d​xμ​d​xν,ds^{2}=\tilde{g}_{\mu\nu}d\tilde{x}^{\mu}d\tilde{x}^{\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}dx^{\nu}\,, (6.15)

We here will not follow this approach further here, but see e.g. [66, 104].

6.2 Four-scalars

We now return to the active approach by studying the simplest tensorial quantity, the four-scalar. Examples of four-scalar are the energy density, ρ\rho, and the scalar field φ{\varphi}, and we shall use the former below.

From Eqs. (2.1) and (2.2) we immediately get the perturbed four-scalar up to second order

ρ=ρ0+δ​ρ1+12​δ​ρ2,\rho=\rho_{0}+\delta\rho_{1}+\frac{1}{2}\delta\rho_{2}\,, (6.16)

using the energy density as an example.

6.2.1 First order

Before we can study the transformation behaviour of the perturbations at first order, we split the generating vector ξ1μ\xi_{1}^{\mu} into a scalar temporal part α1\alpha_{1} and a spatial scalar and vector part, β1\beta_{1} and γ1i{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}, according to

ξ1μ=(α1,β1,i+γ1i),\xi_{1}^{\mu}=\left(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1,}^{~~i}+{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}\right)\,, (6.17)

where the vector part is divergence-free ∂kγ1k=0\partial_{k}{\gamma_{{1}}^{~k}}=0.

Under a first-order transformation a four scalar, here the energy density, ρ\rho, then transforms from Eqs. (6.5) and (1.29) as,

δ​ρ1~=δ​ρ1+ρ0′​α1.\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1}}={\delta\rho_{1}}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}\,. (6.18)

The first-order density perturbation is fully specified by prescribing the first order temporal gauge or time slicing, α1\alpha_{1}.

6.2.2 Second order

At second order, as at first order, we split the generating vector ξ2μ\xi_{2}^{\mu} into a scalar time and scalar and vector spatial part, similarly as at first order, as

ξ2μ=(α2,β2,i+γ2i),\xi_{2}^{\mu}=\left(\alpha_{2},\beta_{2,}^{~~i}+{\gamma_{{2}}^{~i}}\right)\,, (6.19)

where the vector part is divergence-free ∂kγ2k=0\partial_{k}{\gamma_{{2}}^{~k}}=0. We then find from Eqs. (6.6) and (1.29) that a four scalar transforms as

δ​ρ2~=δ​ρ2+ρ0′​α2\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{2}}={\delta\rho_{2}}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\alpha_{2} +\displaystyle+ α1​(ρ0′′​α1+ρ0′​α1′+2​δ​ρ1′)\displaystyle\alpha_{1}\left(\rho_{0}^{\prime\prime}\alpha_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}{\alpha_{1}}^{\prime}+2{\delta\rho_{1}}^{\prime}\right) (6.20)
+\displaystyle+ (2δρ1+ρ0′α1),k(β1,k+γ1k).\displaystyle\left(2{\delta\rho_{1}}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}{\alpha_{1}}\right)_{,k}(\beta_{1,}^{~~k}+{\gamma_{{1}}^{~k}})\,.

We see here already the coupling between vector and scalar perturbations in the last term through the gradient and γ1i{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}. The gauge is only specified once the scalar temporal gauge perturbations at first and second order, α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, and the first order spatial gauge perturbations, β1\beta_{1} and γ1i{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}, are specified.

6.3 Four-vectors

We now turn to four-vectors and their transformation properties. Of particular interest in cosmology is the unit four-velocity uμu^{\mu}, which we defined in Section 4 above 11 1 Note that under a gauge transformation the vector field normal to the constant-η\eta hypersurface, nμn^{\mu} defined in section 3.1, will be replaced by a new vector field normal to the constant-η~\tilde{\eta} hypersurfaces, therefore it is not particularly helpful to study the transformation of nμn^{\mu}. We will study the gauge transformation of the metric tensor in section 6.4, from which we can derive the transformation rules for the hypersurface-orthogonal field and its expansion, shear, etc..

6.3.1 First order

A four-vector transforms at first order, using Eqs. (6.5) and (1.30), as

δ​𝒰1​μ~=δ​𝒰1​μ+𝒰(0)​μ′​α1+𝒰(0)​λ​ξ1,μλ,\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta{\cal{U}}_{1\mu}}=\delta{\cal{U}}_{1\mu}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1,\mu}\,, (6.21)

where we used the fact that in a FRW spacetime background quantities are time dependent only.

For the specific example of the four-velocity, defined in Eq. (4), we find,

v1​i~+B1​i~=v1​i+B1​i−α1,i.\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1i}}+\widetilde{B_{1i}}={v_{1i}}+{B_{1i}}-\alpha_{1,i}\,. (6.22)

Using the transformation of the metric perturbation B1​iB_{1i}, given below in Eq. (6.30), and using the decompositions given in Section 2.2.1 above, we get the transformations for the scalar and vector parts, respectively, at first order

v1~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1}} =\displaystyle= v1−β1′,\displaystyle v_{1}-\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,, (6.23)
vvec⁡(1)i~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{\rm{vec}(1)}^{i}} =\displaystyle= vvec⁡(1)i−γ1i′,\displaystyle v_{\rm{vec}(1)}^{i}-{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}^{\prime}\,, (6.24)

and the perturbed temporal part of uμu^{\mu} does indeed transform as a scalar.

6.3.2 Second order

At second order we find that a four-vector transforms, using Eqs. (6.6) and (1.30), as

δ​𝒰2​μ~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta{\cal{U}}_{2\mu}} =\displaystyle= δ​𝒰2​μ+𝒰(0)​μ′​α2+𝒰(0)​0​α2,μ+𝒰(0)​μ′′​α12+𝒰(0)​μ′​α1,λ​ξ1λ\displaystyle\delta{\cal{U}}_{2\mu}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}^{\prime}\alpha_{2}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)0}\alpha_{2,\mu}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}^{\prime\prime}\alpha_{1}^{2}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}^{\prime}\alpha_{1,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1} (6.25)
+2​𝒰(0)​0′​α1​α1,μ+𝒰(0)​0​(ξ1λ​α1,μ​λ+α1,λ​ξ1,μλ)+2​(δ​𝒰1​μ,λ​ξ1λ+δ​𝒰1​λ​ξ1,μλ),\displaystyle+2{\cal{U}}_{(0)0}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}\alpha_{1,\mu}+{\cal{U}}_{(0)0}\left(\xi^{\lambda}_{1}\alpha_{1,\mu\lambda}+\alpha_{1,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1,\mu}\right)+2\left(\delta{\cal{U}}_{1\mu,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1}+\delta{\cal{U}}_{1\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1,\mu}\right)\,,

where as before we used for the background 𝒰(0)​μ≡𝒰(0)​μ​(η){\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}\equiv{\cal{U}}_{(0)\mu}(\eta) and 𝒰(0)​i=𝟎{\cal{U}}_{(0)i}=\bm{\mathrm{{0}}}.

Focusing again on the four-velocity, Eq. (4), and following a similar procedure as at first order, we find that the second order combined scalar and vector spatial part transforms as

v2​i~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{2i}} =\displaystyle= v2​i−ξ2​i′+𝒳vi,\displaystyle v_{2i}-\xi^{\prime}_{2i}+{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}_{i}\,, (6.26)

where 𝒳vi{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}_{i} contains the terms quadratic in the first order perturbations and is given by

𝒳vi≡\displaystyle{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}_{i}\equiv ξ1​i′​(2​ϕ1+α1′+2​ℋ​α1)−α1​ξ1​i′′\displaystyle\xi^{\prime}_{1i}\left(2{\phi_{{1}}}+\alpha_{1}^{\prime}+2{\cal H}\alpha_{1}\right)-\alpha_{1}\xi^{\prime\prime}_{1i} (6.27)
−ξ1kξ1​i,k′+ξ1k′ξ1​i,k−2α1(v1​i′+ℋv1​i)+2v1​i,kξ1k−2v1kξ1​i,k,\displaystyle-\xi_{1}^{k}\xi^{\prime}_{1i,k}+\xi_{1}^{k\prime}\xi_{1i,k}-2\alpha_{1}\left(v_{1i}^{\prime}+{\cal H}v_{1i}\right)+2v_{1i,k}\xi_{1}^{k}-2v_{1}^{k}\xi_{1i,k}\,,

and we already substituted for the transformation of the metric perturbation B2​iB_{2i}, given below in Eq. (6.48). Decomposing then the second order velocity transformation, Eq. (6.26), into scalar and vector parts, we get the transformations as

v2~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{2}} =\displaystyle= v2−β2′+∇−2𝒳vk,k,\displaystyle v_{2}-\beta_{2}^{\prime}+\nabla^{-2}{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}^{k}_{~,k}\,, (6.28)
vvec⁡(2)i~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{\rm{vec}(2)}^{i}} =\displaystyle= vvec⁡(2)i−γ2i′+𝒳vi−∇−2𝒳vk,ki.\displaystyle v_{\rm{vec}(2)}^{i}-{\gamma_{{2}}^{~i}}^{\prime}+{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}_{i}-\nabla^{-2}{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{v}}}^{k}_{~,ki}\,. (6.29)

6.4 Tensors

6.4.1 First order coordinate transformation

We can now calculate how the first order metric perturbations change under a gauge transformation. We get the change of the δ(1)​g00\delta^{(1)}g_{00} and hence the lapse function ϕ1{\phi_{{1}}} immediately from Eqs. (6.5) and (1.31), since this component of the metric is scalar in nature. The change of the δ(1)​g0​i\delta^{(1)}g_{0i} slightly more involved, since this component contains scalar and vector perturbations. We therefore have to compute the overall transformation of this metric component using Eqs. (6.5) and (1.31), and then split the result for B1​iB_{1i} into its scalar part, B1B_{1}, and its divergence-free part −Si-S_{i}. We therefore get for the combined part B1​iB_{1i},

B~1​i\displaystyle\widetilde{B}_{1i} =\displaystyle= B1​i+ξ1​i′−α1,i,\displaystyle B_{1i}+\xi_{1i}^{\prime}-\alpha_{1,i}\,, (6.30)

and taking the divergence gives for the scalar part,

∇2B~1\displaystyle\nabla^{2}\widetilde{B}_{1} =\displaystyle= ∇2B1+∇2β1′−∇2α1,\displaystyle\nabla^{2}B_{1}+\nabla^{2}\beta_{1}^{\prime}-\nabla^{2}\alpha_{1}\,, (6.31)

which, after “removal” of the Laplacian gives the transformation behaviour of B1B_{1}. We can then subtract the scalar part from Eq. (6.31) and are left with the vector part. The results are given below.

To get the change of the metric functions in the spatial part of the metric under a gauge transformation, we again first use Eqs. (6.5) and (1.31) to get transformation of the spatial part of the metric δ(1)​gi​j\delta^{(1)}g_{ij}, or C1​i​jC_{1ij},

2​C~1​i​j=2​C1​i​j+2​ℋ​α1​δi​j+ξ1​i,j+ξ1​j,i,\displaystyle 2\widetilde{C}_{1ij}=2C_{1ij}+2{\cal H}\alpha_{1}\delta_{ij}+\xi_{1i,j}+\xi_{1j,i}\,, (6.32)

where we reproduce Eq. (2.12) above for convenience,

2​C1​i​j=−2​ψ1​δi​j+2​E1,i​j+2​F1​(i,j)+h1​i​j.2C_{1ij}=-2\psi_{1}\delta_{ij}+2E_{1,ij}+2F_{1(i,j)}+h_{1ij}\,.

Taking the trace of Eq. (6.32) we get

−3​ψ~1+∇2E~1=−3​ψ1+∇2E1+3​ℋ​α1+∇2β1.\displaystyle-3\widetilde{\psi}_{1}+\nabla^{2}\widetilde{E}_{1}=-3\psi_{1}+\nabla^{2}E_{1}+3{\cal H}\alpha_{1}+\nabla^{2}\beta_{1}\,. (6.33)

Now applying the operator ∂i∂j\partial^{i}\partial^{j} to Eq. (6.32) we get a second equation relating the scalar perturbation ψ1\psi_{1} and E1E_{1},

−3​∇~2​ψ1+∇2∇2​E~1=−3​∇2ψ1+∇2∇2​E1+3​ℋ​∇2α1+∇2∇2​β1.\displaystyle-3\widetilde{\nabla}^{2}\psi_{1}+\nabla^{2}\nabla^{2}\widetilde{E}_{1}=-3\nabla^{2}\psi_{1}+\nabla^{2}\nabla^{2}E_{1}+3{\cal H}\nabla^{2}\alpha_{1}+\nabla^{2}\nabla^{2}\beta_{1}\,. (6.34)

Taking the divergence of Eq. (6.32) we get

2​C~1​i​j,j=2​C1​i​j,j+2​ℋ​α1,i+∇2ξ1​i+∇2β1,i.\displaystyle 2\widetilde{C}_{1ij,}^{~~~j}=2C_{1ij,}^{~~~j}+2{\cal H}\alpha_{1,i}+\nabla^{2}\xi_{1i}+\nabla^{2}\beta_{1,i}\,. (6.35)

Substituting in our results for ψ~1\widetilde{\psi}_{1} and E~1\widetilde{E}_{1} we arrive at

∇2F~1​i=∇2F1​i+∇2γ1i.\nabla^{2}\widetilde{F}_{1i}=\nabla^{2}F_{1i}+\nabla^{2}{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}\,. (6.36)

We can sum up the transformations of the first order metric perturbations we have from the above, first for the scalars as

ϕ1~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\phi_{{1}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ1+ℋ​α1+α1′,\displaystyle{\phi_{{1}}}+{\cal H}\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{1}^{\prime}\,, (6.37)
ψ~1\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi}_{1} =\displaystyle= ψ1−ℋ​α1,\displaystyle\psi_{1}-{\cal H}\alpha_{1}\,, (6.38)
B~1\displaystyle\widetilde{B}_{1} =\displaystyle= B1−α1+β1′,\displaystyle B_{1}-\alpha_{1}+\beta_{1}^{\prime}\,, (6.39)
E~1\displaystyle\widetilde{E}_{1} =\displaystyle= E1+β1,\displaystyle E_{1}+\beta_{1}\,, (6.40)

and for the vector perturbations as

S1i~\displaystyle\widetilde{S_{1}^{~i}} =\displaystyle= S1i−γ1i′,\displaystyle S_{1}^{~i}-{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}^{\prime}\,, (6.41)
F1i~\displaystyle\widetilde{F_{1}^{~i}} =\displaystyle= F1i+γ1i.\displaystyle F_{1}^{~i}+{\gamma_{{1}}^{~i}}\,. (6.42)

The first order tensor perturbation is found to be gauge-invariant,

h~1​i​j=h1​i​j.\widetilde{h}_{1ij}=h_{1ij}\,. (6.43)

by substituting Eqs. (6.37) to (6.42) into Eq. (6.32).

For later use, we note that the scalar shear potential, σ1=E1′−B1{\sigma}_{1}=E_{1}^{\prime}-B_{1}, defined in Eq. (3.15) above, and the combination v1+B1v_{1}+B_{1} corresponding to the momentum scalar, transform as

σ1~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\sigma}_{1}} =\displaystyle= σ1+α1,\displaystyle{\sigma}_{1}+\alpha_{1}\,, (6.44)
v1~+B1~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1}}+\widetilde{B_{1}} =\displaystyle= v1+B1−α1.\displaystyle v_{1}+B_{1}-\alpha_{1}\,. (6.45)

6.4.2 Second order gauge transformations

The metric tensor transforms at second order, from Eqs. (6.6) and (1.31), as

δ​gμ​ν(2)~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta g^{(2)}_{\mu\nu}} =\displaystyle= δ​gμ​ν(2)+gμ​ν,λ(0)​ξ2λ+gμ​λ(0)​ξ2,νλ+gλ​ν(0)​ξ2,μλ+2​[δ​gμ​ν,λ(1)​ξ1λ+δ​gμ​λ(1)​ξ1,νλ+δ​gλ​ν(1)​ξ1,μλ]\displaystyle\delta g^{(2)}_{\mu\nu}+g^{(0)}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{2}+g^{(0)}_{\mu\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{2~,\nu}+g^{(0)}_{\lambda\nu}\xi^{\lambda}_{2~,\mu}+2\Big[\delta g^{(1)}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1}+\delta g^{(1)}_{\mu\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\nu}+\delta g^{(1)}_{\lambda\nu}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\mu}\Big] (6.46)
+gμ​ν,λ​α(0)​ξ1λ​ξ1α+gμ​ν,λ(0)​ξ1,αλ​ξ1α+2​[gμ​λ,α(0)​ξ1α​ξ1,νλ+gλ​ν,α(0)​ξ1α​ξ1,μλ+gλ​α(0)​ξ1,μλ​ξ1,να]\displaystyle+g^{(0)}_{\mu\nu,\lambda\alpha}\xi^{\lambda}_{1}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}+g^{(0)}_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}+2\Big[g^{(0)}_{\mu\lambda,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\nu}+g^{(0)}_{\lambda\nu,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\mu}+g^{(0)}_{\lambda\alpha}\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\mu}\xi^{\alpha}_{1~,\nu}\Big]
+gμ​λ(0)​(ξ1,ν​αλ​ξ1α+ξ1,αλ​ξ1,να)+gλ​ν(0)​(ξ1,μ​αλ​ξ1α+ξ1,αλ​ξ1,μα).\displaystyle+g^{(0)}_{\mu\lambda}\left(\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\nu\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}+\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1,~\nu}\right)+g^{(0)}_{\lambda\nu}\left(\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\mu\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1}+\xi^{\lambda}_{1~,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{1,~\mu}\right)\,.

As at first order, in the previous subsection, we get the transformation behaviour for the second order lapse function ϕ2{\phi_{{2}}} straight from the 0−00-0 component of Eq. (6.46), which gives

ϕ2~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\phi_{{2}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ2+ℋ​α2+α2′+α1​[α1′′+5​ℋ​α1′+(ℋ′+2​ℋ2)​α1+4​ℋ​ϕ1+2​ϕ1′]\displaystyle{\phi_{{2}}}+{\cal H}\alpha_{2}+{\alpha_{2}}^{\prime}+\alpha_{1}\left[{\alpha_{1}}^{\prime\prime}+5{\cal H}{\alpha_{1}}^{\prime}+\left({\cal H}^{\prime}+2{\cal H}^{2}\right)\alpha_{1}+4{\cal H}\phi_{1}+2\phi_{1}^{\prime}\right] (6.47)
+2α1′(α1′+2ϕ1)+ξ1​k(α1′+ℋα1+2ϕ1),k\displaystyle+2{\alpha_{1}}^{\prime}\left({\alpha_{1}}^{\prime}+2\phi_{1}\right)+\xi_{1k}\left({\alpha_{1}}^{\prime}+{\cal H}{\alpha_{1}}+2\phi_{1}\right)_{,}^{~k}
+ξ1​k′​[α1,k−2​B1​k−ξ1k′].\displaystyle+\xi_{1k}^{\prime}\left[\alpha_{1,}^{~k}-2B_{1k}-{\xi_{1}^{k}}^{\prime}\right]\,.

The combined scalar and vector 0−i0-i metric part transforms from Eqs. (6.6) and (1.31) as

B~2​i\displaystyle\widetilde{B}_{2i} =\displaystyle= B2​i+ξ2​i′−α2,i+𝒳Bi,\displaystyle B_{2i}+\xi_{2i}^{\prime}-\alpha_{2,i}+{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{B}}}_{i}\,, (6.48)

where B2​iB_{2i} is similarly vector and scalar combined, and we defined 𝒳Bi{{\cal{X}}_{\rm{B}}}_{i} to contain the terms quadratic in the first order perturbations, as
