Although the second-order tensor transformation h2​i​jh_{2ij} is not dependent on the second-order part of the gauge transformation, ξ2μ\xi_{2}^{\mu}, it does depend on first order quantities quadratically. The tensor metric perturbations are no longer gauge-invariant at second and higher order.

6.4.3 The large scale or small kk limit

From Eqs. (6.20), (6.58), and (6.47) we see that on large scales, where gradient terms can be neglected, the definition of the second order perturbations in the “new” coordinate is independent of the spatial coordinate choice (the “threading”) at second order in the gradients. It is therefore sufficient on large scales (at O⁡(k2)O(k^{2})) to specify the time slicing by prescribing α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2}, in order to define gauge-invariant variables [110, 98, 107]. The procedure to neglect the gradient terms, is explained in detail in Ref. [98]. For the approximation to hold one assumes that each quantity can be treated as smooth on some sufficiently large scale. Formally one multiplies each spatial gradient ∂i\partial_{i} by a fictitious parameter kk, and expands the exact equations as a power series in kk, keeping only the zero- and first-order terms, finally setting k=1k=1.

7 Gauge-invariant variables

The notion of invariance under coordinate reparametrisation is central to Einstein’s theory of general relativity. This is both a blessing and a curse in the study of cosmological perturbations. We are free to pick coordinate systems best adapted to the problem at hand, but we also obtain apparently different results depending upon this arbitrary choice of coordinates. This is the gauge problem.

Ultimately physical observables are not dependent on the choice of coordinate, though observables may be different for different observers. All one can do is to specify quantities unambiguously, such that they have a gauge-invariant definition. This is not the same as gauge independence. A quantity like the tensor metric perturbation, h1​i​jh_{1ij}, is truly gauge independent at first order in that the tensor part of the metric perturbation is the same in all gauges. The scalar curvature perturbation, ψ1\psi_{1}, on the other hand is intrinsically gauge-dependent. It is different under different time slicings. (Indeed in the spatially flat slicing the curvature perturbation is zero by construction.) One can construct gauge-invariant combinations, which may be referred to as the gauge-invariant curvature perturbation, but they only correspond with the curvature perturbation in one particular gauge. As a result one can find in the literature many different gauge-invariant curvature perturbations corresponding to the many different choices of gauge, such as Ψ\Psi, ζ\zeta and ℛ{{\cal{R}}}, corresponding to the curvature perturbation in the longitudinal, the uniform density, and the comoving gauge, respectively, to name just three.

In this section we shall show how different gauge invariant combinations of otherwise gauge dependent quantities can be constructed by fixing the otherwise arbitrary coordinate transformations at first order and beyond, yielding gauge invariant definitions of the physical perturbations in specified gauges. Residual gauge degrees of freedom only remain in cases where the coordinate choice is not unambiguously fixed, as in the synchronous gauge.

At first order the tensor metric perturbation, h1​i​jh_{1ij}, is not affected by the mapping, or by the change of coordinate system, and hence is gauge-invariant. Thus we only have to construct gauge-invariant scalar and vector perturbations at first order. However at second order the tensor part of the metric perturbation also becomes gauge-dependent.

At first order we can define scalar and vector type gauge-invariant variables independently of each other, but matters are more complicated at second order. Whereas we can still specify the “proper” second order scalar and vector slicings and threadings independently, we now also have to specify the first order gauge functions of both types simultaneously.

We could specify different gauges at first and second order, but we would be losing the physical interpretation of the quantity thus constructed. We therefore choose the same gauge at first and second order, and at first order the same physical gauge condition for the scalar and vector gauge functions. It is however sometimes necessary to combine different temporal and spatial gauge conditions. For example imposing the uniform density condition only specifies the slicing, and we are free to combine it with a flat threading.

7.1 Longitudinal gauge

7.1.1 First order

The gauge-dependence of the metric perturbations lead Bardeen [7] to propose that only quantities that are explicitly invariant under gauge transformations should be considered. By studying the transformation Eqs. (6.37–6.40), Bardeen22 2 In Bardeen’s notation these gauge-invariant perturbations are given as Φ≡ΦA​Q(0)\Phi\equiv\Phi_{A}Q^{(0)} and Ψ≡−ΦH​Q(0)\Psi\equiv-\Phi_{H}Q^{(0)}. constructed two such quantities [7]

Φ\displaystyle\Phi ≡\displaystyle\equiv ϕ1+ℋ⁡(B1−E1′)+(B1−E1′)′,\displaystyle{\phi_{{1}}}+{\cal H}(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime})+(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime})^{\prime}\,, (7.1)
Ψ\displaystyle\Psi ≡\displaystyle\equiv ψ1−ℋ⁡(B1−E1′).\displaystyle\psi_{1}-{\cal H}\left(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime}\right)\,. (7.2)

These turn out to coincide with the scalar metric perturbations in a particular gauge, called variously the orthogonal zero-shear [7, 66], conformal Newtonian [21, 101] or longitudinal gauge [123]. It may therefore appear that this gauge is somehow preferred over other gauge choices. However any unambiguous choice of time-slicing and threading can be used to define explicitly gauge-invariant perturbations. The longitudinal gauge of Ref. [123] provides but one example.

The two scalar gauge functions, α\alpha and β\beta defined in Eq. (6.17), which represent different choices of time-slicings (choice of spatial hypersurfaces) and threading (choice of spatial coordinates on these hypersurfaces) respectively, allow two of the scalar metric perturbations to be eliminated, implying that the two remaining gauge-invariant combinations should then be gauge-invariant. If we choose to work on spatial hypersurfaces with vanishing shear, we find from Eqs. (6.39),(6.40) and (3.15) that the shear scalar transforms as σ1~=σ1+α1\widetilde{\sigma_{1}}=\sigma_{1}+\alpha_{1} and this implies that to obtain perturbations in the longitudinal gauge starting from arbitrary coordinates we should perform a transformation

α1​ℓ=−σ1=B1−E1′.\alpha_{1\ell}=-{\sigma}_{1}=B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime}\,. (7.3)

This is sufficient to determine the geometrical perturbations ϕ1\phi_{1}, ψ1\psi_{1}, σ1\sigma_{1} or other scalar quantities on these hypersurfaces. In addition, the longitudinal gauge is completely determined by the spatial gauge choice E1​ℓ~=0\widetilde{E_{1\ell}}=0 [and hence from Eq. (7.3) B1​ℓ~=0\widetilde{B_{1\ell}}=0] which requires from Eq. (6.40)

β1​ℓ=−E1.\beta_{1\ell}=-E_{1}\,. (7.4)

The remaining scalar metric perturbations, ϕ1\phi_{1} and ψ1\psi_{1}, are given from Eqs. (6.37) and (6.38) as

ϕ1​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\phi}_{1\ell}} =\displaystyle= ϕ1+ℋ⁡(B1−E1′)+(B1−E1′)′,\displaystyle{\phi_{{1}}}+{\cal H}(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime})+(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime})^{\prime}\,, (7.5)
ψ1​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi_{1\ell}} =\displaystyle= ψ1−ℋ⁡(B1−E1′),\displaystyle\psi_{1}-{\cal H}\left(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime}\right)\,, (7.6)

Note that ϕ1​ℓ~\widetilde{{\phi}_{1\ell}} and ψ1​ℓ~\widetilde{\psi_{1\ell}} are then identical to Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi defined in Eqs. (7.1) and (7.2).

The fluid density perturbation, δ​ρ1\delta\rho_{1}, and scalar velocity, v1v_{1}, are given from (6.18) and (6.23)

δ​ρ1​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1\ell}} =\displaystyle= δ​ρ1+ρ0′​(B1−E1′),\displaystyle\delta\rho_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\left(B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime}\right)\,, (7.7)
v1​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1\ell}} =\displaystyle= v1+E1′.\displaystyle v_{1}+E_{1}^{\prime}\,. (7.8)

These gauge-invariant quantities are simply a gauge-invariant definition of the perturbations in the longitudinal gauge.

This gauge is widely used, for example, throughout Ref. [123]. It has also proven useful for calculations on small scales, since it gives evolution equations closest to the Newtonian ones, e.g. Ref. [54]. Recently it has also become popular in backreaction studies, e.g. [19, 71, 170]. After imposing the gauge-conditions the metric tensor is diagonal, which simplifies many calculations, for example the derivation of the governing equations of the Boltzmann-hierarchy. Moreover we shall show in Section 8 that in many cases of physical interest (in the absence of anisotropic stress) one finds Φ=Ψ\Phi=\Psi and there is only one variable required to describe all scalar metric perturbations.

However, it can be difficult to define quantities in this gauge in the super-horizon limit, since in the super-horizon limit the shear vanishes and hence numerical instabilities can occur on large scales in the longitudinal gauge, see e.g. Refs. [101, 60, 82].

The extension to include vector and tensor metric perturbations is called the Poisson gauge [21, 26]. Tensor metric perturbations are automatically gauge independent at first order (and hence gauge invariant). Eliminating the spatial part of the contravariant vector field nμn^{\mu} in Eq. (3.1) requires both Bℓ~,i\widetilde{B_{\ell}}_{,}^{~i} and Sℓ~i=0\widetilde{S_{\ell}}^{i}=0 which from Eq. (6.41) fixes the vector part of the spatial gauge transformation (6.17)

γ1​ℓi=∫S1i​𝑑η+𝒞^1i​(xj),\gamma_{1\ell}^{i}=\int S_{1}^{i}d\eta+\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}^{i}(x^{j})\,, (7.9)

up to an arbitrary constant 3-vector 𝒞^1i\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}^{i} which depends on the choice of spatial coordinates on an initial hypersurface. The remaining vector metric perturbation is

F1​ℓ~i=F1i′+∫S1idη+𝒞^1i(xj).\widetilde{F_{1\ell}}^{i}=F_{1}^{i\prime}+\int S_{1}^{i}d\eta+\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}^{i}(x^{j})\,. (7.10)

7.1.2 Second order

It is possible to extend the longitudinal, or Poisson, gauge to higher orders. The principle for constructing gauge invariant variables remains the same. We use a physical choice of gauge to specify the vector field ξμ\xi^{\mu} generating the transformation (6.7) from an arbitrary gauge [110, 124]. Requiring first that E2~ℓ=0\widetilde{E_{2}}_{\ell}=0 fixes the scalar part of the spatial gauge using Eq. (6.59), which gives

β2​ℓ=−E2−34∇−2∇−2𝒳i​j,ij+14∇−2𝒳kk.\beta_{2\ell}=-E_{2}-\frac{3}{4}\nabla^{-2}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{ij}_{~~,ij}+\frac{1}{4}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{k}_{~k}\,. (7.11)

Note that having already imposed the Poisson gauge at first order, α1\alpha_{1}, β1\beta_{1} and γ1​i\gamma_{1i} are fixed by Eqs. (7.3), (7.4) and (7.9), and thus so is 𝒳i​j{\cal{X}}_{ij}, given in Eq. (6.54).

Requiring that the scalar part of the perturbed shift function vanishes, B2~ℓ=0\widetilde{B_{2}}_{\ell}=0, then sets the temporal gauge, α2​ℓ\alpha_{2\ell} using Eq. (6.50), while requiring that the vector part vanishes, F2i=𝟎F_{2}^{i}={\bf 0}, can be used along with Eq. (6.62) to fix the vector part of the spatial gauge, γ2​ℓi\gamma_{2\ell}^{i}, up to a constant of integration as at first order, Eq. (7.9).

We then obtain gauge invariant definition of Φ\Phi, Ψ\Psi and other perturbations at second order by substituting these specific gauge transformations into Eq. (6.47) and (6.58) to obtain

ϕ2​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\phi_{{2\ell}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ2+ℋ​α2​ℓ+α2​ℓ′+α1​ℓ​[α1​ℓ′′+5​ℋ​α1​ℓ′+(ℋ′+2​ℋ2)​α1​ℓ+4​ℋ​ϕ1+2​ϕ1′]\displaystyle{\phi_{{2}}}+{\cal H}\alpha_{2\ell}+{\alpha_{2\ell}}^{\prime}+\alpha_{1\ell}\left[{\alpha_{1\ell}}^{\prime\prime}+5{\cal H}{\alpha_{1\ell}}^{\prime}+\left({\cal H}^{\prime}+2{\cal H}^{2}\right)\alpha_{1\ell}+4{\cal H}\phi_{1}+2\phi_{1}^{\prime}\right] (7.12)
+2α1​ℓ′(α1​ℓ′+2ϕ1)+ξ1​ℓ​k(α1​ℓ′+ℋα1​ℓ+2ϕ1),k\displaystyle+2{\alpha_{1\ell}}^{\prime}\left({\alpha_{1\ell}}^{\prime}+2\phi_{1}\right)+\xi_{1\ell k}\left({\alpha_{1\ell}}^{\prime}+{\cal H}{\alpha_{1\ell}}+2\phi_{1}\right)_{,}^{~k}
+ξ1​ℓ​k′​[α1​ℓ,k−2​B1​k−ξ1​ℓk′].\displaystyle+\xi_{1\ell k}^{\prime}\left[\alpha_{1\ell,}^{~k}-2B_{1k}-{\xi_{1\ell}^{k}}^{\prime}\right]\,.
ψ2​ℓ~\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi_{2\ell}} =\displaystyle= ψ2−ℋ​α2​ℓ−14​𝒳ℓ​kk+14​∇−2𝒳ℓ,i​ji​j,\displaystyle\psi_{2}-{\cal H}\alpha_{2\ell}-\frac{1}{4}{\cal{X}}^{~k}_{\ell k}+\frac{1}{4}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{~ij}_{\ell~~,ij}\,, (7.13)

where 𝒳ℓ​i​j{\cal{X}}_{\ell ij} is denotes the quadratic first order terms in Eq. (6.54) using the longitudinal gauge transforms α1​ℓ\alpha_{1\ell} and ξℓ​i\xi_{\ell i}.

The tensor (transverse, tracefree) part of the metric perturbation at second order, hi​jh_{ij} in Eq. (6.63), is not affected by the second order gauge transformations α2\alpha_{2} and ξ2​i\xi_{2i}, but it does depend on the choice of gauge at first order, α1\alpha_{1} and ξ1​i\xi_{1i}. Thus we need to include the corresponding first-order gauge definition to obtain a gauge invariant definition of the tensor metric perturbations at second order.

In particular, recent work on the generation of gravitational waves at second order [117, 126, 5, 18, 16] has calculated the resulting tensor mode in the Poisson gauge. To give a gauge invariant definition of the tensor perturbation in the Poisson gauge one needs to explicitly include the transverse and tracefree (tensor) part of the second order gauge transformation from an arbitrary gauge. From Eqs. (6.63) we obtain the gauge invariant definition of the tensor metric perturbation in the Poisson gauge:

h~2​ℓ​i​j\displaystyle\widetilde{h}_{2\ell ij} =\displaystyle= h2​i​j+𝒳ℓ​i​j+12(∇−2𝒳,klℓ​k​l−𝒳ℓ​kk)δi​j+12∇−2∇−2𝒳,klijℓ​k​l\displaystyle h_{2ij}+{\cal{X}}_{\ell ij}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{\ell kl}_{~~,kl}-{\cal{X}}^{~k}_{\ell k}\right)\delta_{ij}+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{-2}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{\ell kl}_{~~~,klij} (7.14)
+12​∇−2𝒳ℓ​k,i​jk−∇−2(𝒳ℓ​i​k,jk+𝒳ℓ​j​k,ik).\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{~k}_{\ell k,ij}-\nabla^{-2}\left({\cal{X}}_{\ell ik,~~~j}^{~~~~k}+{\cal{X}}_{\ell jk,~~~i}^{~~~~k}\right)\,.

7.2 Spatially flat gauge

7.2.1 First order

An alternative gauge choice, defined purely by local metric quantities is the spatially flat or uniform curvature gauge [66, 62, 63, 65, 161], also called the off-diagonal gauge [27]. In this gauge one selects spatial hypersurfaces on which the induced 3-metric on spatial hypersurfaces is left unperturbed by scalar or vector perturbations, which requires ψ1~=E1~=0\widetilde{\psi_{1}}=\widetilde{E_{1}}=0 and F1~i=𝟎\widetilde{F_{1}}_{i}={\bf 0}. Using Eqs. (6.38), (6.40) and (6.42) this corresponds to a gauge transformation (6.17) where

α1​f​l​a​t=ψ1ℋ,β1​f​l​a​t=−E1,γ1​f​l​a​ti=−F1i.\alpha_{1{\rm{flat}}}=\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\,,\qquad\beta_{1{\rm{flat}}}=-E_{1}\,,\qquad\gamma_{1{\rm{flat}}}^{i}=-F_{1}^{i}\,. (7.15)

The gauge-invariant definitions of the remaining scalar metric degrees of freedom are then from Eqs. (6.37) and (6.39)

ϕ1​f​l​a​t~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\phi}_{1{\rm{flat}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ1+ψ1+(ψ1ℋ)′,\displaystyle{\phi_{{1}}}+\psi_{1}+\left(\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\right)^{\prime}\,, (7.16)
B1​f​l​a​t~\displaystyle\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}} =\displaystyle= B1−E1′−ψ1ℋ.\displaystyle B_{1}-E_{1}^{\prime}-\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\,. (7.17)

These gauge-invariant combinations were denoted 𝒜{\cal A} and ℬ{\cal B} by Kodama and Sasaki [66]. The gauge-invariant definition of the remaining vector metric perturbation is the time derivative of the vector metric perturbation in the Poisson gauge (7.10):

S1​f​l​a​t~i=S1i+F1i′=F1​ℓ~i′.\widetilde{S_{1{\rm{flat}}}}^{i}=S_{1}^{i}+F_{1}^{i\prime}=\widetilde{F_{1\ell}}^{i\prime}\,. (7.18)

Perturbations of scalar quantities in this gauge, such as the density perturbation, have gauge invariant definitions from Eq. (6.18):

δ​ρ1​f​l​a​t~=δ​ρ1+ρ0′​ψ1ℋ,\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=\delta\rho_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\,, (7.19)

and the velocity potential (6.23) is given from Eq. (6.23):

v1​f​l​a​t~=v1+E1′.\widetilde{v_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=v_{1}+E_{1}^{\prime}\,. (7.20)

The shear perturbation in the spatially flat gauge is given by σ1​f​l​a​t~=−B1​f​l​a​t~\widetilde{\sigma_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=-\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}}. This is closely related to the curvature perturbation in the zero-shear (longitudinal) gauge, ψℓ~=Ψ\widetilde{\psi_{\ell}}=\Psi, given in Eqs. (7.2) or (7.6),

B1​f​l​a​t~=−ψ1​ℓ~ℋ=−Ψℋ.\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=-\frac{\widetilde{\psi_{1\ell}}}{{\cal H}}=-\frac{\Psi}{{\cal H}}\,. (7.21)

Gauge-invariant quantities, such as B1​f​l​a​t~\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}} or ψ1​ℓ~\widetilde{\psi_{1\ell}} are proportional to the displacement between two different choices of spatial hypersurface,

B1​f​l​a​t~=−ψ1​ℓ~ℋ=α1​f​l​a​t−α1​ℓ,\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=-\frac{\widetilde{\psi_{1\ell}}}{{\cal H}}=\alpha_{1{\rm{flat}}}-\alpha_{1\ell}\,, (7.22)

which would vanish for a homogeneous cosmology.

In some circumstances it is more convenient to use the spatially-flat gauge-invariant variables instead of those in the longitudinal gauge. For instance, when calculating the evolution of perturbations during a collapsing “pre Big Bang” era the perturbations ϕ1​f​l​a​t~\widetilde{{\phi}_{1{\rm{flat}}}} and B1​f​l​a​t~\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}} may remain small even when Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi become large [27, 39]. On the other hand the metric perturbation B1​f​l​a​t~\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}} grows on large scales in radiation or matter dominated eras, B1​f​l​a​t~∝ℋ−1∝η\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{flat}}}}\propto{\cal H}^{-1}\propto\eta, when the longitudinal gauge metric perturbation Ψ\Psi remains constant.

Note that the scalar field perturbation on spatially flat hypersurfaces,

δ​φ1​f​l​a​t~≡δ​φ1+φ0′​ψ1ℋ,\widetilde{\delta{\varphi}_{1{\rm{flat}}}}\equiv\delta\varphi_{{1}}+\varphi_{0}^{\prime}\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\,, (7.23)

is the gauge-invariant Sasaki-Mukhanov variable [145, 120], often denoted 𝒬{\cal{Q}}.

7.2.2 Second order

At second order we get from the gauge condition ψ2~=0\widetilde{\psi_{2}}=0 using Eq. (6.58)

α2​f​l​a​t=ψ2ℋ+14​ℋ​[∇−2𝒳flat,i​ji​j−𝒳flat​kk],\displaystyle\alpha_{2{\rm{flat}}}=\frac{\psi_{2}}{{\cal H}}+\frac{1}{4{\cal H}}\left[\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{ij}_{{\rm{flat}},ij}-{\cal{X}}^{k}_{{\rm{flat}}k}\right]\,, (7.24)

where we get 𝒳flat​i​j{\cal{X}}_{{\rm{flat}}ij} from Eq. (6.54) using the first order gauge generators given above, as

+1ℋ​[ψ1,i​(2​B1​j+ξ1​f​l​a​t​j′)+ψ1,j​(2​B1​i+ξ1​f​l​a​t​i′)]−2ℋ2​ψ1,i​ψ1,j\displaystyle+\frac{1}{{\cal H}}\Big[\psi_{1,i}\left(2B_{1j}+\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}j}^{\prime}\right)+\psi_{1,j}\left(2B_{1i}+\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}i}^{\prime}\right)\Big]-\frac{2}{{\cal H}^{2}}\psi_{1,i}\psi_{1,j}
+2ℋ​ψ1​(ξ1​f​l​a​t​(i,j)′+4​ℋ​ξ1​f​l​a​t​(i,j))+2​ξ1​f​l​a​tk​ξ1​f​l​a​t​(i,j)​k+2​ξ1​f​l​a​t​k,i​ξ1​f​l​a​t,jk,\displaystyle+\frac{2}{{\cal H}}\psi_{1}\left(\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}(i,j)}^{\prime}+4{\cal H}\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}(i,j)}\right)+2\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}}^{k}\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}(i,j)k}+2\xi_{1{\rm{flat}}k,i}\xi_{1{\rm{flat}},j}^{k}\,,

where we define

The trace of Eq. (7.2.2) is then

The second order tensor perturbation is in the flat gauge

h~2​f​l​a​t​i​j\displaystyle\widetilde{h}_{2{\rm{flat}}ij} =\displaystyle= h2​i​j+𝒳flat​i​j+12​(∇−2𝒳flat,k​lk​l−𝒳flat​kk)​δi​j+12​∇−2​∇−2𝒳flat,k​l​i​jk​l\displaystyle h_{2ij}+{\cal{X}}_{{\rm{flat}}ij}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{kl}_{{\rm{flat}},kl}-{\cal{X}}^{k}_{{\rm{flat}}k}\right)\delta_{ij}+\frac{1}{2}\nabla^{-2}\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{kl}_{{\rm{flat}},klij} (7.29)

As an example of a matter variable we choose the energy density, which in the flat gauge is

δ​ρ2​f​l​a​t~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{2{\rm{flat}}}} =\displaystyle= δ​ρ2+ρ0′ℋ​ψ2+ρ0′4​ℋ​(∇−2𝒳flat,i​ji​j−𝒳flat​kk)\displaystyle{\delta\rho_{2}}+\frac{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}\psi_{2}+\frac{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}{4{\cal H}}\left(\nabla^{-2}{\cal{X}}^{ij}_{{\rm{flat}},ij}-{\cal{X}}^{k}_{{\rm{flat}}k}\right) (7.30)

To show the relation between gauge-invariant perturbations defined in the flat gauge and those previously defined in the longitudinal gauge we note that in the longitudinal gauge we have

2​C1​ℓ~i​j=−2​Ψ​δi​j+2​F1​ℓ~(i,j)+h1​i​j,2\widetilde{C_{1\ell}}_{ij}=-2\Psi\delta_{ij}+2\widetilde{F_{1\ell}}_{(i,j)}+h_{1ij}\,, (7.31)

and the first-order gauge shifts to the flat gauge, Eqs. (7.15), become

α1​f​l​a​t|ℓ=Ψℋ,β1​f​l​a​t|ℓ=0,γ1​f​l​a​ti=−F1​ℓ~i.\alpha_{1{\rm{flat}}}|_{\ell}=\frac{\Psi}{{\cal H}}\,,\qquad\beta_{1{\rm{flat}}}|_{\ell}=0\,,\qquad\gamma_{1{\rm{flat}}}^{i}=-\widetilde{F_{1\ell}}^{i}\,. (7.32)

If we can neglect the first-order vector and tensor perturbations, F1​ℓ~i\widetilde{F_{1\ell}}_{i} and h1​i​jh_{1ij}, then we have

+ρ0′2​ℋ{E1,k​lE1,k​l+∇2E1,kE1,k−2ψ1∇2(E1′ℋ+2E1)−ψ1,kℋ(2B1+E1′−ψ1ℋ),k\displaystyle+\frac{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}{2{\cal H}}\Bigg\{E_{1,kl}E_{1,}^{~kl}+\nabla^{2}E_{1,k}E_{1,}^{~k}-2\psi_{1}\nabla^{2}\left(\frac{E_{1}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}+2E_{1}\right)-\frac{\psi_{1,k}}{{\cal H}}\left(2B_{1}+E_{1}^{\prime}-\frac{\psi_{1}}{{\cal H}}\right)_{,k}

This expression was first derived in Ref. [110], however with a different, incorrect sub-horizon part [133]. On super-horizon scales, where gradient terms can be neglected, we recover the expressions given in Ref. [105].

7.3 Synchronous gauge

The synchronous gauge is defined by ϕ~=B~i=0\widetilde{{\phi}}=\widetilde{B}_{i}=0, so that the proper time for observers at fixed spatial coordinates coincides with cosmic time in the FRW background, i.e., d​τ=a​d​ηd\tau=ad\eta. This simplifies dynamical equations as the time derivatives can be directly related to proper time derivatives. This gauge is very popular for numerical studies, and used in many Boltzmann solvers such as CMBFAST [154]. It is also popular in the older literature [177, 131].

The gauge condition at first order is ϕ1~=B1~i=0\widetilde{{\phi_{{1}}}}=\widetilde{B_{1}}_{i}=0, which from Eqs. (6.37) and (6.39) gives

α1​s​y​n\displaystyle\alpha_{1{\rm{syn}}} =\displaystyle= −1a​(∫a​ϕ1​𝑑η−𝒞1​(xi)),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{a}\left(\int a\phi_{1}d\eta-{\cal{C}}_{1}(x^{i})\right)\,, (7.36)
β1​s​y​n\displaystyle\beta_{1{\rm{syn}}} =\displaystyle= ∫(α1​s​y​n−B1)​𝑑η+𝒞^1​(xi),\displaystyle\int\left(\alpha_{1{\rm{syn}}}-B_{1}\right)d\eta+\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}(x^{i})\,, (7.37)
γ1​s​y​ni\displaystyle\gamma_{1{\rm{syn}}}^{i} =\displaystyle= ∫S1i​𝑑η+𝒞^1i​(xi).\displaystyle\int S_{1}^{i}d\eta+\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}^{i}(x^{i})\,. (7.38)

This does not determine the time-slicing unambiguously and we are left with two arbitrary scalar functions of the spatial coordinates, 𝒞1{\cal{C}}_{1} and 𝒞^1\hat{\cal{C}}_{1}. Note that 𝒞^1,i+𝒞^1​i\hat{\cal{C}}_{1,i}+\hat{\cal{C}}_{1i} affects only the labelling of the coordinates on the initial spatial hypersurface, but 𝒞1{\cal{C}}_{1} affects scalar perturbations on spatial hypersurfaces. We are left with two non-zero geometrical scalar perturbations,

ψ1​s​y​n~\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi_{1{\rm{syn}}}} =\displaystyle= ψ1+ℋa​(∫a​ϕ1​𝑑η−𝒞⁡(xi)),\displaystyle\psi_{1}+\frac{{\cal H}}{a}\left(\int a\phi_{1}d\eta-{\cal{C}}(x^{i})\right)\,, (7.39)
σ~1​s​y​n\displaystyle\widetilde{\sigma}_{1{\rm{syn}}} =\displaystyle= σ1+α1​s​y​n−B1,\displaystyle{\sigma}_{1}+\alpha_{1{\rm{syn}}}-B_{1}\,, (7.40)

and the matter variables are

δ​ρ1​s​y​n~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1{\rm{syn}}}} =\displaystyle= δ​ρ1−ρ0′a​(∫a​ϕ1​𝑑η−𝒞⁡(xi)),\displaystyle\delta\rho_{1}-\frac{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}{a}\left(\int a\phi_{1}d\eta-{\cal{C}}(x^{i})\right)\,, (7.41)
v1​s​y​n~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1{\rm{syn}}}} =\displaystyle= v1+B1−α1​s​y​n.\displaystyle v_{1}+B_{1}-\alpha_{1{\rm{syn}}}\,. (7.42)

Thus it is not possible to define gauge-invariant quantities in general using this gauge condition [114]. This gauge was originally used by Lifshitz in his pioneering work on perturbations in a FRW spacetime [87] (see also Ref. [75]). He dealt with the residual gauge freedom by eliminating the unphysical gauge modes through symmetry arguments.

To remove the ambiguity, we can follow Ref. [28] and choose the initial velocity of cold dark matter to be zero, v1​c​d​m~≡0\widetilde{v_{1{\rm cdm}}}\equiv 0, which fixes the residual gauge freedom

𝒞1​(x)=a⁡(v1​c​d​m+B1).{\cal{C}}_{1}(x)=a(v_{1{\rm cdm}}+B_{1})\,. (7.43)

Note that for pressureless matter, momentum conservation equation ensures that a⁡(v1​c​d​m+B1)a(v_{1{\rm cdm}}+B_{1}) is a constant (see Section 8).

7.4 Comoving orthogonal gauge

The comoving gauge is defined by choosing spatial coordinates such that the 3-velocity of the fluid vanishes, v~i=0\widetilde{v}_{i}=0. Orthogonality of the constant-η\eta hypersurfaces to the 4-velocity, uμu^{\mu}, then requires v~i+B~i=0\widetilde{v}_{i}+\widetilde{B}_{i}=0, which shows that the momentum vanishes as well. From Eqs. (6.39) and (6.23) this implies

α1​c​o​m\displaystyle\alpha_{1{\rm{com}}} =\displaystyle= v1+B1,\displaystyle v_{1}+B_{1}\,,
β1​c​o​m\displaystyle\beta_{1{\rm{com}}} =\displaystyle= ∫v1​𝑑η+𝒞^​(xi),\displaystyle\int v_{1}d\eta+\hat{\cal{C}}(x^{i})\,, (7.44)

where 𝒞^​(xi)\hat{\cal{C}}(x^{i}) represents a residual gauge freedom, corresponding to a constant shift of the spatial coordinates. All the 3-scalars like curvature, expansion, acceleration and shear are independent of 𝒞^​(xi)\hat{\cal{C}}(x^{i}). Applying the above transformation from arbitrary coordinates, the scalar perturbations in the comoving orthogonal gauge can be written as

ϕ1​c​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{{{\phi}}_{1{\rm{com}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ1+ℋ⁡(v1+B1)+(v1′+B1′),\displaystyle{\phi_{{1}}}+{\cal H}\left(v_{1}+B_{1}\right)+\left(v_{1}^{\prime}+B_{1}^{\prime}\right)\,, (7.45)
ℛ≡ψ1​c​o​m~\displaystyle{{\cal{R}}}\equiv\widetilde{\psi_{1{\rm{com}}}} =\displaystyle= ψ1−ℋ⁡(v1+B1),\displaystyle\psi_{1}-{\cal H}\left(v_{1}+B_{1}\right)\,, (7.46)
σ1​c​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{{\sigma}_{1{\rm{com}}}} =\displaystyle= v1+E1′.\displaystyle v_{1}+E_{1}^{\prime}\,. (7.47)

Defined in this way, these combinations are gauge-invariant under transformations of their component parts in exactly the same way as, for instance, Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi defined in Eqs. (7.1) and (7.2).

Note that the curvature perturbation in the comoving gauge given above, Eq. (7.46) was used (with a constant pre-factor) by Lukash [91]. It was later employed by Lyth and denoted ℛ\cal{R} in his seminal paper, [92], and in many subsequent works, e.g. [83] and [86].

The density perturbation on the comoving orthogonal hypersurfaces is given by Eqs. (6.18) and (7.4) in gauge-invariant form as

δ​ρ1​c​o​m~=δ​ρ1+ρ0′​(v1+B1),\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1{\rm{com}}}}=\delta\rho_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\left(v_{1}+B_{1}\right)\,, (7.48)

and corresponds to the gauge-invariant density perturbation ϵm​E0​Q(0)\epsilon_{m}E_{0}Q^{(0)} in the notation of Bardeen [7]. The gauge-invariant scalar density perturbation Δ\Delta introduced in Refs. [25, 46] corresponds to δ​ρ~1​c​o​m,ii/ρ0\delta\tilde{\rho}_{1{\rm{com}},i}^{~~~i}/\rho_{0}.

If we wish to write these gauge-invariant quantities in terms of the metric perturbations rather than the velocity potential then we can use the Einstein equations, presented in section 8, to obtain

v1+B1=ℋ​ϕ1+ψ1′ℋ′−ℋ2.v_{1}+B_{1}=\frac{{\cal H}\phi_{1}+\psi_{1}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}\,. (7.49)

In particular we note that we can write the comoving curvature perturbation, given in Eq. (7.46), in terms of the longitudinal gauge-invariant quantities as

ℛ=Ψ−ℋ⁡(ℋ​Φ+Ψ′)ℋ′−ℋ2,{{\cal{R}}}=\Psi-\frac{{\cal H}({\cal H}\Phi+\Psi^{\prime})}{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}\,, (7.50)

which coincides the quantity denoted ζ\zeta by Mukhanov, Feldman and Brandenberger in Ref. [123].

By comparing the definitions of the energy-momentum tensor for a single fluid and a single scalar field in Sections 4.1 and 5.1 we can relate the v1+B1v_{1}+B_{1} to δ​φ1\delta\varphi_{{1}}, which allows one to rewrite the definition of the comoving curvature perturbations, Eq. (7.46), as

ℛ=ψ1+ℋφ0′​δ​φ1.{{\cal{R}}}=\psi_{1}+\frac{{\cal H}}{{\varphi}_{0}^{\prime}}\delta\varphi_{{1}}\,. (7.51)

From the definition above we immediately that the comoving curvature perturbation is related to the field fluctuation on flat slices, defined in Eq. (7.23), by

δ​φ1​f​l​a​t~=φ0′ℋ​ℛ.\widetilde{{\delta\varphi}_{1{\rm{flat}}}}=\frac{\varphi_{0}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}{{\cal{R}}}\,. (7.52)

For extensions to the multi-field case see Section 8.2.4.

7.5 Total matter gauge

This gauge is also known as the velocity orthogonal isotropic gauge [66] but here we follow the terminology of Ref. [84]. It is closely related to comoving orthogonal and longitudinal gauges.

To fix the temporal gauge we require the total momentum potential on spatial hypersurfaces to vanish

v1~+B1~=0.\widetilde{v_{1}}+\widetilde{B_{1}}=0\,. (7.53)

In addition we require E1~=0\widetilde{E_{1}}=0 and F1~i=0\widetilde{F_{1}}_{i}=0, which fixes the spatial gauge. These require

α1​t​o​m=v1+B1,β1​t​o​m=−E1,γ1​t​o​mi=−F1i.\displaystyle\alpha_{1{\rm{tom}}}=v_{1}+B_{1}\,,\qquad\beta_{1{\rm{tom}}}=-E_{1}\,,\qquad\gamma_{1{\rm{tom}}}^{i}=-F_{1}^{i}\,. (7.54)

We therefore get the metric perturbations in the total matter gauge related to the comoving orthogonal and longitudinal gauge perturbations:

ϕ1​t​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{{{\phi}}_{1{\rm{tom}}}} =\displaystyle= ϕ1​c​o​m~,\displaystyle\widetilde{{{\phi}}_{1{\rm{com}}}}\,, (7.55)
ψ1​t​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi_{1{\rm{tom}}}} =\displaystyle= ψ1​c​o​m~,\displaystyle\widetilde{\psi_{1{\rm{com}}}}\,, (7.56)
B1​t​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{tom}}}} =\displaystyle= −v1​ℓ~,\displaystyle-\widetilde{v_{1\ell}}\,, (7.57)

and for the matter quantities we get in the total matter gauge

δ​ρ1​t​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1{\rm{tom}}}} =\displaystyle= δ​ρ1​c​o​m~,\displaystyle\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1{\rm{com}}}}\,, (7.58)
v1​t​o​m~\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1{\rm{tom}}}} =\displaystyle= v1​ℓ~.\displaystyle\widetilde{v_{1\ell}}\,. (7.59)

Note that in the total matter gauge velocity potential is not identically zero (unlike in the comoving orthogonal gauge), but equal to the shear potential, v1​t​o​m~=σ1​t​o​m~=−B1​t​o​m~\widetilde{v_{1{\rm{tom}}}}=\widetilde{{\sigma}_{1{\rm{tom}}}}=-\widetilde{B_{1{\rm{tom}}}}, which also coincides with velocity potential in longitudinal gauge.

7.6 Uniform density gauge

Alternatively we can use the matter to pick out a foliation of uniform density hypersurfaces on which to define perturbed quantities.

7.6.1 First order

Using Eq. (6.18) we see that δ​ρ1~=0\widetilde{\delta\rho_{1}}=0 implies a temporal gauge transformation

α1​δ​ρ=−δ​ρ1ρ0′.\alpha_{1{\delta\rho}}=-\frac{\delta\rho_{1}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\,. (7.60)

On these hypersurfaces the gauge-invariant curvature perturbation is [40, 114]

−ζ1≡ψ1​δ​ρ~=ψ1+ℋ​δ​ρ1ρ0′.-\zeta_{1}\equiv\widetilde{\psi_{1{\delta\rho}}}=\psi_{1}+{\cal H}\frac{\delta\rho_{1}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\,. (7.61)

The sign is chosen to coincide with ζ\zeta defined in Refs. [9, 8]33 3 Note, that ζ1\zeta_{1} defined in Eq. (7.61) is related to the curvature perturbation ζSBB\zeta_{\rm{SBB}} defined in Ref. [143] by ζSBB≡3​ζ1\zeta_{\rm{SBB}}\equiv 3\zeta_{1}.. There is still the freedom to choose the spatial gauge. In particular we can choose either B~\tilde{B}, E~\tilde{E} or v~\tilde{v} to be zero and thus fix β\beta.

Note that ζ1\zeta_{1} is simply related to the density perturbation in the flat gauge, Eq. (7.19) by

−ζ1=ℋρ0′​δ​ρ1​f​l​a​t.-\zeta_{1}=\frac{{\cal H}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{1{\rm{flat}}}\,. (7.62)

The curvature perturbation in the uniform-density gauge is also closely related to the comoving curvature perturbation (7.46). At first order we have

ζ1=−ℛ1−ℋρ0′​δ​ρ1​c​o​m,\zeta_{1}=-{{\cal{R}}}_{1}-\frac{{\cal H}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{1{\rm{com}}}\,, (7.63)

where δ​ρ1​c​o​m\delta\rho_{1{\rm{com}}} is the comoving density perturbation (7.48). In Section 8 we shall use the Einstein equations to show that ζ1\zeta_{1} and ℛ1{{\cal{R}}}_{1} differ only by an overall minus sign in the large scale limit where the comoving density perturbation vanishes.

7.6.2 Second order

The transformation behaviour of scalars at second order, Eq. (6.20), allows us to define the temporal gauge corresponding to uniform density hypersurfaces as

α2​δ​ρ=−δ​ρ2ρ0′−α1ρ0′(ρ0′′α1+ρ0′α1′+2δρ1′)−1ρ0′(2δρ1+ρ0′α1),k(β1,k+γ1k).\alpha_{2{\delta\rho}}=-\frac{\delta\rho_{2}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}-\frac{\alpha_{1}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\left(\rho_{0}^{\prime\prime}\alpha_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}^{\prime}+2\delta\rho_{1}^{\prime}\right)-\frac{1}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\left(2\delta\rho_{1}+\rho_{0}^{\prime}\alpha_{1}\right)_{,k}\left(\beta_{1,}^{~~k}+{\gamma_{{1}}^{~k}}\right)\,. (7.64)

Using then the definition of uniform density hypersurfaces at first order, Eq. (7.60), and choosing a spatially flat threading by using Eq. (7.15), we finally get

α2​δ​ρ=1ρ0′​[−δ​ρ2+δ​ρ1′ρ0′​δ​ρ1+(E1,k+F1k)​δ​ρ1,k].\alpha_{2{\delta\rho}}=\frac{1}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\left[-\delta\rho_{2}+\frac{\delta\rho_{1}^{\prime}}{\rho_{0}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{1}+\left(E_{1,}^{~~k}+F_{1}^{~k}\right)\delta\rho_{1,k}\right]\,. (7.65)
