8 Dynamics

In this section we give the Einstein equations governing the evolution of the FRW background and perturbations in general relativity. This will allow us to derive some key properties of the perturbation variables, such as the conservation of the curvature perturbation ζ\zeta on super-horizon scales in the adiabatic case.

In general relativity the Einstein equations relate the local spacetime curvature to the local energy-momentum:

Gμ​ν=8​π​G​Tμ​ν.G_{\mu\nu}=8\pi GT_{\mu\nu}\,. (8.1)

In more general theories of gravity we can still equate the local spacetime curvature, Gμ​νG_{\mu\nu}, with an effective energy-momentum, though this may not be simply related to the energy-momentum tensor derived, say, from the matter Lagrangian. Moreover, many modified gravity theories, including Brans-Dicke gravity or higher-order theories, may be rewritten in terms of general relativity plus non-minimally coupled matter fields through a conformal rescaling of coordinates [102, 173]. In this review we will restrict our analysis to general relativity.

We can project the tensor equation (8.1) into components tangent to and orthogonal to the timelike 4-vector field, nμn^{\mu} defined in Eq. (3.4), which defines the coordinate system (see section 3). This gives two constraint equations for the metric perturbations, which we will refer to as the energy and momentum constraint equations. We also have two evolution equations driven by the trace and trace-free parts of the pressure. Through the Bianchi identities, ∇μGνμ=0\nabla_{\mu}G^{\mu}_{\nu}=0, the field equations (8.1) imply the local conservation the total energy and momentum,

∇μTμ​ν=0.\nabla_{\mu}T^{\mu\nu}=0\,. (8.2)

which can similarly be split into energy and momentum conservation equations with respect to a given coordinate system.

In the case of multiple matter components the total energy-momentum tensor is the sum of the energy-momentum tensors of the individual fluids, T(α)μ​νT^{\mu\nu}_{(\alpha)}, given in Eq. (4.20). For each fluid the local energy-momentum “conservation” equation (4.21), has an energy-momentum transfer 4-vector, Q(α)νQ^{\nu}_{(\alpha)} on the right-hand-side, which is zero only for non-interacting fluids. However local conservation of the total energy-momentum imposes the constraint Eq. (4.22).

We also have at our disposal the equations of motion for specific matter fields, such as the Klein-Gordon equation for canonical scalar fields, φI\varphi_{I}, with interaction potential energy UU:

□​φI=d​Ud​φI.\Box\varphi_{I}=\frac{dU}{d\varphi_{I}}\,. (8.3)

In the following we equate terms order by order in a perturbative expansion about a homogeneous background spacetime.

8.1 Background

The Einstein equations (8.1) give the Friedmann constraint and evolution equation for the background FRW universe

ℋ2\displaystyle{\cal H}^{2} =\displaystyle= 8​π​G3​a2​ρ,\displaystyle\frac{8\pi G}{3}a^{2}\rho\,, (8.4)
ℋ′\displaystyle{\cal H}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= −4​π​G3​a2​(ρ+3​P),\displaystyle-\frac{4\pi G}{3}a^{2}\left(\rho+3P\right)\,, (8.5)

and energy-momentum conservation, Eq. (8.2), gives the continuity equation

ρ′=−3​ℋ​(ρ+P),\rho^{\prime}=-3{\cal H}\left(\rho+P\right)\,, (8.6)

where ρ\rho and PP are the total energy density and the total pressure, a prime denotes a derivative with respect to conformal time, η\eta, the scale factor is aa, and ℋ≡a′/a{\cal H}\equiv a^{\prime}/a is the conformal Hubble parameter.

The total density and the total pressure are related to the density and pressure of the component fluids by

∑αρα=ρ,∑αPα=P.\sum_{\alpha}\rho_{\alpha}=\rho\,,\qquad\sum_{\alpha}P_{\alpha}=P\,. (8.7)

The continuity equation (4.21) for each individual fluid in the background is [66]

ρα′=−3​ℋ​(ρα+Pα)+a​Qα,\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}=-3{\cal H}\left(\rho_{\alpha}+P_{\alpha}\right)+aQ_{\alpha}\,, (8.8)

where the energy transfer to the α\alpha-fluid is given by the time component of the energy-momentum transfer vector

Qα≡−uμ​Q(α)μ.Q_{\alpha}\equiv-u_{\mu}Q^{\mu}_{(\alpha)}\,. (8.9)

Equation (4.22) implies that the energy transfer obeys the constraint

∑αQα=0.\sum_{\alpha}Q_{\alpha}=0\,. (8.10)

Homogeneous scalar fields in the FRW metric obey the Klein-Gordon equation

φI′′+2​ℋ​φI′+a2​d​Ud​φI=0.\varphi_{I}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}\varphi_{I}^{\prime}+a^{2}\frac{dU}{d\varphi_{I}}=0\,. (8.11)

It is sometimes useful to identify the kinetic energy density and (isotropic) pressure of each field as

ρI=PI=12​a−2​φI′2\rho_{I}=P_{I}=\frac{1}{2}a^{-2}\varphi_{I}^{\prime 2} (8.12)

The Klein-Gordon equation (8.11) then implies an energy transfer of the form given by Eq. (8.8)

a​QI=−φ′​d​Ud​φI.aQ_{I}=-\varphi^{\prime}\frac{dU}{d\varphi_{I}}\,. (8.13)

where this energy is transferred to the potential energy

ρU=−PU=U,\rho_{U}=-P_{U}=U\,, (8.14)

and overall energy conservation (8.10) implies

QU=−∑IQI=a−1U′.Q_{U}=-\sum_{I}Q_{I}=a^{-1}U^{\prime}\,. (8.15)

8.2 First order scalar perturbations

In the following we discuss the linear constraint and evolution equations for inhomogeneous perturbations at first order. We omit the subscript “1” denoting the order of the perturbations to avoid unnecessary clutter.

8.2.1 Einstein equations

The scalar metric perturbations in an arbitrary gauge are related to matter perturbations via the first-order energy and momentum constraints [66, 123]

3​ℋ​(ψ′+ℋ​ϕ)−∇2[ψ+ℋ​σ]\displaystyle 3{\cal H}\left(\psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}{\phi}\right)-\nabla^{2}\left[\psi+{\cal H}{\sigma}\right] =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​δ​ρ,\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}\delta\rho, (8.16)
ψ′+ℋ​ϕ\displaystyle\psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}{\phi} =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​(ρ+P)​V\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}(\rho+P)V (8.17)

where the total covariant velocity perturbation is given by

V≡v+B,V\equiv v+B\,, (8.18)

and vv is the total scalar velocity potential (4.5).

In a specific gauge, such as the spatially flat gauge these can be written in terms of the corresponding gauge-invariant quantities. For instance, in the spatially flat gauge we have

3​ℋ2​ϕflat−ℋ​∇2σflat\displaystyle 3{\cal H}^{2}{\phi}_{\rm{flat}}-{\cal H}\nabla^{2}{\sigma}_{\rm{flat}} =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​δ​ρflat,\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}\delta\rho_{\rm{flat}}, (8.19)
ℋ​ϕflat\displaystyle{\cal H}{\phi}_{\rm{flat}} =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​(ρ+P)​Vflat,\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}(\rho+P)V_{\rm{flat}}\,, (8.20)

which makes it straightforward to eliminate the metric variables ϕflat{\phi}_{\rm{flat}} and σflat=−Bflat{\sigma}_{\rm{flat}}=-B_{\rm{flat}} in favour of the energy and momentum in the flat gauge.

Alternatively in the longitudinal gauge the shear terms are absent and we obtain first order differential equations for the curvature perturbation

3​ℋ​(Ψ′+ℋ​Φ)−∇2Ψ\displaystyle 3{\cal H}\left(\Psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}\Phi\right)-\nabla^{2}\Psi =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​δ​ρℓ,\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}\delta\rho_{\ell}, (8.21)
Ψ′+ℋ​Φ\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}\Phi =\displaystyle= −4​π​G​a2​(ρ+P)​vℓ.\displaystyle-4\pi Ga^{2}(\rho+P)v_{\ell}\,. (8.22)

Typically one then uses these equations to eliminate the density and velocity perturbations, δ​ρℓ\delta\rho_{\ell} and vℓv_{\ell}, in terms of the metric perturbations in the longitudinal gauge.

The same energy and momentum constraints can be re-written in terms of gauge invariant variables to give expressions for the curvature perturbation in the uniform-density gauge (7.61) and the comoving curvature perturbation (7.46), respectively, in terms of the longitudinal gauge metric perturbations (7.1) and (7.2):

Ψ′+ℋ​Φ−ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ​Ψ−13​ℋ​∇2Ψ=ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ​ζ,\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}\Phi-\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}}\Psi-\frac{1}{3{\cal H}}\nabla^{2}\Psi=\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}}\zeta\,, (8.23)
Ψ′+ℋ​Φ−ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ​Ψ=−ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ​ℛ.\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}\Phi-\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}}\Psi=-\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}}{{\cal{R}}}\,. (8.24)

These can be combined to give the gauge-invariant generalisation of the Newtonian Poisson equation

∇2Ψ=−3​(ℋ′−ℋ2)​(ζ+ℛ)=4​π​G​a2​δ​ρcom,\nabla^{2}\Psi=-3\left({\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}\right)(\zeta+{{\cal{R}}})=4\pi Ga^{2}\delta\rho_{\rm com}\,, (8.25)

relating the longitudinal gauge curvature perturbation (7.2) to the comoving density perturbation (7.48). We see that the comoving density perturbation is suppressed relative to the metric perturbation Ψ\Psi on large scales, and that ζ\zeta and −ℛ-{{\cal{R}}} coincide in the large scale limit so long as Ψ\Psi is finite in this limit44 4 Note that Eq. (8.24) shows that the variable denoted ζ\zeta in the review by Mukhanov, Feldman and Brandenberger: ζMFB≡Φ−ℋ⁡(Φ′+ℋ​Φ)ℋ′−ℋ2,\zeta_{\rm MFB}\equiv\Phi-\frac{{\cal H}(\Phi^{\prime}+{\cal H}\Phi)}{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}\,, (8.26) coincides with the comoving curvature perturbation when Ψ=Φ\Psi=\Phi..

The perturbed Einstein equations at first order also yield two evolution equations for the scalar metric perturbations

ψ′′+2​ℋ​ψ′+ℋ​ϕ′+(2​ℋ′+ℋ2)​ϕ=4​π​G​a2​(δ​P+23​∇2Π),\displaystyle\psi^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}\psi^{\prime}+{\cal H}{\phi}^{\prime}+\left(2{\cal H}^{\prime}+{\cal H}^{2}\right){\phi}=4\pi Ga^{2}\left(\delta P+\frac{2}{3}\nabla^{2}\Pi\right)\,, (8.27)
σ′+2​ℋ​σ+ψ−ϕ=8​π​G​a2​Π,\displaystyle{\sigma}^{\prime}+2{\cal H}{\sigma}+\psi-{\phi}=8\pi Ga^{2}\Pi\,, (8.28)

where Π\Pi is the scalar part of the (tracefree) anisotropic stress, defined in Eq. (4.10).

Equation (8.28) in a general gauge can be interpreted as the evolution equation for the scalar shear, but in the longitudinal gauge it becomes a constraint equation for the gauge-invariant perturbations Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi, defined in Eqs. (7.1) and (7.2),

Ψ−Φ=8​π​G​a2​Π,\Psi-\Phi=8\pi Ga^{2}\Pi\,, (8.29)

and hence we have Ψ=Φ\Psi=\Phi in the absence of anisotropic stresses.

Equation (8.27) then provides a second-order evolution equation for the metric perturbation in the longitudinal gauge driven by isotropic pressure:

Ψ′′+3​ℋ​Ψ′+(2​ℋ′+ℋ2)​Ψ=4​π​G​a2​δ​P.\Psi^{\prime\prime}+3{\cal H}\Psi^{\prime}+\left(2{\cal H}^{\prime}+{\cal H}^{2}\right)\Psi=4\pi Ga^{2}\delta P\,. (8.30)

For adiabatic perturbations we can relate the pressure to the density, δ​P=cs2​δ​ρ\delta P=c_{s}^{2}\delta\rho where cs2c_{s}^{2} is the adiabatic sound speed, in which case (8.30) and (8.16) yield a closed second-order differential equation [123]

Ψ′′+3​(1+cs2)​ℋ​Ψ′+[2​ℋ′+(1+3​cs2)​ℋ2−cs2​∇2]​Ψ=0.\Psi^{\prime\prime}+3(1+c_{s}^{2}){\cal H}\Psi^{\prime}+[2{\cal H}^{\prime}+(1+3c_{s}^{2}){\cal H}^{2}-c_{s}^{2}\nabla^{2}]\Psi=0\,. (8.31)

8.2.2 Energy and momentum conservation

Energy-momentum conservation gives evolution equations for the perturbed energy and momentum

δ​ρ′+3​ℋ​(δ​ρ+δ​P)−3​(ρ+P)​ψ′+(ρ+P)​∇2(V+σ)=0,\displaystyle\delta\rho^{\prime}+3{\cal H}\left(\delta\rho+\delta P\right)-3\left(\rho+P\right)\psi^{\prime}+(\rho+P)\nabla^{2}\left(V+{\sigma}\right)=0\,, (8.32)
V′+(1−3​cs2)​ℋ​V+ϕ+1ρ+P​(δ​P+23​∇2Π)=0,\displaystyle V^{\prime}+(1-3c^{2}_{\rm s}){\cal H}V+\phi+\frac{1}{\rho+P}\left(\delta P+\frac{2}{3}\nabla^{2}\Pi\right)=0\,, (8.33)

where cs2c^{2}_{\rm s} is the adiabatic speed of sound, defined as

cs2≡P′ρ′.c^{2}_{\rm s}\equiv\frac{P^{\prime}}{\rho^{\prime}}\,. (8.34)

From the momentum conservation equation in the total matter gauge, such that V=0V=0, we see that the acceleration is proportional to the pressure perturbation: (ρ+P)​ϕ=δ​P+(2/3)​∇2Π(\rho+P)\phi=\delta P+(2/3)\nabla^{2}\Pi. Alternatively, for pressureless, non-interacting dust we have (a​V)′+a​ϕ=0(a{V})^{\prime}+a{\phi}=0 and hence the scalar velocity potential redshifts as V∝1/aV\propto 1/a in a synchronous gauge.

Re-writing the energy conservation equation (8.32) in terms of the curvature perturbation on uniform-density hypersurfaces, ζ\zeta in (7.61), we obtain the important result

ζ′=−ℋ​δ​Pnadρ+P−ΣV,\zeta^{\prime}=-{\cal H}\frac{\delta P_{\rm nad}}{\rho+P}-{\Sigma_{V}}\,, (8.35)

where δ​Pnad\delta P_{\rm nad} is the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation, defined in (9.5), and Σ\Sigma describes the divergence of the velocity in the longitudinal gauge, Eq. (7.8) or, equivalently, the scalar shear along comoving worldlines [96]

ΣV≡13​∇2(V+σ)=13​∇2vℓ~.{\Sigma_{V}}\equiv\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\left(V+{\sigma}\right)=\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\widetilde{v_{\ell}}\,. (8.36)

Thus the curvature perturbation on uniform-density hypersurfaces is constant for adiabatic perturbations on large scales when the shear of comoving worldlines becomes negligible. This follows directly from local energy conservation and holds independently of the gravitational field equations [176, 159, 22, 33].

Using the definition of ζ\zeta and Ψ\Psi in Eqs. (7.61) and (7.2) and the constraint equation for the comoving density perturbation (8.25), we have

ΣVℋ=∇23​ℋ2​(ζ+Ψ)+2​ρ3​(ρ+P)​(∇2ℋ2)2​Ψ.\frac{\Sigma_{V}}{{\cal H}}=\frac{\nabla^{2}}{3{\cal H}^{2}}\left(\zeta+\Psi\right)+\frac{2\rho}{3(\rho+P)}\left(\frac{\nabla^{2}}{{\cal H}^{2}}\right)^{2}\Psi\,. (8.37)

Thus we see that ζ\zeta is constant for adiabatic perturbations (δ​Pnad=0\delta P_{\rm nad}=0) on super-Hubble scales (k/ℋ≪1k/{\cal H}\ll 1), so long as Ψ\Psi remains finite. This makes ζ\zeta a convenient variable to characterise the primordial density perturbation on super-Hubble scales, either during a period of inflation in the very early universe, or in the subsequent radiation dominated era. This is an excellent approximation throughout reheating at the end of inflation and the subsequent radiation era on scales relevant for observations of degree-scale anisotropies in the cosmic microwave background and large-scale galaxy surveys [84].

Conversely, local variations in the pressure leading to a non-adiabatic pressure perturbation, δ​Pnad\delta P_{\rm nad}, will lead to a change in the curvature perturbation ζ\zeta on super-Hubble scales [116, 50, 89]. This mechanism is at the heart of the curvaton scenario for the origin of large scale structure in the universe [48, 95, 118].

8.2.3 Multiple fluids

The perturbations in the total energy-momentum can be related to the perturbations of individual fluids by

∑αδ​ρα=δ​ρ,∑αδ​Pα=δ​P,∑αΠα=Π,\sum_{\alpha}\delta\rho_{\alpha}=\delta\rho\,,\qquad\sum_{\alpha}\delta P_{\alpha}=\delta P\,,\qquad\sum_{\alpha}\Pi_{\alpha}=\Pi\,, (8.38)

and

V=∑γργ+Pγρ+P​Vγ,V=\sum_{\gamma}\frac{\rho_{\gamma}+P_{\gamma}}{\rho+P}V_{\gamma}\,, (8.39)

where δ​ρα\delta\rho_{\alpha} and δ​Pα\delta P_{\alpha} are the perturbed energy density and the perturbed pressure of the α\alpha-fluid, respectively, and Vα{V_{\alpha}} is the covariant velocity perturbation of the α\alpha-fluid defined as

Vα≡vα+B,{V_{\alpha}}\equiv v_{\alpha}+B\,, (8.40)

where vαv_{\alpha} is the scalar velocity potential of the α\alpha-fluid.

The perturbed energy transfer 4-vector, Eq. (4.21), for individual fluids including terms up to first order, is written as [66, 113]

Q(α)​0\displaystyle Q_{(\alpha)0} =\displaystyle= −a​Qα​(1+ϕ)−a​δ​Qα,\displaystyle-aQ_{\alpha}(1+\phi)-a\delta Q_{\alpha}\,,
Q(α)​i\displaystyle Q_{(\alpha)i} =\displaystyle= (fα+aQαV),i,\displaystyle\left(f_{\alpha}+aQ_{\alpha}V\right)_{,i}\,, (8.41)

and Eq. (4.22) implies that the perturbed energy and momentum transfer obey the constraints

∑αδ​Qα=0,∑αfα=0.\sum_{\alpha}\delta Q_{\alpha}=0\,,\quad\sum_{\alpha}f_{\alpha}=0\,. (8.42)

Note that the momentum transfer, fαf_{\alpha}, is by convention [66, 111] defined with respect to the total momentum, VV, so is non-zero only if the momentum transfer vanishes in the total matter frame (V=0V=0).

The perturbed energy conservation equation for a particular fluid, including energy transfer, is then obtained by the first-order part of the time-component of the perturbed continuity equation (4.21) to give [66, 104]

δ​ρα′+3​ℋ​(δ​ρα+δ​Pα)−3​(ρα+Pα)​ψ′+(ρα+Pα)​∇2(Vα+σ)=a​Qα​ϕ+a​δ​Qα,\delta\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}+3{\cal H}(\delta\rho_{\alpha}+\delta P_{\alpha})-3\left(\rho_{\alpha}+P_{\alpha}\right)\psi^{\prime}+(\rho_{\alpha}+P_{\alpha})\nabla^{2}\left({V_{\alpha}}+{\sigma}\right)=aQ_{\alpha}\phi+a\delta Q_{\alpha}\,, (8.43)

The momentum conservation equation of the α\alpha-fluid is

Vα′\displaystyle{V}_{\alpha}^{\prime} +\displaystyle+ [a​Qαρα+Pα​(1+cα2)+(1−3​cα2)​ℋ]​Vα+ϕ\displaystyle\left[\frac{aQ_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}+P_{\alpha}}(1+c^{2}_{\alpha})+(1-3c^{2}_{\alpha}){\cal H}\right]{V_{\alpha}}+\phi (8.44)
+\displaystyle+ 1ρα+Pα​[δ​Pα+23​∇2Πα−a​Qα​V−fα]=0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\rho_{\alpha}+P_{\alpha}}\left[\delta P_{\alpha}+\frac{2}{3}\nabla^{2}\Pi_{\alpha}-aQ_{\alpha}V-f_{\alpha}\right]=0\,,

where cα2≡Pα′/ρα′c^{2}_{\alpha}\equiv P_{\alpha}^{\prime}/\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime} is the adiabatic sound speed of the α\alpha-fluid and a2​[Πα,i​j−(1/3)​δi​j​∇2Πα]a^{2}[\Pi_{\alpha,ij}-(1/3)\delta_{ij}\nabla^{2}\Pi_{\alpha}] is the scalar anisotropic stress of that fluid. The total adiabatic sound speed, Eq. (8.34), is the weighted sum of the adiabatic sound speeds of the individual fluids,

cs2=∑αρα′ρ′​cα2.c^{2}_{\rm{s}}=\sum_{\alpha}\frac{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}{\rho^{\prime}}c^{2}_{\alpha}\,. (8.45)

We recover the evolution equation for the total density perturbation (8.32) from Eq. (8.43) by summing over all fluids, using Eq. (8.38) and the constraint (8.42).

Analogous to the curvature perturbation on uniform-total-density hypersurfaces, ζ\zeta defined in Eq. (7.61), we can define a gauge-invariant perturbation on the uniform-α\alpha-density hypersurfaces

ζα≡−ψ−ℋ​δ​ραρα′.\zeta_{\alpha}\equiv-\psi-{\cal H}\frac{\delta\rho_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\,. (8.46)

The perturbed energy conservation equation for each fluid can then be written as

ζα′\displaystyle\zeta_{\alpha}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= 3​ℋ2ρα′​δ​Pintr,α−Σα−∇23​ℋ​[a​Qαρα′​ℛα]\displaystyle 3\frac{{\cal H}^{2}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta P_{{\rm intr},\alpha}-\Sigma_{\alpha}-\frac{\nabla^{2}}{3{\cal H}}\left[\frac{aQ_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}{{\cal{R}}}_{\alpha}\right] (8.47)
−(ℋa)′​a​Qαρα′​(δ​ραρα′−δ​ρρ′)−ℋρα′​(δ​Qα−Qα′ρα′​δ​ρα),\displaystyle-\left(\frac{{\cal H}}{a}\right)^{\prime}\frac{aQ_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\left(\frac{\delta\rho_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}-\frac{\delta\rho}{\rho^{\prime}}\right)-\frac{{\cal H}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\left(\delta Q_{\alpha}-\frac{Q_{\alpha}^{\prime}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{\alpha}\right)\,,

where the intrinsic non-adiabatic pressure perturbation of each fluid is given by

δ​Pintr,α≡δ​Pα−cα2​δ​ρα,\delta P_{\rm{intr},\alpha}\equiv\delta P_{\alpha}-c^{2}_{\alpha}\delta\rho_{\alpha}\,, (8.48)

the scalar shear along worldlines comoving with the α\alpha-fluid is

Σα≡13​∇2(σ+Vα),\Sigma_{\alpha}\equiv\frac{1}{3}\nabla^{2}\left(\sigma+V_{\alpha}\right)\,, (8.49)

and, extending Eq. (7.46), the curvature perturbation comoving with the α\alpha-fluid is

ℛα≡ψ+ℋ⁡(vα+B).{{\cal{R}}}_{\alpha}\equiv\psi+{\cal H}(v_{\alpha}+B)\,. (8.50)

Thus we see that ζα\zeta_{\alpha} is constant on large scales for adiabatic perturbations of any perfect fluid, with δ​Pintr,α=0\delta P_{\rm{intr},\alpha}=0, whose energy is conserved, Qα=0Q_{\alpha}=0 [176]. In fact we shall show later that ζα\zeta_{\alpha} is constant even in the presence of energy transfer, Qα≠0Q_{\alpha}\neq 0, so long as that energy transfer is adiabatic [111].

8.2.4 Multiple fields

If we consider NN scalar fields with Lagrangian density

ℒ=−U⁡(φ1,⋯,φN)−12​∑I=1Ngμ​ν​φI,μ​φI,ν,{{\cal L}}=-U(\varphi_{1},\cdots,\varphi_{N})-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I=1}^{N}g^{\mu\nu}\varphi_{I,\mu}\varphi_{I,\nu}\,, (8.51)

and minimal coupling to gravity, then the total energy, pressure and momentum perturbations are given by

δ​ρ\displaystyle\delta\rho =\displaystyle= ∑I[a−2​φI′​(δ​φI′−φI′​ϕ1)+UI​δ​φI],\displaystyle\sum_{I}\left[a^{-2}\varphi_{I}^{\prime}\left({\delta\varphi}_{I}^{\prime}-\varphi_{I}^{\prime}{\phi_{{1}}}\right)+U_{I}\delta\varphi_{I}\right]\,, (8.52)
δ​P\displaystyle\delta P =\displaystyle= ∑I[a−2​φI′​(δ​φI′−φI′​ϕ1)−UI​δ​φI],\displaystyle\sum_{I}\left[a^{-2}\varphi_{I}^{\prime}\left({\delta\varphi}_{I}^{\prime}-\varphi_{I}^{\prime}{\phi_{{1}}}\right)-U_{I}\delta\varphi_{I}\right]\,, (8.53)
(ρ+P)(v+B),i\displaystyle(\rho+P)(v+B)_{,i} =\displaystyle= −∑Ia−1φI′δφI,i,\displaystyle-\sum_{I}a^{-1}{\varphi}_{I}^{\prime}\delta\varphi_{I,i}\,, (8.54)

where UI≡∂U/∂φIU_{I}\equiv\partial U/\partial\varphi_{I}. These then give the gauge-invariant comoving density perturbation (7.48)

δ​ρm=a−2​∑I[φI′​(δ​φI′−φI′​ϕ1)−(φI′′−ℋ​φI′)​δ​φI].\displaystyle\delta\rho_{m}=a^{-2}\sum_{I}\left[\varphi_{I}^{\prime}\left({\delta\varphi}_{I}^{\prime}-\varphi_{I}^{\prime}{\phi_{{1}}}\right)-(\varphi_{I}^{\prime\prime}-{\cal H}\varphi_{I}^{\prime})\delta\varphi_{I}\right]\,. (8.55)

The comoving density is sometimes used to represent the total matter perturbation, but for a single scalar field it is proportional to the non-adiabatic pressure (9.5):

δ​Pnad=−2a2U,φ3​ℋ​φ′​δ​ρcom.\delta P_{\rm nad}=-\frac{2a^{2}U_{,\varphi}}{3{\cal H}\varphi^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{\rm{com}}\,. (8.56)

From the Einstein constraint equation (8.25) this will vanish on large scales (k/a​H→0k/aH\to 0) if Ψ\Psi remains finite, and hence single scalar field perturbations become adiabatic in this large-scale limit, even without assuming slow-roll [52, 104].

The anisotropic stress, πi​j\pi_{ij}, vanishes to linear order for any number of scalar fields minimally coupled to gravity.

The first-order scalar field perturbations obey the wave equation

δ​φI′′+2​ℋ​δ​φI′−∇2δ​φI+a2​∑JUI​J​δ​φJ=−2​a2​UI​ϕ1+φI′​[ϕ1′+3​ψ′−∇2σ].\displaystyle{\delta\varphi}_{I}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}{\delta\varphi}_{I}^{\prime}-{\nabla^{2}}\delta\varphi_{I}+a^{2}\sum_{J}U_{IJ}\delta\varphi_{J}=-2a^{2}U_{I}{\phi_{{1}}}+\varphi_{I}^{\prime}\left[{{\phi_{{1}}}}^{\prime}+3{\psi}^{\prime}-{\nabla^{2}}{\sigma}\right].

where the terms on the right-hand-side represent the effect of metric perturbations at first-order (sometimes called the gravitational back-reaction).

The scalar field wave equation in a perturbed FRW cosmology can most easily be written in closed form in terms of the field perturbations in the spatially flat gauge, defined in Eq. (7.23), which in the multi-field case have the gauge invariant definitions

δ​φflat​I≡δ​φI+φI′ℋ​ψ.{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}I}\equiv\delta\varphi_{I}+\frac{\varphi_{I}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}\psi\,. (8.58)

Note that since the scalar field can be thought of as a potential for the 4-velocity, this variable is a rescaling of the curvature perturbation on the comoving-orthogonal hypersurface for each field

δ​φflat​I=φI′ℋ​ℛI.{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}I}=\frac{\varphi_{I}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}{{\cal{R}}}_{I}\,. (8.59)

Using the Einstein equations to eliminate the metric perturbations on the right-hand-side of Eq. (8.2.4) yields [146, 64, 128, 164]

δ​φflat​I′′+2​ℋ​δ​φflat​I′−∇2δ​φflat​I+a2​[∑JUI​J−8​π​Ga2​(a2​φI′​φJ′ℋ)′]​δ​φflat​J=0.{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}I}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}I}^{\prime}-{\nabla^{2}}{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}I}+a^{2}\left[\sum_{J}U_{IJ}-\frac{8\pi G}{a^{2}}\left(\frac{a^{2}\varphi_{I}^{\prime}\varphi_{J}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}\right)^{\prime}\right]{\delta\varphi}_{{\rm{flat}}J}=0\,. (8.60)

The effect of gravitational coupling is now evident due to the terms proportional to Newton’s gravitational constant. It is also evident that this gravitational coupling vanishes at first order for fields whose time derivative vanishes in the background solution, which is why at lowest order in a slow-roll approximation during inflation one can neglect the gravitational coupling.

In the next section we will discuss how the coupled equations for multiple fields may be partially decoupled by identifying the adiabatic and isocurvature field perturbations on large scales.

8.3 First order vector perturbations

The divergence-free part of the 3-momentum [see Eqs. (2.11), (4.5) and (4.13)]

δ​qi=(ρ+P)​(vvec​i−Si),{\delta q}_{i}=(\rho+P)(v_{{\rm vec}i}-S_{i})\,, (8.61)

obeys the momentum conservation equation

δ​qi′+4​ℋ​δ​qi=−∇2Πi,{\delta q}_{i}^{\prime}+4{\cal H}\delta q_{i}=-\nabla^{2}\Pi_{i}\,, (8.62)

where the vector part of the anisotropic stress, Eq. (4.10), is given by a2​∂(iCLOSEΠOPENj)a^{2}\partial_{(i}\Pi_{j)}. The gauge-invariant vector metric perturbation is then directly related to the divergence-free part of the momentum via the constraint equation

∇2(Fi′+Si)=−16​π​G​a2​δ​qi.\nabla^{2}\left({F}_{i}^{\prime}+S_{i}\right)=-16\pi Ga^{2}\delta q_{i}\,. (8.63)

Thus the Einstein equations constrain the gauge-invariant vector metric perturbation, Fi′+SiF_{i}^{\prime}+S_{i}, to vanish in the presence of only scalar fields, for which the divergence-free momentum necessarily vanishes.

Equation (8.63) shows that vector metric perturbations can be supported only by divergence-free momenta, but even then equation (8.62) shows that the vector perturbations are redshifted away by the Hubble expansion on large scales unless they are driven by an anisotropic stress.

8.4 First order tensor perturbations

There is no constraint equation for the tensor perturbations as these are the free gravitational degrees of freedom (gravitational waves). The spatial part of the Einstein equations yields a wave equation

hi​j′′+2​ℋ​hi​j′−∇2hi​j=8​π​G​a2​Πi​j,{h}_{ij}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}{h}_{ij}^{\prime}-{\nabla^{2}}h_{ij}=8\pi Ga^{2}\Pi_{ij}\,, (8.64)

where Πi​j(T​T)\Pi_{ij}^{(TT)} is the transverse and tracefree part of the anisotropic stress (4.10).

We can decompose arbitrary tensor perturbations into eigenmodes of the spatial Laplacian, ∇2ei​j=−(k2/a2)​ei​j\nabla^{2}e_{ij}=-(k^{2}/a^{2})e_{ij}, with comoving wavenumber kk, and scalar amplitude h⁡(t)h(t):

hi​j=h⁡(t)​ei​j(+,×)​(x),h_{ij}=h(t)e_{ij}^{(+,\times)}(x)\,, (8.65)

with two possible polarisation states, ++ and ×\times. In the absence of any such anisotropic stress, e.g., in the presence of scalar fields and perfect fluids, the amplitude, defined in Eq. (8.65), of the tensor metric perturbation with comoving wavenumber, kk, obeys the wave equation for a massless scalar field (8.2.4) in an unperturbed FRW metric.

h′′+2​ℋ​h′+k2​h=0.{h}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}h^{\prime}+k^{2}h=0\,. (8.66)

9 Adiabatic and entropy perturbations

9.1 Multiple fluids

We will refer to primordial perturbations as the perturbations at the epoch of primordial nucleosynthesis. The abundances of the light elements provide constraints on the matter content and expansion rate of the universe at this epoch, so we will assume that the material content of the universe is known (photons, neutrinos, baryonic matter and cold dark matter) and the gravitational laws are described by general relativity. This is expected to be some time after an early inflationary epoch when the perturbations originated as vacuum fluctuations on much smaller scales. By the time of primordial nucleosynthesis, the scales responsible for the large scale structure of our observable universe today were far outside the Hubble scale and well described by large scale limit.

In the standard Hot Big Bang the entropy density of the universe is dominated by the number of relativistic particles and for most of the history of the universe it is proportional to the number of photons, s=1.8​gs​nγs=1.8g_{s}n_{\gamma}, where gsg_{s} is the effective number of light species [70]. In particular the perturbed baryon-entropy ratio nB/sn_{B}/s (assuming gsg_{s} remains constant) is given by [116]

SB≡δ⁡(nB/nγ)nB/nγ=δ​nBnB−δ​nγnγ.S_{B}\equiv\frac{\delta(n_{B}/n_{\gamma})}{n_{B}/n_{\gamma}}=\frac{\delta n_{B}}{n_{B}}-\frac{\delta n_{\gamma}}{n_{\gamma}}\,. (9.1)

Written in terms of the energy density of photons, ργ∝nγ4/3\rho_{\gamma}\propto n_{\gamma}^{4/3}, and baryons, ρB∝nB\rho_{B}\propto n_{B}, at the time of primordial nucleosynthesis this becomes

SB=δ​ρBρB−34​δ​ργργ.S_{B}=\frac{\delta\rho_{B}}{\rho_{B}}-\frac{3}{4}\frac{\delta\rho_{\gamma}}{\rho_{\gamma}}\,. (9.2)

More generally, density perturbations in an nn-component system can be decomposed into an overall density perturbation and n−1n-1 relative density perturbations between the different components. The overall density perturbation is naturally gauge-dependent, however the gauge transformation rule for the linear density perturbation (6.18) suggests a natural gauge-invariant definition of the relative density perturbation at first-order,

δ​ρI​J∝δ​ρI−ρI′ρJ′​δ​ρJ,\delta\rho_{IJ}\propto\delta\rho_{I}-\frac{\rho_{I}^{\prime}}{\rho_{J}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{J}\,, (9.3)

corresponding to the density perturbation of fluid II on surfaces of uniform density of the fluid JJ. Comparing this expression with the conventional definition of the primordial baryon-entropy perturbation (9.2) suggests a gauge-invariant definition of the relative perturbation between any two fluids [113, 111]

SI​J≡3​ℋ​(δ​ρJρJ′−δ​ρIρI′)≡3​(ζI−ζJ),S_{IJ}\equiv 3{\cal H}\left(\frac{\delta\rho_{J}}{\rho_{J}^{\prime}}-\frac{\delta\rho_{I}}{\rho_{I}^{\prime}}\right)\equiv 3\left(\zeta_{I}-\zeta_{J}\right)\,, (9.4)

which reduces to baryon-entropy perturbation (9.2) for SB≡SB​γS_{B}\equiv S_{B\gamma}. Hence we refer to SI​JS_{IJ} as the relative entropy perturbation for two fluids. It is the correct generalisation of the the entropy perturbation defined in Ref. [66] to the case of non-interacting fluids.

The non-adiabatic pressure perturbation is given by

δ​Pnad≡δ​P−P′ρ′​δ​ρ.\delta P_{\rm nad}\equiv\delta P-\frac{P^{\prime}}{\rho^{\prime}}\delta\rho\,. (9.5)

For a detailed recent discussion of the non-adiabatic pressure see Ref. [37].

In a system of more than one fluids the total non-adiabatic pressure perturbation, δ​Pnad\delta P_{\rm nad}, may be further split into two parts [66],

δ​Pnad≡δ​Pintr+δ​Prel.\delta P_{\rm nad}\equiv\delta P_{\rm intr}+\delta P_{\rm rel}\,. (9.6)

The first part is due to the intrinsic entropy perturbation of each fluid

δ​Pintr=∑αδ​Pnad,α,\delta P_{\rm intr}=\sum_{\alpha}\delta P_{\rm{nad},\alpha}\,, (9.7)

where the intrinsic non-adiabatic pressure perturbation of each fluid was given in Eq. (8.48). The second part of the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation (9.6) is due to the relative entropy perturbation 𝒮α​β\cal{S}_{\alpha\beta} between different fluids (9.4)

δPrel≡−16​ℋ​ρ′∑α,βρα′ρβ′(cα2−cβ2)𝒮α​β.\delta P_{\rm rel}\equiv-\frac{1}{6{\cal H}\rho^{\prime}}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}\rho_{\beta}^{\prime}\left(c^{2}_{\alpha}-c^{2}_{\beta}\right){\cal{S}}_{\alpha\beta}\,. (9.8)

In analogy with the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation for each fluid (8.48), we can identify an intrinsic non-adiabatic part of the energy transfer perturbation [113, 111] that appears in the perturbed energy conservation equation for each fluid (8.43)

δ​Qintr,α≡δ​Qα−Qα′ρα′​δ​ρα.\delta Q_{{\rm intr},\alpha}\equiv\delta Q_{\alpha}-\frac{Q_{\alpha}^{\prime}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta\rho_{\alpha}\,. (9.9)

This is automatically zero if the local energy transfer QαQ_{\alpha} is a function of the local density ρα\rho_{\alpha} so that δ​Qα=(d​Qα/d​ρα)​δ​ρα\delta Q_{\alpha}=(d{Q}_{\alpha}/d\rho_{\alpha})\delta\rho_{\alpha}, just as the intrinsic non-adiabatic pressure perturbation (8.48) vanishes when δ​Pα=(d​Pα/d​ρα)​δ​ρα\delta P_{\alpha}=(d{P}_{\alpha}/d\rho_{\alpha})\delta\rho_{\alpha}.

We can also identify in Eq. (8.43) a relative non-adiabatic energy transfer

δ​Qrel,α\displaystyle\delta Q_{{\rm rel},\alpha} =\displaystyle= Qα​ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ2​(δ​ραρα′−δ​ρρ′)\displaystyle Q_{\alpha}\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}^{2}}\left(\frac{\delta\rho_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}-\frac{\delta\rho}{\rho^{\prime}}\right) (9.10)
=\displaystyle= −Qα6​ℋ​ρ∑βρβ′𝒮α​β,\displaystyle-\frac{Q_{\alpha}}{6{\cal H}\rho}\sum_{\beta}\rho_{\beta}^{\prime}{\cal{S}}_{\alpha\beta}\,,

due to the presence of relative entropy perturbations whenever the background energy transfer is non-zero, Qα≠0Q_{\alpha}\neq 0.

The perturbed energy conservation Eq. (8.47) for each fluid can then be written as

ζα′\displaystyle\zeta_{\alpha}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= 3​ℋ2ρα′​δ​Pintr,α−ℋρα′​(δ​Qintr,α+δ​Qrel,α)−Σα−∇23​ℋ​[a​Qαρα′​ℛα]\displaystyle 3\frac{{\cal H}^{2}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\delta P_{{\rm intr},\alpha}-\frac{{\cal H}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}\left(\delta Q_{{\rm intr},\alpha}+\delta Q_{{\rm rel},\alpha}\right)-\Sigma_{\alpha}-\frac{\nabla^{2}}{3{\cal H}}\left[\frac{aQ_{\alpha}}{\rho_{\alpha}^{\prime}}{{\cal{R}}}_{\alpha}\right] (9.11)

where the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation of each fluid is given by Eq. (8.48) and the non-adiabatic energy transfer is given by Eqs. (9.9) and (9.10). We thus see that ζα\zeta_{\alpha} is constant for adiabatic perturbations in the large scale limit where the shear of comoving worldlines, Σα\Sigma_{\alpha} defined in Eq. (8.49), vanishes [111].

More generally [96] one finds a conserved perturbation whenever there is a local conservation equation of the form d​y/d​τ=−θ​f​(y)dy/d\tau=-\theta f(y), where θ\theta is the local expansion rate and τ\tau the proper time along comoving worldlines. When one integrates this conservation equation one finds the local logarithmic expansion as a function of yy:

N~=∫θ​𝑑τ=∫d​yf⁡(y)≡F⁡(y).\tilde{N}=\int\theta d\tau=\int\frac{dy}{f(y)}\equiv F(y)\,. (9.12)

Thus the difference δ​F=F⁡(yB)−F⁡(yA)\delta F=F(y_{B})-F(y_{A}) evaluated along different worldlines remains a fixed constant of integration if one evaluates δ​F\delta F on constant time hypersurfaces separated by a fixed expansion, and spatially flat hypersurfaces provide a suitable time-slicing on large scales. The classic example of such a conserved quantity is the curvature perturbation on uniform density hypersurfaces, ζ\zeta defined in Eq. (7.61), which is conserved on large scales when P=P⁡(ρ)P=P(\rho) and thus the perturbations are adiabatic. But as we have seen the same result holds for the curvature perturbation on uniform-density hypersurfaces for any fluid whose pressure perturbation and energy transfer is adiabatic.

Thus the matter isocurvature perturbation (9.2) is constant on large scales if there is negligible energy transfer between non-relativistic matter and radiation. However at even higher energies we can still define a conserved perturbation associated with conserved baryon number density [97]

ζ~B=δ​nBnB−ψ\tilde{\zeta}_{B}=\frac{\delta n_{B}}{n_{B}}-\psi (9.13)

so long as we have a conserved quantum number associated with baryon number. The observed stability of the proton implies that baryon number is conserved up to very high energy, possibly the GUT scale, and thus it should be possible to relate any primordial baryon isocurvature perturbation to physics at very high energies.

9.2 Multiple fields

In the background FRW cosmology driven by multiple scalar fields it is possible to identify an adiabatic direction along the background trajectory in field space

r^I=φI′φI′2.\hat{r}_{I}=\frac{\varphi_{I}^{\prime}}{\sqrt{\varphi_{I}^{\prime 2}}}\,. (9.14)

The background solution, even in the presence of multiple fields, can then be described in terms of an effective single field, rr, obeying the usual Klein-Gordon equation

r′′+2​ℋ​r′+Ur=0.r^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}r^{\prime}+U_{r}=0\,. (9.15)

where r′=∑Ir^I​φI′{r^{\prime}}=\sum_{I}\hat{r}_{I}\varphi_{I}^{\prime} and Ur=∑Ir^I​UIU_{r}=\sum_{I}\hat{r}_{I}U_{I}. However field perturbations need not follow this background trajectory and we encounter qualitatively different behaviour from that in the single field case when we consider inhomogeneous perturbations about the background trajectory.

In analogy with our treatment of fluid perturbations one can identify adiabatic and isocurvature field perturbations in a cosmology with more than one scalar field. Indeed even a single scalar field, φ\varphi, can support a non-adiabatic pressure perturbation, given in Eq. (8.56). We refer to this as the intrinsic pressure perturbation for the field. However this intrinsic non-adiabatic perturbation for a single field is proportional to the comoving density perturbation and thus vanishes in a scalar field dominated universe on large scales according to Eq. (8.25), leaving effectively only adiabatic perturbations in this large scale limit.

For multiple fields we can perform a local rotation in field space to identify the adiabatic part of arbitrary perturbations along the background trajectory [109, 52]

δ​r≡∑Ir^I​δ​φI.\delta r\equiv\sum_{I}\hat{r}_{I}\delta\varphi_{I}\,. (9.16)

The generalisation to non-canonical fields with arbitrary metric in field space is given in Refs. [55, 41].

Field perturbations orthogonal to the adiabatic field are isocurvature field perturbations, or entropy perturbations in analogy with the fluid density perturbations (9.2),

δ​sI​J∝δ​φIφI′−δ​φJφJ′.\delta s_{IJ}\propto\frac{\delta\varphi_{I}}{\varphi_{I}^{\prime}}-\frac{\delta\varphi_{J}}{\varphi_{J}^{\prime}}\,. (9.17)

Note that the adiabatic field perturbation is naturally gauge-dependent, whereas the isocurvature field perturbations are gauge-independent at first order. For simplicity we will consider the case of two scalar fields where the direction in field space is given by the angle θ\theta, see Figure 1, so that r^=(cos⁡θ,sin⁡θ)\hat{r}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta). We then have

δ​r=cos⁡θ​δ​φ1+sin⁡θ​δ​φ2,\displaystyle\delta r=\cos\theta\delta\varphi_{1}+\sin\theta\delta\varphi_{2}\,, (9.18)
δ​s=−sin⁡θ​δ​φ1+cos⁡θ​δ​φ2\displaystyle\delta s=-\sin\theta\delta\varphi_{1}+\cos\theta\delta\varphi_{2} (9.19)

and we will work with the adiabatic field perturbation in the spatially flat gauge

δ​rflat=δ​r+r′ℋ​ψ,\delta r_{\rm{flat}}=\delta r+\frac{r^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}\psi\,, (9.20)

Note that δ​rflat\delta r_{\rm{flat}} is thus proportional to the total comoving curvature perturbation

ℛ=ψ+ℋr′​δ​r=ℋr′​δ​rflat.{{\cal{R}}}=\psi+\frac{{\cal H}}{r^{\prime}}\delta r=\frac{{\cal H}}{r^{\prime}}\delta r_{\rm{flat}}\,. (9.21)

since the adiabatic field, rr, is the potential for the total velocity, uμ∝d​r/d​xμu_{\mu}\propto dr/dx^{\mu}.

The adiabatic and isocurvature field perturbations obey the coupled evolution equations [52]

δ​rflat′′+2​ℋ​δ​rflat′+[k2+a2​Ur​r−θ′2−8​π​Ga2​(a2​r′2ℋ)′]​δ​rflat\displaystyle{\delta r}^{\prime\prime}_{\rm{flat}}+2{\cal H}{\delta r}^{\prime}_{\rm{flat}}+\left[{k^{2}}+a^{2}U_{rr}-{\theta}^{\prime 2}-\frac{8\pi G}{a^{2}}\left(\frac{a^{2}r^{\prime 2}}{{\cal H}}\right)^{\prime}\right]\delta r_{\rm{flat}}
=2​(θ′​δ​s)′−2​(a2​Urr′+ℋ′ℋ)​θ′​δ​s,\displaystyle=2(\theta^{\prime}\delta s)^{\prime}-2\left(\frac{a^{2}U_{r}}{r^{\prime}}+\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}}{{\cal H}}\right)\theta^{\prime}\delta s\,, (9.22)
δ​s′′+2​ℋ​δ​s′+(k2+a2​Us​s+3​θ′2)​δ​s=θ′r′​k22​π​G​Ψ,\displaystyle{\delta s}^{\prime\prime}+2{\cal H}{\delta s}^{\prime}+\left({k^{2}}+a^{2}U_{ss}+3{\theta}^{\prime 2}\right)\delta s=\frac{\theta^{\prime}}{r^{\prime}}\frac{k^{2}}{2\pi G}\Psi\,, (9.23)

where

Ur​r\displaystyle U_{rr} ≡\displaystyle\equiv (cos2⁡θ)​U11+(sin⁡2​θ)​U12+(sin2⁡θ)​U22,\displaystyle(\cos^{2}\theta)U_{11}+(\sin 2\theta)U_{12}+(\sin^{2}\theta)U_{22}, (9.24)
Us​s\displaystyle U_{ss} ≡\displaystyle\equiv (sin2⁡θ)​U11−(sin⁡2​θ)​U12+(cos2⁡θ)​U22.\displaystyle(\sin^{2}\theta)U_{11}-(\sin 2\theta)U_{12}+(\cos^{2}\theta)U_{22}. (9.25)

We can identify a purely adiabatic mode where δ​s=0\delta s=0 and remains zero on large scales. However a non-zero isocurvature perturbation appears as a source term in the perturbed inflaton equation (9.2) whenever θ′≠0{\theta}^{\prime}\neq 0 and the inflaton trajectory is curved in field space. Note that θ′{\theta}^{\prime} is given by [52]

θ′=−a2​Usr′,\theta^{\prime}=-\frac{a^{2}U_{s}}{r^{\prime}}\,, (9.26)

where Us=(cos⁡θ)​U2−(sin⁡θ)​U1U_{s}=(\cos\theta)U_{2}-(\sin\theta)U_{1} is the potential gradient orthogonal to the inflaton trajectory in field space. In the slow-roll approximation the background field always follows the potential gradient so the adiabatic-isocurvature coupling is suppressed in this slow-roll limit the integrated effect of isocurvature field perturbations on the adiabatic field perturbation cannot in general be neglected.

Equation (9.2) shows that the isocurvature perturbation δ​s\delta s works as a source term for the adiabatic curvature perturbation. This is in fact clearly seen if we take the time derivative of the comoving curvature perturbation (9.21):

ℛ′=ℋℋ′−ℋ2​k2​Ψ+2​ℋr′​θ′​δ​s.{{\cal{R}}}^{\prime}=\frac{{\cal H}}{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{k^{2}}\Psi+\frac{2{\cal H}}{r^{\prime}}{\theta^{\prime}}\delta s\,. (9.27)

Therefore ℛ{\cal R} (or equivalently ζ\zeta) is not conserved even in the large-scale limit in the presence of an isocurvature field perturbation, δ​s\delta s, with a non-straight trajectory in field space (θ′≠0{\theta}^{\prime}\neq 0).

By contrast, the solution for the isocurvature field perturbation is independent of any initial adiabatic perturbation on large-scales. The adiabatic perturbation provides a source term for the isocurvature field only through the spatial gradient of the longitudinal gauge metric potential, Ψ\Psi, which rapidly becomes negligible on super-Hubble scales during slow-roll inflation.

10 Perturbations from inflation

The standard hot big bang model of cosmology has a major shortcoming in that there is no causal explanation for the existence of primordial density perturbations on super-Hubble scales during the radiation dominated era. The CMB, and in particular the acoustic peaks in the temperature and polarisation anisotropies seen by the WMAP satellite [74] provide strong evidence that these primordial density perturbations do exist on scales much larger than the causal horizon at early times. The detailed distribution of primordial inhomogeneities is left as an unexplained initial condition in the standard hot big bang.

The primary success of inflation [155, 56] is to give a model for the origin of the primordial density perturbations from vacuum fluctuations during a period of accelerated expansion at very early times. This relies on speculative and uncertain physics - in particular it requires some form of energy density with negative pressure in general relativity - but the unexpected discovery that the universe is accelerating today appears to show that cosmological inflation does happen. Zero-point vacuum fluctuations of any light, weakly-coupled scalar field will be stretched up to super-Hubble scales during inflation and leave an approximately scale-invariant and Gaussian distribution of perturbations on large scales [122, 58, 156, 57, 9, 119, 145, 120].

The simplest model for inflation is that it is driven by a vacuum (potential) energy density which is a function of one or more scalar fields. We can describe the homogeneous FRW solution using the inflaton field, rr, which describes the evolution along the trajectory, r^\hat{r} defined in Eq. (9.14), in a possibly multi-dimensional field space. For a sufficiently flat potential the evolution can be well-described by the slow-roll approximation which assumes that the energy density is potential dominated

ℋ2≃8​π​G​a23​U​(r).{\cal H}^{2}\simeq\frac{8\pi Ga^{2}}{3}U(r)\,. (10.1)

This is equivalent to requiring that the first slow-roll parameter is small:

ϵ≡−H˙H2=−ℋ′−ℋ2ℋ2≪1.\epsilon\equiv-\frac{\dot{H}}{H^{2}}=-\frac{{\cal H}^{\prime}-{\cal H}^{2}}{{\cal H}^{2}}\ll 1\,. (10.2)

Note that the condition for accelerated expansion requires ϵ<1\epsilon<1. In terms of the potential we have

ϵ≃116​π​G​(UrU)2,\epsilon\simeq\frac{1}{16\pi G}\left(\frac{U_{r}}{U}\right)^{2}\,, (10.3)

We also assume the universe is overdamped, such that

3​ℋ​r′≃−a2​Ur.3{\cal H}r^{\prime}\simeq-a^{2}U_{r}\,. (10.4)

This implies that we can neglect the decaying mode of the overdamped system and we have a unique trajectory in field space for a single field. This is a self-consistent approximation when the inflaton field is light compared with the Hubble scale, which requires that the second slow-roll parameter is small:

|ηr​r|≪1where​ηr​r≡Ur​r3​H2.|\eta_{rr}|\ll 1\quad{\rm where}\ \eta_{rr}\equiv\frac{U_{rr}}{3H^{2}}\,. (10.5)

In the two-field model described in section 9.2, allowing for non-adiabatic perturbations, we can define three parameters [175], ηr​r\eta_{rr}, ηr​s\eta_{rs} and ηs​s\eta_{ss}, describing the curvature of the potential, where in general we have

ηI​J≡18​π​G​UI​JU.\eta_{IJ}\equiv\frac{1}{8\pi G}\frac{U_{IJ}}{U}\,. (10.6)

The background slow-roll solution is described in terms of the slow-roll parameters by

r˙2≃23​ϵ​U,H−1​θ˙≃−ηr​s,\dot{r}^{2}\simeq\frac{2}{3}\epsilon U\,,\quad H^{-1}\dot{\theta}\simeq-\eta_{rs}\,, (10.7)

while the perturbations on large scales (comoving wavenumber k≪ℋk\ll{\cal H}) obey

H−1​δ​r˙flat\displaystyle H^{-1}\dot{\delta r}_{\rm{flat}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq (2​ϵ−ηr​r)​δ​rflat−2​ηr​s​δ​s,\displaystyle\left(2\epsilon-\eta_{rr}\right)\delta r_{\rm{flat}}-2\eta_{rs}\delta s\,,
H−1​δ​s˙\displaystyle H^{-1}\dot{\delta s} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −ηs​s​δ​s,\displaystyle-\eta_{ss}\delta s\,, (10.8)

where we neglect spatial gradients. Although Us≃0U_{s}\simeq 0 at lowest order in slow-roll, this does not mean that the inflaton and entropy perturbations decouple. θ˙\dot{\theta} given by Eq. (10.7) is in general non-zero at first-order in slow-roll and large-scale entropy perturbations do affect the evolution of the adiabatic perturbations when ησ​s≠0\eta_{\sigma s}\neq 0.

While the general solution to the two second-order perturbation equations (9.2) and (9.23) has four independent modes, the two first-order slow-roll equations (10) give the approximate form of the squeezed state on large scales. This has only two modes which we can describe in terms of the dimensionless comoving curvature and isocurvature perturbations:

ℛ≡ℋr′​δ​rflat,𝒮≡ℋr′​δ​s.{{\cal{R}}}\equiv\frac{{\cal H}}{r^{\prime}}\delta r_{\rm{flat}}\,,\quad{\cal{S}}\equiv\frac{{\cal H}}{r^{\prime}}\delta s\,. (10.9)

The normalisation of ℛ{{\cal{R}}} coincides with the standard definition of the comoving curvature perturbation, Eq. (7.46). The normalisation of the dimensionless entropy during inflation, 𝒮{\cal{S}}, is chosen here coincide with Ref. [175]. It can be related to the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation (9.5) on large scales

δ​Pnad≃−ϵ​ηr​s​H22​π​G​𝒮.\delta P_{\rm nad}\simeq-\epsilon\eta_{rs}\frac{H^{2}}{2\pi G}{\cal{S}}\,. (10.10)

The slow-roll approximation can provide a useful approximation to the instantaneous evolution of the fields and their perturbations on large scales during slow-roll inflation, but is not expected to remain accurate when integrated over many Hubble times, where inaccuracies can accumulate. In single-field inflation the constancy of the comoving curvature perturbation after Hubble exit, which does not rely on the slow-roll approximation, is crucial in order to make accurate predictions of the primordial perturbations using the slow-roll approximation only around Hubble crossing. In a two-field model we must describe the evolution after Hubble exit in terms of a general transfer matrix:

(ℛ𝒮)=(1Tℛ𝒮0T𝒮𝒮)​(ℛ𝒮)∗.\left(\begin{array}[]{c}{{{\cal{R}}}}\\ {{\cal{S}}}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&{T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}\\ 0&{T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}{{\cal{R}}}\\ {\cal{S}}\end{array}\right)_{*}\,. (10.11)

On large scales the comoving curvature perturbation still remains constant for the purely adiabatic mode, corresponding to 𝒮=0{\cal{S}}=0, and adiabatic perturbations remain adiabatic. These general results are enough to fix two of the coefficients in the transfer matrix, but Tℛ𝒮{T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}} and T𝒮𝒮{T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}} remain to be determined either within a given theoretical model, or from observations, or ideally by both. The scale-dependence of the transfer functions depends upon the inflaton-entropy coupling at Hubble exit during inflation and can be given in terms of the slow-roll parameters as [175]

∂∂ln⁡k​Tℛ𝒮\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\ln k}{T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}} =\displaystyle= 2​ηr​s+(2​ϵ−ηr​r+ηs​s)​Tℛ𝒮,\displaystyle 2\eta_{rs}+(2\epsilon-\eta_{rr}+\eta_{ss}){T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}\,,
∂∂ln⁡k​T𝒮𝒮\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\ln k}{T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}} =\displaystyle= (2​ϵ−ηr​r+ηs​s)​T𝒮𝒮.\displaystyle(2\epsilon-\eta_{rr}+\eta_{ss}){T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}\,. (10.12)

10.1 Initial power spectra

The expectation value of the fluctuations of a homogeneous field are given by

⟨δ​φI​(𝐤1)​δ​φI​(𝐤2)⟩=(2​π)3​δ3​(𝐤1+𝐤2)​Pδ​φI​(k1),\langle\delta\varphi_{I}({\bf k}_{1})\delta\varphi_{I}({\bf k}_{2})\rangle=(2\pi)^{3}\delta^{3}({\bf k}_{1}+{\bf k}_{2})P_{\delta\varphi_{I}}(k_{1})\,, (10.13)

where angle brackets denote the ensemble average (i.e., the average over infinitely many realisations of the field, which is equivalent to taking the spatial average in an infinite space). The dimensionless power spectrum of the field (equivalently the variance of the field per logarithmic range of kk) is given by

𝒫δ​φI​(k)=4​π​k3(2​π)3​Pδ​φI​(k).{\cal P}_{\delta\varphi_{I}}(k)=\frac{4\pi k^{3}}{(2\pi)^{3}}P_{\delta\varphi_{I}}(k)\,. (10.14)

For weakly-coupled, light fields we can neglect interactions on wavelengths below the Hubble scale, so that vacuum fluctuations correspond to [86]

Pδ​φI​(k)=12​k​a2.P_{\delta\varphi_{I}}(k)=\frac{1}{2ka^{2}}\,. (10.15)

This gives rise to the power spectrum of field fluctuations on the Hubble scale (k=ℋ=a​Hk={\cal H}=aH) during inflation given by

𝒫δ​φI≃(H2​π)∗2,{\cal P}_{\delta\varphi_{I}}\simeq\left(\frac{H}{2\pi}\right)_{*}^{2}\,, (10.16)

where we use a ∗* to denote quantities evaluated at Hubble-exit. If a field has a mass comparable to the Hubble scale or larger then the vacuum fluctuations on wavelengths greater than the effective Compton wavelength are suppressed. In addition fluctuations in strongly interacting fields may develop correlations before Hubble exit. But during slow-roll inflation the correlation between vacuum fluctuations in weakly coupled, light fields at Hubble-exit is suppressed by slow-roll parameters. This remains true under a local rotation in fields space to another orthogonal basis such as the instantaneous inflaton and entropy directions (9.18) and (9.19) in field space.

The curvature and isocurvature power spectra at Hubble-exit are given by

𝒫ℛ|∗≃𝒫𝒮|∗≃(H22​π​σ˙)∗2≃83​(Uϵ​MPl4)∗,\left.{\cal P}_{{{\cal{R}}}}\right|_{*}\simeq\left.{\cal P}_{{\cal{S}}}\right|_{*}\simeq\left(\frac{H^{2}}{2\pi\dot{\sigma}}\right)_{*}^{2}\simeq\frac{8}{3}\left(\frac{U}{\epsilon M_{\rm Pl}^{4}}\right)_{*}\,, (10.17)

while the cross-correlation is first-order in slow-roll [55, 30],

𝒞ℛ𝒮|∗≃−2​C​ηr​s​𝒫ℛ|∗,\left.{\cal C}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}\right|_{*}\simeq-2C\eta_{rs}\left.{\cal P}_{{{\cal{R}}}}\right|_{*}\,, (10.18)

where C=2−ln⁡2−γ≈0.73C=2-\ln 2-\gamma\approx 0.73 and γ\gamma is the Euler number. The normalisation chosen for the dimensionless entropy perturbation in Eq. (10.9) ensures that the curvature and isocurvature fluctuations have the same power at horizon exit [175]. The spectral tilts at horizon-exit are also the same and are given by

Δ​nℛ|∗≃Δ​n𝒮|∗≃−6​ϵ+2​ηr​r.\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}\simeq\Delta n_{\cal{S}}|_{*}\simeq-6\epsilon+2\eta_{rr}\,. (10.19)

where Δ​nX≡d​ln⁡𝒫X/d​ln⁡k\Delta n_{X}\equiv d\ln{\cal P}_{X}/d\ln k.

The tensor perturbations (8.64) are decoupled from scalar metric perturbations at first-order and hence the power spectrum has the same form as in single field inflation. Thus the power spectrum of gravitational waves on super-Hubble scales during inflation is given by

𝒫T|∗≃16​H2π​MPl2≃1283​U∗MPl4,\left.{\cal P}_{\rm T}\right|_{*}\simeq\frac{16H^{2}}{\pi M_{\rm Pl}^{2}}\simeq\frac{128}{3}\frac{U_{*}}{M_{\rm Pl}^{4}}\,, (10.20)

and the spectral tilt is

Δ​nT|∗≃−2​ϵ.\Delta n_{\rm T}|_{*}\simeq-2\epsilon\,. (10.21)

10.2 Primordial power spectra

The resulting primordial power spectra on large scales can be obtained simply by applying the general transfer matrix (10.11) to the initial scalar perturbations. The scalar power spectra probed by astronomical observations are thus given by [175]

𝒫ℛ\displaystyle{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}} =\displaystyle= (1+Tℛ𝒮2)​𝒫ℛ|∗\displaystyle(1+T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}^{2}){\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*} (10.22)
𝒫𝒮\displaystyle{\cal P}_{\cal{S}} =\displaystyle= T𝒮𝒮2​𝒫ℛ|∗\displaystyle T_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}^{2}{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*} (10.23)
𝒞ℛ𝒮\displaystyle{\cal C}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}} =\displaystyle= Tℛ𝒮​T𝒮𝒮​𝒫ℛ|∗.\displaystyle T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}T_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}\,. (10.24)

Note that the primordial curvature and isocurvature perturbations from inflation are in general correlated [76] (see also [28, 168, 4]). The cross-correlation can be given in terms of a dimensionless correlation angle:

cos⁡Θ≡𝒞ℛ𝒮𝒫ℛ​𝒫𝒮=Tℛ𝒮1+Tℛ𝒮2.\cos\Theta\equiv\frac{{\cal C}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}}{\sqrt{{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}{\cal P}_{\cal{S}}}}=\frac{T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}}{\sqrt{1+T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}^{2}}}\,. (10.25)

We see that if we can determine the dimensionless correlation angle, Θ\Theta, from observations, then this determines the off-diagonal term in the transfer matrix

Tℛ𝒮=cot⁡Θ,T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}=\cot\Theta\,, (10.26)

and we can in effect measure the contribution of the entropy perturbation during two-field inflation to the resultant curvature primordial perturbation. In particular this allows us in principle to deduce from observations the power spectrum of the curvature perturbation at Hubble-exit during two-field slow-roll inflation [175]:

𝒫ℛ|∗=𝒫ℛ​sin2⁡Θ.{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}={\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}\sin^{2}\Theta\,. (10.27)

The scale-dependence of the resulting scalar power spectra depends both upon the scale-dependence of the initial power spectra and of the transfer coefficients. The spectral tilts are given from Eqs. (10.22–10.24) by

Δ​nℛ\displaystyle\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}} =\displaystyle= Δ​nℛ|∗+H∗−1​(∂Tℛ𝒮/∂t∗)​sin⁡2​Θ,\displaystyle\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}+H_{*}^{-1}(\partial{T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}/\partial t_{*})\sin 2\Theta\,,
Δ​n𝒮\displaystyle\Delta n_{\cal{S}} =\displaystyle= Δ​nℛ|∗+2​H∗−1​(∂ln⁡T𝒮𝒮/∂t∗),\displaystyle\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}+2H_{*}^{-1}(\partial\ln{T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}/\partial t_{*})\,, (10.28)
Δ​n𝒞\displaystyle\Delta n_{\cal C} =\displaystyle= Δ​nℛ|∗+H∗−1​[(∂Tℛ𝒮/∂t∗)​tan⁡Θ+(∂ln⁡T𝒮𝒮/∂t∗)],\displaystyle\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}|_{*}+H_{*}^{-1}\left[(\partial{T}_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}/\partial t_{*})\tan\Theta+(\partial\ln{T}_{{\cal{S}}{\cal{S}}}/\partial t_{*})\right]\,,

where we have used Eq. (10.26) to eliminate Tℛ𝒮T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}} in favour of the observable correlation angle Θ\Theta. Substituting Eq. (10.19) for the tilt at Hubble-exit, and Eqs. (10) for the scale-dependence of the transfer functions, we obtain [175]

Δ​nℛ\displaystyle\Delta n_{{{\cal{R}}}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −(6−4​cos2⁡Θ)​ϵ\displaystyle-(6-4\cos^{2}\Theta)\epsilon
+2​(ηr​r​sin2⁡Θ+2​ηr​s​sin⁡Θ​cos⁡Θ+ηs​s​cos2⁡Θ),\displaystyle+2\left(\eta_{rr}\sin^{2}\Theta+2\eta_{rs}\sin\Theta\cos\Theta+\eta_{ss}\cos^{2}\Theta\right)\,,
Δ​n𝒮\displaystyle\Delta n_{\cal{S}} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −2​ϵ+2​ηs​s,\displaystyle-2\epsilon+2\eta_{ss}\,, (10.29)
Δ​n𝒞\displaystyle\Delta n_{\cal C} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −2​ϵ+2​ηs​s+2​ηr​s​tan⁡Θ.\displaystyle-2\epsilon+2\eta_{ss}+2\eta_{rs}\tan\Theta\,.

Although the overall amplitude of the transfer functions are dependent upon the evolution after Hubble-exit and through reheating into the radiation era, the spectral tilts can be expressed solely in terms of the slow-roll parameters at Hubble-exit during inflation and the correlation angle, Θ\Theta, which can in principle be observed.

If the primordial curvature perturbation results solely from the adiabatic inflaton field fluctuations during inflation then we have Tℛ𝒮=0T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}=0 in Eq. (10.22) and hence cos⁡Θ=0\cos\Theta=0 in Eqs. (10.2), which yields the standard single field result

Δ​nℛ≃−6​ϵ+2​ηr​r.\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}\simeq-6\epsilon+2\eta_{rr}\,. (10.30)

Any residual isocurvature perturbations must be uncorrelated with the adiabatic curvature perturbation (at first-order in slow-roll) with spectral index

Δ​n𝒮≃−2​ϵ+2​ηs​s.\Delta n_{\cal{S}}\simeq-2\epsilon+2\eta_{ss}\,. (10.31)

On the other hand, if the observed primordial curvature perturbation is produced due to some entropy field fluctuations during inflation, we have Tℛ𝒮≫1T_{{{\cal{R}}}{\cal{S}}}\gg 1 and sin⁡Θ≃0\sin\Theta\simeq 0. In a two-field inflation model any residual primordial isocurvature perturbations will then be completely correlated (or anti-correlated) with the primordial curvature perturbation and we have

Δ​nℛ≃Δ​n𝒞≃Δ​n𝒮≃−2​ϵ+2​ηs​s.\Delta n_{{\cal{R}}}\simeq\Delta n_{\cal C}\simeq\Delta n_{\cal{S}}\simeq-2\epsilon+2\eta_{ss}\,. (10.32)

The gravitational wave power spectrum is frozen-in on large scales, independent of the scalar perturbations, and hence

𝒫T=𝒫T|∗.{\cal P}_{\rm T}={\cal P}_{\rm T}|_{*}\,. (10.33)

Thus we can derive a modified consistency relation [86] between observables applicable in the case of two-field slow-roll inflation:

𝒫T𝒫ℛ≃−8​Δ​nT​sin2⁡Θ.\frac{{\cal P}_{\rm T}}{{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}}\simeq-8\Delta n_{\rm T}\sin^{2}\Theta\,. (10.34)

This relation was first obtained in Ref. [10] at the end of two-field inflation, and verified in Ref. [169] for slow-roll models. But it was realised in Ref. [175] that this relation also applies to the primordial perturbation spectra in the radiation era long after two-field slow-roll inflation has ended and hence may be tested observationally.

More generally, if there is any additional source of the scalar curvature perturbation, such as additional scalar fields during inflation, then this could give an additional contribution to the primordial scalar curvature spectrum without affecting the gravitational waves, and hence the more general result is the inequality [158, 146]:

𝒫T𝒫ℛ≤−8​Δ​nT​sin2⁡Θ.\frac{{\cal P}_{\rm T}}{{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}}\leq-8\Delta n_{\rm T}\sin^{2}\Theta\,. (10.35)

This leads to a fundamental difference when interpreting the observational constraints on the amplitude of primordial tensor perturbations in multiple inflation models. In single field inflation, observations directly constrain r=[𝒫T/𝒫ℛ]∗r=[{\cal P}_{\rm T}/{\cal P}_{{\cal{R}}}]_{*} and hence, from Eqs. (10.17) and (10.20), the slow-roll parameter ϵ\epsilon. However in multiple field inflation, non-adiabatic perturbations can enhance the power of scalar perturbations after Hubble exit and hence observational constraints on the amplitude of primordial tensor perturbations do not directly constrain the slow-roll parameter ϵ\epsilon.

Current CMB data alone require r<0.55r<0.55 (assuming power-law primordial spectra) [74] which in single-field models is interpreted as requiring ϵ<0.04\epsilon<0.04. But in multiple field models ϵ\epsilon could be larger if the primordial density perturbation comes from non-adiabatic perturbations during inflation.

11 Non-linear evolution and non-Gaussianity

A powerful technique to calculate the primordial curvature perturbation resulting from many inflation models, including multi-field models, is to note that the curvature perturbation ζ\zeta defined in Eq. (7.61) can be interpreted as a perturbation in the local expansion [156, 157, 146, 98]

ζ=δ​N,\zeta=\delta N\,, (11.1)

where δ​N\delta N is the perturbed expansion to uniform-density hypersurfaces with respect to spatially flat hypersurfaces, which is given to first-order by

ζ=−H​δ​ρflatρ˙,\zeta=-H\frac{\delta\rho_{\rm{flat}}}{\dot{\rho}}\,, (11.2)

where δ​ρflat\delta\rho_{\rm{flat}} must be evaluated on spatially flat (ψ=0\psi=0) hypersurfaces (see Sections 3.2 and 7.6).

An important simplification arises on large scales where anisotropy and spatial gradients can be neglected, and the local density, expansion, etc., obeys the same evolution equations as in a homogeneous FRW universe [144, 146, 147, 176, 96, 136, 98]. Thus we can use the homogeneous FRW solutions to describe the local evolution, which is known as the “separate universe” approach [144, 146, 147, 176, 136]. In particular we can evaluate the perturbed expansion in different parts of the universe resulting from different initial values for the fields during inflation using the homogeneous background solutions [146].

In the slow-roll approximation the integrated expansion on super-Hubble scales from some initial spatially flat hypersurface up to a subsequent fixed density hypersurface (say at the epoch of primordial nucleosynthesis) is some function of the local field values on the initial hypersurface, N⁡(φI|ψ)N(\varphi_{I}|_{\psi}). More generally we expect this to hold whenever we can neglect the decaying mode for the field perturbations on super-Hubble scales. The resulting primordial curvature perturbation on the uniform-density hypersurface is then

ζ=∑INI​δ​φI​flat,\zeta=\sum_{I}N_{I}\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}}\,, (11.3)

where NI≡∂N/∂φIN_{I}\equiv\partial N/\partial\varphi_{I} and δ​φI​flat\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}} is the field perturbation on some initial spatially-flat hypersurfaces during inflation (8.58). In particular the power spectrum for the primordial density perturbation in a multi-field inflation can be written (at leading order) in terms of the field perturbations after Hubble-exit as

𝒫ζ=∑INI2​𝒫δ​φI​flat.{\cal P}_{\zeta}=\sum_{I}N_{I}^{2}{\cal P}_{\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}}}\,. (11.4)

This approach is readily extended to estimate the non-linear effect of field perturbations on the metric perturbations [147, 96, 94, 98]. We can take Eq. (11.1) as our definition of the non-linear primordial curvature perturbation, ζ\zeta, so that in the radiation dominated era the non-linear extension of Eq. (11.2) is given by [98]

ζ=14​ln⁡(ρflatρ0),\zeta=\frac{1}{4}\ln\left(\frac{\rho_{\rm{flat}}}{\rho_{0}}\right)\,, (11.5)

where ρflat​(t,𝐱)\rho_{\rm{flat}}(t,{\bf x}) is the perturbed (inhomogeneous) density evaluated on a spatially flat hypersurface and ρ0​(t)\rho_{0}(t) is the background (homogeneous) density. See Refs. [136, 138, 139, 78, 79, 80] for alternative approaches to define the non-linear extension of ζ\zeta.

This non-linear curvature perturbation as a function of the initial field fluctuations can simply be expanded as a Taylor expansion [94, 150, 31, 151]

ζ≃∑INI​δ​φI​flat+12​∑I,JNI​J​δ​φI​flat​δ​φJ​flat+16​∑I,J,KNI​J​K​δ​φI​flat​δ​φJ​flat​δ​φK​flat+….\zeta\simeq\sum_{I}N_{I}\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I,J}N_{IJ}\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}}\delta\varphi_{J{\rm{flat}}}+\frac{1}{6}\sum_{I,J,K}N_{IJK}\delta\varphi_{I{\rm{flat}}}\delta\varphi_{J{\rm{flat}}}\delta\varphi_{K{\rm{flat}}}+\ldots\,. (11.6)

where we now identify (11.3) as the leading-order term.

We expect the field perturbations at Hubble-exit to be close to Gaussian for weakly coupled scalar fields during inflation [103, 149, 137, 150, 152]. In this case the bispectrum of the primordial curvature perturbation at leading (fourth) order, can be written as [49, 73]

Bζ​(𝐤1,𝐤2,𝐤3)\displaystyle B_{\zeta}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2},\mathbf{k}_{3}) =\displaystyle= 65​fN​L​[Pζ​(k1)​Pζ​(k2)+Pζ​(k2)​Pζ​(k3)+Pζ​(k3)​Pζ​(k1)].\displaystyle\frac{6}{5}{f_{NL}}\left[P_{\zeta}(k_{1})P_{\zeta}(k_{2})+P_{\zeta}(k_{2})P_{\zeta}(k_{3})+P_{\zeta}(k_{3})P_{\zeta}(k_{1})\right]\,. (11.7)

where Pζ​(k)=2​π2​𝒫ζ​(k)/k3P_{\zeta}(k)=2\pi^{2}{\cal P}_{\zeta}(k)/k^{3}, and the dimensionless non-linearity parameter is given, using the δ​N\delta N-formalism, by55 5 Note, that the factor “5/65/6” in Eq. (11.8) is a historical convention, due to the original definition [73] which was given in terms of the Newtonian potential, which on large scales in the matter era is given by Φ=−(3/5)​ζ\Phi=-(3/5)\zeta. [94]

fN​L=56​NA​NB​NA​B(NC​NC)2.{f_{NL}}=\frac{5}{6}\frac{N_{A}N_{B}N^{AB}}{\left(N_{C}N^{C}\right)^{2}}\,. (11.8)

Similarly to the bispectrum, the connected part of the trispectrum in this case can be written as [151, 31]

Tζ​(𝐤1,𝐤2,𝐤3,𝐤4)\displaystyle T_{\zeta}(\mathbf{k}_{1},\mathbf{k}_{2},\mathbf{k}_{3},\mathbf{k}_{4}) =\displaystyle= τN​L​[Pζ​(|𝐤1+𝐤3|)​Pζ​(k3)​Pζ​(k4)+(11​perms)]\displaystyle\tau_{NL}\left[P_{\zeta}(|{\bf k}_{1}+{\bf k}_{3}|)P_{\zeta}(k_{3})P_{\zeta}(k_{4})+(11\,\,\rm{perms})\right] (11.9)
+5425​gN​L​[Pζ​(k2)​Pζ​(k3)​Pζ​(k4)+(3​perms)].\displaystyle+\frac{54}{25}g_{NL}\left[P_{\zeta}(k_{2})P_{\zeta}(k_{3})P_{\zeta}(k_{4})+(3\,\,\rm{perms})\right]\,.

where

τN​L\displaystyle\tau_{NL} =\displaystyle= NA​B​NA​C​NB​NC(ND​ND)3,\displaystyle\frac{N_{AB}N^{AC}N^{B}N_{C}}{(N_{D}N^{D})^{3}}\,, (11.10)
gN​L\displaystyle g_{NL} =\displaystyle= 2554​NA​B​C​NA​NB​NC(ND​ND)3.\displaystyle\frac{25}{54}\frac{N_{ABC}N^{A}N^{B}N^{C}}{(N_{D}N^{D})^{3}}\,. (11.11)

The expression for τN​L\tau_{NL} was first given in [2]. Note that we have factored out products in the trispectrum with different kk dependence in order to define the two kk independent non-linearity parameters τN​L\tau_{NL} and gN​Lg_{NL}. This gives the possibility that observations may be able to distinguish between the two parameters [130].

In many cases there is single direction in field-space, χ\chi, which is responsible for perturbing the local expansion, N⁡(χ)N(\chi), and hence generating the primordial curvature perturbation (11.6). For example this would be the inflaton field in single field models of inflation, or it could be a late-decaying scalar field [116, 89, 48] as in the curvaton scenario [95, 118]. In this case the curvature perturbation (11.6) is given by

ζ≃N′​δ​χflat+12​N′′​δ​χflat2+16​N′′′​δ​χflat3+…,\zeta\simeq N^{\prime}\delta\chi_{\rm{flat}}+\frac{1}{2}N^{\prime\prime}\delta\chi^{2}_{\rm{flat}}+\frac{1}{6}N^{\prime\prime\prime}\delta\chi^{3}_{\rm{flat}}+\ldots\,, (11.12)

and the non-Gaussianity of the primordial perturbation has the simplest “local” form

ζ=ζ1+35​fN​L​ζ12+925​gN​L​ζ13+…\zeta=\zeta_{1}+\frac{3}{5}f_{NL}\zeta_{1}^{2}+\frac{9}{25}g_{NL}\zeta_{1}^{3}+\ldots (11.13)

where ζ1=N′​δ​χflat\zeta_{1}=N^{\prime}\delta\chi_{\rm{flat}} is the leading-order Gaussian curvature perturbation and the non-linearity parameters fN​Lf_{NL} and gN​Lg_{NL}, are given by [94, 148]

fN​L\displaystyle f_{NL} =\displaystyle= 56​N′′(N′)2,\displaystyle\frac{5}{6}\frac{N^{\prime\prime}}{(N^{\prime})^{2}}\,, (11.14)
gN​L\displaystyle g_{NL} =\displaystyle= 2554​N′′′(N′)3,\displaystyle\frac{25}{54}\frac{N^{\prime\prime\prime}}{(N^{\prime})^{3}}\,, (11.15)

The primordial bispectrum and trispectrum are then given by Eqs. (11.7) and (11.9), where the non-linearity parameters fN​Lf_{NL} and gN​Lg_{NL}, given in Eqs. (11.8) and (11.11), reduce to Eqs. (11.14) and (11.15) respectively, and τN​L\tau_{NL} given in Eq.(11.10) reduces to

τN​L\displaystyle\tau_{NL} =\displaystyle= (N′′)2(N′)4=3625​fN​L2.\displaystyle\frac{(N^{\prime\prime})^{2}}{(N^{\prime})^{4}}=\frac{36}{25}f_{NL}^{2}\,. (11.16)

Thus τN​L\tau_{NL} is proportional to fN​L2f_{NL}^{2} (first shown in [130] using the Bardeen potential, and in [94] using this notation). However the trispectrum could be large even when the bispectrum is small because of the gN​Lg_{NL} term [130, 148].

In the case of where the primordial curvature perturbation is generated solely by adiabatic fluctuations in the inflaton field, rr, the curvature perturbation is non-linearly conserved on large scales [96, 98, 79] and we can calculate N′N^{\prime}, N′′N^{\prime\prime}, N′′′N^{\prime\prime\prime}, etc, at Hubble-exit. In terms of the slow-roll parameters, we find

N′\displaystyle N^{\prime} =\displaystyle= Hφ˙≃121mPl1ϵ∼𝒪(ϵ−1/2),\displaystyle\frac{{H}}{\dot{{\varphi}}}\simeq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{m_{\rm{Pl}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\epsilon}}\sim{\mathcal{O}}\left(\epsilon^{-1/2}\right)\,, (11.17)
N′′\displaystyle N^{\prime\prime} ≃\displaystyle\simeq −12​1mPl2​1ϵ​(ηr​r−2​ϵ)∼𝒪⁡(1),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{m_{\rm{Pl}}^{2}}\frac{1}{\epsilon}(\eta_{rr}-2\epsilon)\sim{\mathcal{O}}\left(1\right)\,, (11.18)
N′′′\displaystyle N^{\prime\prime\prime} ≃\displaystyle\simeq 12​1mPl3​1ϵ​ϵ​(ϵ​ηr​r−ηr​r2+12​ξr2)∼𝒪⁡(ϵ1/2),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{m_{\rm{Pl}}^{3}}\frac{1}{\epsilon\sqrt{\epsilon}}\left(\epsilon\eta_{rr}-\eta_{rr}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\xi_{r}^{2}\right)\sim{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{1/2})\,, (11.19)

where we have used the reduced Planck mass mPl2=(8​π​G)−1m_{\rm{Pl}}^{2}=(8\pi G)^{-1} and introduced the second-order slow-roll parameter ξσ2=mPl4​Ur​Ur​r​r/U2\xi_{\sigma}^{2}=m_{\rm{Pl}}^{4}U_{r}U_{rrr}/U^{2}. Hence the non-linearity parameters for single field inflation, (11.14) and (11.15), are given by

fN​L\displaystyle f_{NL} =\displaystyle= 56​(ηr​r−2​ϵ),\displaystyle\frac{5}{6}(\eta_{rr}-2\epsilon)\,, (11.20)
gN​L\displaystyle g_{NL} =\displaystyle= 2554​(2​ϵ​ηr​r−2​ηr​r2+ξr2).\displaystyle\frac{25}{54}\left(2\epsilon\eta_{rr}-2\eta_{rr}^{2}+\xi_{r}^{2}\right)\,. (11.21)

with τN​L\tau_{NL} given by Eq. (11.16). Although there are additional contributions to the primordial bispectrum and trispectrum coming from the intrinsic non-Gaussianity of the field perturbations at Hubble-exit, these are also suppressed by slow-roll parameters in slow-roll inflation. Thus the primordial non-Gaussianity is likely to be too small to ever be observed in the conventional inflaton scenario of single-field slow-roll inflation [1, 103]. Indeed any detection of primordial non-Gaussianity fN​L>1f_{NL}>1 would appear to rule out this inflaton scenario.

However significant non-Gaussianity can be generated due to non-adiabatic field fluctuations. Thus far it has proved difficult to generate detectable non-Gaussianity in the curvature perturbation during conventional slow-roll inflation, even in multiple field models [140, 171], though see Refs. [32, 38]. But detectable non-Gaussianity might be produced in non-slow-roll [36] or non-canonical scalar field inflation [3, 81], or when the curvature perturbation is generated from isocurvature field perturbations at the end of inflation [20, 93], during inhomogeneous reheating [44, 69, 178, 45, 72, 29], or some time after inflation has ended in the curvaton model [95, 99, 11, 107, 148].

12 Summary and outlook

Linear perturbations have become part of the standard toolbox of modern cosmology. Earlier confusion surrounding apparently different behaviour found in different coordinate bases has largely been resolved through the use of variables which have gauge-invariant definitions. In Section 7 we have emphasised the physical interpretation of these gauge-invariant variables.

The power spectrum of primordial perturbations revealed by the cosmic microwave background and large scale galaxy surveys is a powerful probe of inflationary models of the very early universe, and a challenge for alternative theories. Linear theory enables us to relate the primordial spectra to quantum fluctuations in the metric and matter fields at much higher energies. In the simplest single field inflation models, it is possible to equate the primordial density perturbation with the curvature perturbation, ζ\zeta defined in Eq. (7.61), during inflation which remains constant on large scales for adiabatic density perturbations. More generally, if one allows for non-adiabatic perturbations then it becomes necessary to allow for variation in the curvature perturbation, even on super-Hubble scales. Nonetheless it is still possible in many cases to identify the primordial density perturbation with a perturbed expansion in the δ​N\delta N approach described in Section 11 where the integrated expansion, NN, is a function of the local field values on spatially flat slices during inflation. As one goes beyond the textbook examples, it becomes necessary to have a clear physical definition of the perturbation variables to consistently extend the background FRW equations to the inhomogeneous perturbations.

The new frontier in the study of cosmological perturbations is the study of non-linear primordial perturbations, at second-order and beyond. Many of the familiar certainties of linear perturbation theory no longer apply. We have shown in Section 6 that quantities that were automatically gauge-independent at first order (including the non-adiabatic pressure perturbation, anisotropic stress, and the tensor metric perturbation) become gauge dependent at second order. We have shown in Section 7 that it is possible to use the same methodology to construct gauge-invariant variables at second (and higher) order. A variable with an unambiguous physical meaning will have a gauge invariant definition. The resulting gauge invariant definitions inevitably become more complicated than those at first order and we have only presented explicit definitions at second order for a few cases. Likewise we have not attempted to present the second order dynamical equations in a comprehensive manner as was done at first order in Section 8. Our aim has been to provide an introduction to some of the issues that arise at higher order. Early works on non-linear and second order perturbation theory include Refs. [166, 131], more recently see also Refs. [134, 167, 129, 125, 126, 127].

Non-linearities allow additional information to be gleaned from the primordial perturbations. Much effort is currently being devoted to the study of higher-order correlations. Non-Gaussianity in the distribution of primordial density perturbations would reveal interactions beyond the linear theory. Such interactions are minimal (suppressed by slow-roll parameters) in the simplest single field inflation model, so any detection of primordial non-Gaussianity would cause a major upheaval in our thinking about the very early universe. In principle the δ​N\delta N approach can be easily extended to higher-orders, simply by extending the Taylor series for the integrated expansion as a function of the field perturbations beyond linear order. This enables one to compute higher-order correlation functions for ζ\zeta as shown in Section 11. The challenge is then to develop transfer functions to relate the primordial ζ\zeta to observables beyond linear order [15, 12, 13, 14], although large primordial non-Gaussianity (e.g., fN​L≫1{f_{NL}}\gg 1) is expected to dominate over non-linearity in the transfer functions.

The Klein-Gordon equation in closed form at second order shows that at second order scalar perturbations will also be sourced by terms quadratic in first order field perturbations [106, 112]. This and second order perturbation theory in general, provides an alternative to using the δ​N\delta N formalism in calculating the primordial non-gaussianity fN​L{f_{NL}} [153]. The main advantage of perturbation theory is that it can also be extended to sub-horizon scales, whereas the δ​N\delta N formalism is only valid on super-horizon scales, and in some cases it has been shown to be numerically more efficient [107].

Typically non-linear effects are going to be small, given that scalar metric perturbations are only of order 10−510^{-5}. Primordial tensor modes are smaller, and vector modes are effectively zero during scalar field driven inflation. But the additional information available from higher-order correlations and the use of optimised filters for specific forms of non-Gaussianity means that there are already impressive constraints on the degree of primordial Gaussianity.

Qualitatively new effects appear beyond linear order. The non-linearity of the field equations inevitably leads to mixing between scalar, vector and tensor modes and the existence of primordial density perturbations then inevitably generates vector and tensor modes [117, 126, 5, 18, 90]. As shown in Section 6, if we continue studies of scalar perturbations to higher order then the distinction between the different types of perturbations becomes gauge dependent and consistent computation will require careful (gauge invariant) definition of the variables being used.

Appendix A Definitions and notation

A.1 Notation

The sign convention is (+++) in the classification of Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler [115].

Tensor indices:
Greek indices, such as α,β,…,μ,ν,…\alpha,\beta,\dots,\mu,\nu,\dots, run from 0 to 33. Latin indices, such as a,b,…,i,j,…a,b,\dots,i,j,\dots, run from 1 to 33, that is only over spatial dimensions.

Spatial three-vectors are written in boldface, i.e. 𝐯≡vi\bm{\mathrm{{v}}}\equiv v^{i}, whenever convenient.

Throughout this work we use the units c=ℏ=1c=\hbar=1.

A.2 Definitions

The connection coefficient is defined as

Γβ​μγ=12​gα​γ​(gα​β,μ+gα​μ,β−gβ​μ,α).\Gamma^{\gamma}_{\beta\mu}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\alpha\gamma}\left(g_{\alpha\beta,\mu}+g_{\alpha\mu,\beta}-g_{\beta\mu,\alpha}\right)\,. (1.22)

The Riemann tensor is defined as

Rβ​μ​να=Γβ​ν,μα−Γβ​μ,να+Γλ​μα​Γβ​νλ−Γλ​να​Γβ​μλ.R^{\alpha}_{~\beta\mu\nu}=\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\beta\nu,\mu}-\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\beta\mu,\nu}+\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\lambda\mu}\Gamma^{\lambda}_{\beta\nu}-\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\lambda\nu}\Gamma^{\lambda}_{\beta\mu}\,. (1.23)

The Ricci tensor is a contraction of the Riemann tensor and given by

Rμ​ν=Rμ​α​να,R_{\mu\nu}=R^{\alpha}_{~\mu\alpha\nu}\,, (1.24)

and the Ricci scalar is given by contracting the Ricci tensor

R=Rμμ.R=R^{\mu}_{~\mu}\,. (1.25)

The Einstein tensor is defined as

Gμ​ν=Rμ​ν−12​gμ​ν​R.G_{\mu\nu}=R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R\,. (1.26)

The covariant derivatives are denoted by

;μ ≡∇μCovariant​differentiation​with​respect​to​gμ​ν.\displaystyle\equiv\nabla_{\mu}~~~{\rm{Covariant~differentiation~with~respect~to}}~g_{\mu\nu}\,.

Partial derivatives are denoted by

X,i≡∂X∂xi.X_{,i}\equiv\frac{\partial X}{\partial x^{i}}\,. (1.27)

V(i,j)≡12​(Vi,j+Vj,i),V[i,j]≡12​(Vi,j−Vj,i).V_{(i,j)}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(V_{i,j}+V_{j,i}\right)\,,\qquad V_{[i,j]}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(V_{i,j}-V_{j,i}\right)\,. (1.28)

A.3 Lie derivatives

The Lie derivatives with respect to a vector field ξμ\xi^{\mu} of a scalar φ{\varphi}, a covariant vector vμv_{\mu}, and a covariant tensor tμ​νt_{\mu\nu} are given by (see e.g. Ref. [160])

£ξ​φ\displaystyle\pounds_{\xi}{\varphi} =\displaystyle= ξλφ,λ,\displaystyle\xi^{\lambda}{\varphi}_{,\lambda}\,, (1.29)
£ξ​vμ\displaystyle\pounds_{\xi}v_{\mu} =\displaystyle= vμ,αξα+vαξα,μ,\displaystyle v_{\mu,\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}+v_{\alpha}\xi^{\alpha}_{,~\mu}\,, (1.30)
£ξ​tμ​ν\displaystyle\pounds_{\xi}t_{\mu\nu} =\displaystyle= tμ​ν,λξλ+tμ​λξλ,ν+tλ​νξλ,μ.\displaystyle t_{\mu\nu,\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}+t_{\mu\lambda}\xi^{\lambda}_{,~\nu}+t_{\lambda\nu}\xi^{\lambda}_{,~\mu}\,. (1.31)

A.4 Covariant derivatives

The covariant derivatives of a scalar φ{\varphi}, a covariant vector VμV_{\mu}, and a covariant tensor tμ​νt_{\mu\nu} are given by (e.g. [160])

φ;μ\displaystyle{\varphi}_{;\mu} =\displaystyle= φ,μ,\displaystyle{\varphi}_{,\mu}\,,
Vμ;ν\displaystyle V_{\mu;\nu} =\displaystyle= Vμ,ν−Γμ​να​Vα,\displaystyle V_{\mu,\nu}-\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\mu\nu}V_{\alpha}\,,
tμ​ν;λ\displaystyle t_{\mu\nu;\lambda} =\displaystyle= tμ​ν,λ−Γμ​λα​tα​ν−Γν​λβ​tβ​μ.\displaystyle t_{\mu\nu,\lambda}-\Gamma^{\alpha}_{\mu\lambda}t_{\alpha\nu}-\Gamma^{\beta}_{\nu\lambda}t_{\beta\mu}\,. (1.32)
